The underlying root is associated with the idea of being brutish or senseless, which may reflect the name's original sense, but in the text it simply identifies an individual.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon — appearing only once in the entire Old Testament — so virtually nothing can be said about its usage beyond this single genealogical reference.

definition: A place name in southern Judah, listed among the towns in Joshua's territorial allotments.
article: Adadah is a town mentioned once in the Old Testament, in Joshua 15:22, as part of the list of cities assigned to the tribe of Judah in the Negev region. The name appears only as a proper noun in this single verse, making it purely a geographical identifier with no broader semantic usage in the Hebrew Bible. Strong's notes a connection to a root meaning 'festival,' but since the word functions exclusively as a place name in the text, that root meaning has no practical bearing on how a reader encounters it.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon with only one occurrence, and the site's exact historical or archaeological identification remains uncertain.

definition: Shachatsом is a place name in the tribal territory of Issachar, mentioned as a border landmark in Joshua 19.
article: Shachatsom (also spelled Shahazimah) appears twice in Joshua 19:22, where it marks a boundary point in the allotment of the tribe of Issachar. It occurs nowhere else in the Old Testament. Strong's connects the name to a root meaning 'proudly,' suggesting the place name may carry that sense, but its exact location in ancient Canaan has not been identified with certainty.
caution: This word appears only in Joshua 19:22, making it effectively a hapax in terms of geographic context, and its precise location remains unidentified; the spelling 'Shahazimah' comes from a marginal reading rather than the main text tradition.

definition: A personal name belonging to at least three Israelite men mentioned in the post-exilic period.
article: Mattenai is a proper name appearing 3 times across Ezra and Nehemiah, always identifying Israelite individuals in the post-exilic restoration community. In Ezra 10, two different men named Mattenai are listed among those who had married foreign women, while Nehemiah 12 names a Mattenai among priestly family heads. The KJV renders the name consistently as 'Mattenai' across all three occurrences, and Strong's connects it to the root meaning 'liberal' or 'gift.'
caution: With only 3 occurrences all functioning as a proper name, the underlying meaning of the name itself cannot be verified from OT usage alone, and confidence in the etymology is low.

definition: To whisper quietly or mumble in a secretive way, especially when casting a spell or charm.
article: This verb describes low, hushed speech — the kind of murmuring associated with secret conversation or the muttering of a magician working a charm. It appears only 3 times across 2 books, split between Psalms (2×) and 2 Samuel (1×), and carries a somewhat darker, conspiratorial or magical tone depending on context. The two attested stems, Hithpael and Piel, both suggest deliberate, focused action rather than casual speech. Strikingly, the LXX translators rendered this word as ἄβυσσος ("abyss" or "deep") and κῦμα ("wave"), choices that are quite distant from the Hebrew sense and offer little help in clarifying the word's meaning.
caution: With only 3 occurrences and LXX translations that diverge sharply from the expected meaning, confidence in the full semantic range is low, and the precise nuance in each context remains uncertain.

definition: A personal name meaning 'Jehovah will cause to dwell,' borne by one Israelite in the genealogies of Simeon.
article: Yoshibyah is a proper name appearing once in the Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 4:35, within a genealogical list of Simeonite clan leaders. The name combines the Hebrew root for 'to dwell' or 'to settle' with the divine name Yah, yielding the sense 'Jehovah will cause to dwell.' The KJV renders it simply as Josibiah, offering no translation of its meaning. Nothing further is recorded about this individual beyond his place in the lineage.
caution: With only a single occurrence in a genealogical list, nothing can be said about the word's usage beyond its function as a personal name.

definition: A round or flat cake of bread, specifically the barley loaf that appears in Gideon's dream.
article: This rare noun refers to a round or flattened cake, likely of bread or grain. It appears only twice in the Old Testament, both occurrences in Judges 7:13, describing the barley loaf in a Midianite soldier's dream that Gideon overhears — a vivid image that encourages him before battle. The LXX uses κρίθινος ("of barley") alongside verbs of rolling and recounting, reflecting the ancient translators' sense of a tumbling loaf, which fits the dream's action of a bread cake rolling into the Midianite camp.
caution: This word occurs only in a single verse (cited twice in the same context), making it effectively a hapax legomenon with very limited evidence for its precise meaning; confidence in the definition is low.

definition: A siege or the physical siege-works surrounding a city, and by extension the distress and confinement that such entrapment brings.
article: מָצוֹר comes from the root meaning to hem in or encircle, and it covers both the act of besieging a city and the earthworks and barriers the besiegers construct around it. Deuteronomy alone accounts for five uses, mostly in vivid descriptions of the horrors of being trapped inside a besieged city — making that book the word's most concentrated context. The LXX translators chose περιοχή ("surrounding" or "encirclement") five times, confirming that ancient readers heard the idea of being hemmed in as the word's core meaning rather than the strength of a fortress. The KJV's wide range of glosses — from "siege" to "bulwark" to "tower" — reflects the same root idea seen from two angles: the attacker's encircling works and the defender's desperate confinement.
caution: The word's range between an offensive siege and a defensive stronghold creates genuine ambiguity in some passages, and the moderate confidence rating reflects that scholars do not always agree which sense is primary in a given context.

definition: A personal name (Pilcha) belonging to an Israelite who signed the covenant in Nehemiah's time.
article: Pilcha is a personal name appearing once in the Old Testament, in Nehemiah 10:25, among the list of leaders who sealed the covenant renewal under Nehemiah. The KJV simply transliterates the name as 'Pilcha.' Strong's connects it to a root meaning 'slicing,' but for readers of Scripture this functions purely as a proper name with no broader semantic range to explore.
caution: This word occurs only once in the entire Old Testament (a hapax in terms of name attestation), and its underlying root meaning has no practical bearing on how it functions in context; no LXX evidence was supplied to clarify ancient understanding.

definition: An Aramaic word meaning an enormous, uncountable multitude, typically rendered as ten thousand times ten thousand.
article: This Aramaic term denotes an overwhelmingly large number, conventionally translated as 'ten thousand times ten thousand,' signifying a quantity beyond ordinary reckoning. It appears all three of its Old Testament occurrences in a single verse, Daniel 7:10, describing the countless throng of heavenly beings standing before the Ancient of Days. The LXX renders this with similar large-number language, reinforcing that the intent is rhetorical vastness rather than a precise mathematical figure.
caution: With only 3 occurrences all in one verse of Daniel, and Strong's definition simply cross-referencing another form of the same root, the precise semantic range of this Aramaic word is very difficult to establish independently.

definition: To sow or scatter seed in a field, and by extension to plant, produce offspring, or spread something broadly.
article: זָרַע most commonly means to sow seed in a field, as in the agricultural laws of Leviticus and the creation narrative of Genesis 1, where plants yield seed 'after their kind.' Its range extends naturally to human reproduction (conceiving or bearing seed) and to the figurative spreading of peoples or ideas. The LXX translators chose σπείρω — the standard Greek word for sowing — an overwhelming 42 out of 43 times, confirming that ancient readers understood this as solidly agricultural language even when used metaphorically.
caution: The single KJV gloss 'κλοπή' (theft) in the LXX data appears to be a textual anomaly and may reflect a scribal variant rather than a genuine semantic sense of the Hebrew root.

definition: A personal name meaning 'in the counsel of Yahweh,' belonging to an Israelite mentioned in Nehemiah's account of Jerusalem's wall repair.
article: Besodejah appears exactly once in the Old Testament, in Nehemiah 3:6, where his son Melatiah helped repair the Old Gate of Jerusalem. The name is built from the preposition 'in,' the noun סוֹד (counsel or intimate circle), and the divine name Yah — essentially meaning 'in Yahweh's counsel.' Because it is a proper name, the LXX simply transliterates it rather than translating it, offering no additional semantic insight.
caution: With only a single occurrence, nothing can be said about this individual beyond the one verse in Nehemiah, and the name's precise meaning depends on the interpretation of the underlying root סוֹד.

definition: A personal name meaning 'given by the king,' belonging to a royal official mentioned in the reign of Josiah.
article: Nethan-melech appears only in 2 Kings 23:11, where he is identified as a court official (a chamberlain or officer) whose chamber stood near the temple entrance, and whose horses connected to sun worship were removed by Josiah. The name itself combines the Hebrew roots for 'given' and 'king.' The LXX is split in its rendering: once it transliterates the name as Nathanan (treating it as a proper name), and once it renders the location as γαζοφυλάκιον ('treasury' or 'storehouse'), suggesting some uncertainty about whether the text referred to the man or his official post.
caution: With only 2 occurrences in a single verse, and the LXX showing inconsistency between transliterating a name and rendering a location, the exact role and identity of this figure remain uncertain.

definition: A grain stalk with its head of kernels, or by extension a flowing stream or channel of water.
article: This word covers two distinct physical pictures that share the idea of something that grows or flows outward: the head of a grain plant and a running watercourse. The great majority of its 19 occurrences appear in Genesis 41, where Pharaoh dreams of seven fat ears of grain and seven thin ones — accounting for 10 of the word's uses. The LXX translators almost always chose the Greek word στάχυς, meaning 'ear of grain,' showing that ancient readers saw that as the word's dominant sense, even though the KJV also renders it as 'flood' and 'channel' in other passages. The famous episode in Judges 1 — where pronunciation of this word exposed Ephraimite soldiers — is the origin of the English word 'shibboleth.'
caution: Strong's flags this word as having two quite different meanings (grain-ear and watercourse) that scholars believe share a root but whose connection is uncertain, and the low confidence tier reflects ongoing discussion about whether these are truly one word or two homonyms.

definition: The nose or face, and by extension anger or wrath, since ancient Hebrew associated passionate breathing through the nose with emotion.
article: אַף covers a physical and an emotional domain that Hebrew treats as naturally connected: the nose (or nostrils) as a body part, and the hot, rapid breathing that signals rage. In prose narrative it often refers literally to the nose or face (as in Gen 2:7, the breath of life through the nostrils), while in the Psalms, Isaiah, and Jeremiah it overwhelmingly signals divine or human anger. The LXX translators confirm this emotional sense was primary in their reading, rendering the word as ὀργή or θυμός — the two main Greek words for wrath and fury — a combined 130 times out of 276 occurrences. The phrase 'slow to anger' in Hebrew is literally 'long of nose,' a vivid idiom this word makes possible.

definition: An adverb meaning 'empty-handed' or 'without result,' describing action done without adequate provision, payment, or effect.
article: רֵיקָם functions as an adverb expressing the idea of emptiness in a practical, concrete sense — most often that someone departs or is sent away without what they deserve or need. In Exodus it appears in commands not to appear before God or release servants 'empty-handed,' making the core meaning vivid: without proper provision or compensation. It can also shade into the abstract sense of acting 'without cause' or 'in vain,' as seen in the Psalms. The LXX overwhelmingly renders it with κενός ('empty'), confirming that ancient readers heard the concrete sense of emptiness first and foremost.
caution: The confidence tier is flagged as low, and the single occurrence rendered ἀποπίπτω ('to fall away') and another as βάσανος ('torment') in the LXX suggest translators occasionally struggled with the word's sense in context, indicating some interpretive uncertainty.

definition: The Babylonian name given to one of Daniel's three companions in the book of Daniel.
article: Abed-nego is a Babylonian name assigned to one of Daniel's companions — known by his Hebrew name Azariah — when he entered service in Nebuchadnezzar's court. This specific form of the name (H5664) appears only 2 times, both in Daniel 1:7, which records the renaming event itself. The far more common form of the name (H5665) is used throughout the rest of Daniel, including the famous fiery furnace narrative. The KJV consistently renders it as
caution: The meaning of the Babylonian name itself is uncertain and disputed, and this particular Hebrew spelling appears only twice, making it a rare variant form with very limited attestation.

definition: Gezer, a Canaanite city in the lowlands of Palestine that appears in military and territorial boundary contexts.
article: Gezer is a specific place name referring to a well-known Canaanite city located in the Shephelah lowlands of Palestine. It appears 15 times across 5 books, concentrated especially in Joshua (5×), 1 Chronicles (4×), and 1 Kings (3×), reflecting its importance in conquest narratives, tribal boundaries, and Solomonic administrative records. The LXX translations are unusual — rendering the name twice as φόρος (tribute) and once as ἐκκεντέω (to pierce through) — suggesting ancient translators occasionally misread or reinterpreted the text rather than consistently treating it as a proper noun.
caution: The confidence tier for this entry is marked low, and the inconsistent LXX renderings raise genuine uncertainty about whether all 15 occurrences reliably point to the same city or whether some textual confusion exists in the manuscript tradition.

definition: An exclamatory or conditional particle meaning 'look!' or 'if,' used to draw attention or introduce a supposition.
article: הֵן serves two related functions: it either calls the reader's attention to something striking — much like saying 'Look!' or 'Listen!' — or it introduces a conditional clause meaning 'if.' Its most common rendering in the Septuagint is ἰδού ('behold/look!'), appearing 191 times that way, which confirms the exclamatory sense was dominant for ancient readers. It appears 318 times across 31 books, with the heaviest concentration in the prophetic books — Jeremiah, Isaiah, and Ezekiel — where dramatic attention-getting language is especially common. The grammatical data shows it functions primarily as a particle (217 times), though it also appears as a definite article (99 times), reflecting a distinct but related usage.
caution: The 99 occurrences tagged as 'definite article' likely reflect a separate homographic form rather than the same particle, so readers should note the entry blends two grammatically distinct words that happen to share the same spelling.

definition: To blow away or scatter, used of dispersing people to distant corners or ends.
article: This rare Hebrew verb appears only once in the Old Testament, in Deuteronomy 32:26, where God contemplates scattering Israel. The KJV renders it 'scatter into corners,' blending the idea of blowing away with dispersal to remote places. Strong's connects the root to a puffing or blowing action, suggesting the image of wind driving something away entirely.
caution: This word occurs only once in the entire Old Testament (a hapax legomenon), making its precise meaning difficult to verify and heavily dependent on context and ancient interpretation.

definition: A measured or portioned piece of food distributed to people, likely a cut of meat or similar provisions.
article: This rare word appears only twice in the Old Testament, both times in parallel accounts of David distributing food to the assembled people (2 Samuel 6:19 and 1 Chronicles 16:3). The KJV renders it 'good piece of flesh,' suggesting a cut of meat, though the exact nature of the portion is uncertain. The Septuagint consistently uses διαμερίζω, meaning 'to divide' or 'distribute,' which points to the word's core idea of a measured-out share rather than any specific food item.
caution: Strong's marks the derivation as uncertain, the word is effectively a near-hapax appearing only in parallel passages, and scholars disagree on whether it denotes a piece of meat, a date cake, or some other portion of food.

definition: Wealth, honour, or high status — the quality of being costly, valuable, or held in great esteem.
article: יְקָר covers the range from concrete material wealth to the abstract sense of honour and high social standing. Its strong concentration in Esther (10 of 17 occurrences) fits that book's royal court setting, where the word describes the king's splendour and the dignity conferred on favoured officials. The LXX most often renders it with δοξάζω ('to glorify'), showing that ancient translators heard the word's dominant sense as honour and glory rather than mere monetary value.
caution: Confidence in the precise nuance is rated low, and the distribution is heavily skewed toward Esther, which makes it harder to establish the full semantic range with certainty.

definition: Amraphel is a foreign king of Shinar who allied with other rulers against the cities of the plain in Genesis 14.
article: Amraphel appears only twice in the Old Testament, both times in Genesis 14, where he is named as the king of Shinar and one of four kings who made war against five kings of the plain. The name is translated simply as 'Amraphel' in every ancient version, including the LXX, offering no interpretive help. His origin and the meaning of his name remain unknown, with Strong's explicitly noting the derivation is uncertain and possibly foreign.
caution: The name's etymology is entirely uncertain — Strong's labels it possibly foreign in origin — and the figure appears only in one chapter with no further biblical attestation, making confident historical or linguistic identification impossible.

definition: A personal name referring to an Israelite man listed in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles.
article: Resheph is a proper name appearing once in the Old Testament, in the genealogy of Ephraim in 1 Chronicles 7:25. The name shares its form with a common noun meaning flame or burning coal, but here it functions purely as a personal name with no further narrative context. Its single occurrence offers no information about the person beyond his place in the family line.
caution: This name appears only once in the entire OT, making any deeper analysis of its significance or background impossible from the biblical text alone.

definition: A precious or distinguished thing, especially choice produce, fruit, or other valued natural goods.
article: מֶגֶד refers to something eminent or distinguished, most concretely the valuable yields of land and nature. Its 8 occurrences are split between Deuteronomy (5×) and Song of Solomon (3×): in Deuteronomy 33 it appears repeatedly in Moses' blessing of Joseph, piling up images of heaven's dew, deep waters, and the finest fruits of sun and moon, while in Song of Solomon it describes desirable fruits and pleasures. The LXX translators reached for ὥρα — a Greek word for the beauty of a season or its ripe produce — suggesting ancient readers heard in מֶגֶד the sense of prime, timely abundance rather than mere monetary value.
caution: Confidence is rated low, the root is unattested in Hebrew beyond this noun, and the precise semantic boundaries between 'precious thing' in general and 'choice agricultural produce' in particular remain uncertain.

definition: To alter or change something, shifting it from one state or appearance to another.
article: שָׁנָא means to alter or change, appearing only 3 times across 2 Kings, Ecclesiastes, and Lamentations. The Qal stem carries the basic sense of changing, while the Pual stem (passive) describes something being changed or transformed by an outside force. The KJV consistently renders it simply as 'change,' suggesting translators saw little ambiguity in its meaning across these varied contexts.
caution: This root is nearly a hapax, appearing only 3 times with low confidence assigned by lexicographers, and its relationship to the more common root שָׁנָה (H8138) is disputed — the two may overlap or be variant spellings of the same verb.

definition: A gentile adjective identifying someone from Horonaim, used exclusively as an ethnic label for Sanballat, Nehemiah's opponent.
article: Choronite (or Horonite in the KJV) denotes a person from a place called Horonaim, though the exact location of that city is uncertain. All three occurrences appear in Nehemiah alone, each referring to Sanballat the Horonite, a leading adversary of the Jerusalem rebuilding project. Because the word functions purely as an ethnic label, its semantic range is extremely narrow — it answers only the question of where Sanballat came from, not anything about character or social role.
caution: The location of Horonaim itself is disputed, and whether Sanballat's hometown was in Moab, Samaria, or elsewhere remains unresolved, making the precise meaning of this ethnic label uncertain.

definition: An adjective meaning enduring or long-established, and thus highly valued or precious.
article: עָתֵק appears only once in the Old Testament, in Proverbs 8:18, where Wisdom declares that riches and honor accompany her. The word carries the sense of something old and established, and therefore genuinely valuable — not merely expensive but proven over time. The KJV renders it 'durable,' capturing the enduring quality behind the worth. Its single appearance in the wisdom literature of Proverbs fits a context where lasting, reliable goods are contrasted with fleeting wealth.
caution: With only one occurrence in the entire Old Testament, this is effectively a hapax legomenon, and its precise nuance — whether the emphasis falls on antiquity, durability, or intrinsic value — cannot be confirmed from usage patterns alone.

definition: A Hebrew personal name referring primarily to the famous reforming king of Judah, son of Amon, who reigned in Jerusalem around 640–609 BC.
article: Josiah is a personal name borne most famously by the king of Judah who launched sweeping religious reforms after the discovery of the Book of the Law in the temple (2 Kings 22–23). The name appears 53 times across 7 books, with the heaviest concentration in Jeremiah (18×), 2 Chronicles (17×), and 2 Kings (13×), reflecting how significant this king was to the prophetic and historical traditions of the period. The LXX consistently translates the name as Ἰωσίας, the direct Greek form that passes into the New Testament and church tradition as

definition: Joyful gladness or rejoicing, used to describe a celebratory, exuberant state of delight.
article: חֶדְוָה means joy or gladness, appearing only twice in the Old Testament — once in 1 Chronicles and once in Nehemiah, both in celebratory contexts. Its most famous occurrence is Nehemiah 8:10, where 'the joy of the LORD is your strength.' The LXX's translation choices are striking: the ancient translators rendered it as ἔπαινος (praise) and καύχημα (boasting or pride), suggesting they heard in it not just quiet happiness but an outward, expressive delight that overflows into celebration.
caution: With only 2 occurrences across the entire Old Testament and low confidence assigned by lexicographers, the full semantic range of this word is difficult to establish with certainty.

definition: Destruction or utter ruin, referring to the complete perishing of a people or group.
article: אָבְדַן means destruction or complete perishing, derived from the root אָבַד (to perish or be destroyed). It appears only once in the Old Testament, in Esther 8:6, where Esther pleads before the king about the threatened annihilation of her people. Notably, the LXX rendered it as πατρίς (homeland or native country), which is a striking departure — suggesting ancient translators may have interpreted the verse's focus as the loss of one's people and homeland rather than destruction itself.
caution: This word is a hapax legomenon, appearing only once in the entire Hebrew Old Testament, which makes confident assessment of its full semantic range impossible.

definition: A proper name for a place, likely an early name for Jerusalem, meaning 'peaceful' or 'complete.'
article: שָׁלֵם (Shalem) appears only twice in the Old Testament — once in Genesis 14:18, where Melchizedek is called king of Salem, and once in Psalm 76:3, where Salem is paired with Zion. The name carries the sense of 'peaceful' or 'whole,' sharing its root with the familiar word shalom. The KJV consistently renders it as 'Salem,' and most ancient readers understood it as an early designation for Jerusalem. Interestingly, the LXX uses ἀπατάω (meaning 'to deceive') in one instance, which is puzzling and may reflect a textual or translation anomaly rather than the word's actual meaning.
caution: With only 2 occurrences and an unexpected LXX rendering of ἀπατάω ('to deceive'), confidence in the full picture of this entry is low — the LXX choice may signal a textual variant or scribal confusion rather than the word's true sense.

definition: An exclamation of triumph, mockery, or malicious delight, roughly equivalent to 'Aha!' or 'Ha!'
article: הֶאָח is an interjection used to express gloating or contemptuous satisfaction, most often voiced by enemies rejoicing over someone's downfall. It appears 12 times across 4 books, with 7 occurrences in Psalms — consistently placed in the mouths of those mocking the afflicted. The word's emotional color is negative: it is the shout of someone delighting in another's trouble. Notably, the LXX once renders it with παρανομέω, a verb meaning 'to act lawlessly,' suggesting ancient translators heard in this cry not just emotion but the wickedness of those uttering it.
caution: The grammatical role is listed as 'definite article' for all 12 occurrences, which appears to be a tagging error in the source data — the word is clearly an interjection, not an article, so the confidence tier is low and users should be aware of possible parsing inconsistencies.

definition: A proper name referring to a place in ancient Palestine, likely meaning 'springs' in Hebrew.
article: Gallim is a proper place name appearing twice in the Old Testament — once in 1 Samuel 25:44 and once in Isaiah 10:30. It appears to be a town in the territory of Israel, named from the Hebrew root for 'springs.' The KJV consistently renders it simply as 'Gallim' without translation, treating it as a fixed geographical name.
caution: With only 2 occurrences across 2 books and no LXX translation evidence provided, the exact location and full significance of Gallim remain uncertain.

definition: A personal name meaning 'brother of majesty' or 'brother of renown,' borne by an Israelite leader appointed to help divide Canaan.
article: Achihud appears exactly once in the Old Testament, in Numbers 34:27, where he is named as the representative of the tribe of Asher in the division of the promised land. The name combines the Hebrew words for 'brother' and 'majesty' or 'renown,' suggesting a sense of noble kinship. Because it is a proper name with a single occurrence, its meaning functions more as a bearer's identifier than as a word with semantic range.
caution: This word occurs only once in the entire Old Testament, making it a hapax legomenon; almost nothing can be said about the person beyond this single reference.

definition: A thorny, prickly weed or bramble that grows in neglected, overgrown places.
article: חָרוּל refers to some kind of prickly or thorny plant that takes over neglected land. It appears only 3 times in the Old Testament, always in poetic or prophetic contexts — Job, Proverbs, and Zephaniah — where overgrown weeds signal ruin, poverty, or desolation. The LXX renders it with φρύγανον, a Greek word for dry brushwood or thornbushes, reinforcing the picture of wild, useless, and unpleasant vegetation. Together these contexts consistently paint חָרוּל as a plant marker of abandonment and decay.
caution: With only 3 occurrences and an unused root, the precise plant species cannot be identified with confidence; 'nettle,' 'bramble,' and other thorny weeds have all been proposed by translators.

definition: To loathe or regard as detestable, especially in the context of ritually unclean creatures and forbidden things.
article: שָׁקַץ describes an intense aversion — not mere dislike, but active abhorrence directed at something considered deeply impure or forbidden. All 6 verbal occurrences appear in the Piel stem, which intensifies the action, so the word always carries a strong, deliberate sense of treating something as utterly detestable. The word concentrates heavily in Leviticus (4 times) and Deuteronomy (2 times), almost entirely in laws about unclean animals and forbidden objects, which tells us its primary home is the ritual-purity world. The LXX most often chose βδελύσσω — the same Greek word used for moral revulsion and abomination — showing that ancient readers understood this as the strongest possible language of rejection.
caution: The low confidence tier and sparse attestation (7 occurrences across only 3 books) leave some uncertainty about the full semantic range; scholars debate how sharply to distinguish ritual disgust from moral loathing in this root.

definition: A state of confusion, disarray, or utter perplexity, especially in the context of crisis or judgment.
article: מְבוּכָה (mebukah) describes a condition of bewildering confusion or perplexity, derived from the root בּוּך, which conveys being lost or thrown into disorder. It appears only twice in the Old Testament, both times in prophetic books — once in Isaiah 22:5, describing a day of tumult and chaos, and once in Micah 7:4, portraying the confusion that comes upon those caught in judgment. Its exclusive appearance in two prophetic texts gives it a distinctly solemn, crisis-oriented register.
caution: This word occurs only twice in the entire Old Testament (a near-hapax), and the KJV translates it the same way both times, offering very little range of evidence to confirm or nuance its meaning beyond 'perplexity.'

definition: A force or capacity in persons or resources — covering military armies, physical strength, moral virtue, and material wealth.
article: חָיִל is one of Hebrew's broadest power-words, stretching across military, physical, economic, and moral domains wherever force or capacity is at work. It appears 234 times across 31 books, with especially heavy use in the historical books (Jeremiah, Chronicles, Kings) where armies and campaigns dominate. The LXX overwhelmingly chose δύναμις ("power, force") 114 times — the same word NT authors use for divine power — signaling that ancient readers heard the word as raw, versatile capacity rather than any single English gloss. The famous description of the capable wife in Proverbs 31 uses this word (אֵשֶׁת חַיִל), showing the moral-and-practical register: she is a woman of חָיִל, not just wealth or muscle but excellent, effective force of character.

definition: A day in the literal sense (sunrise to sunset or a full 24-hour period), or more broadly any defined span of time, season, or era.
article: יוֹם is the standard Hebrew word for 'day,' but its range stretches far beyond a single rotation of the earth. It can mean the daylight hours, a full calendar day, a lifetime, an era, or simply 'a time when' something happens — context is everything. With 2,304 occurrences spread across all 39 books of the Old Testament, it is one of the most common nouns in the Hebrew Bible, appearing most densely in narrative and legal texts like Deuteronomy, Genesis, and Numbers. The LXX almost always renders it with Greek ἡμέρα (1,794 times), confirming its core meaning as 'day,' but the remaining renderings — including σήμερον ('today') and various relational particles — reflect how often יוֹם functions adverbially to anchor an event in time rather than simply name a unit of it.

definition: A cutting or shaping tool used in woodworking, likely an axe or chisel for hewing timber.
article: מַעֲצָד refers to a tool used to cut or shape wood, derived from a root meaning 'to hew.' It appears only twice in the entire Old Testament — once in Isaiah 44:12 and once in Jeremiah 10:3 — both times in the context of a craftsman fashioning an idol from timber. The KJV renders it as both 'ax' and 'tongs,' suggesting some uncertainty about the exact tool, though the woodworking context strongly favors a cutting implement like an axe or adze.
caution: With only 2 occurrences and a root described as unused, the precise identification of this tool is uncertain — the spread between 'ax' and 'tongs' in KJV translation reflects genuine scholarly disagreement about what instrument is meant.

definition: The gullet or throat, referring to the passage through which food and drink are swallowed.
article: לֹעַ refers to the gullet or throat, the channel through which food passes when swallowed. It appears only once in the entire Old Testament, in Proverbs 23:2, where the reader is warned to put a knife to their throat if they are a person given to appetite — a vivid, hyperbolic call to self-restraint at the table. The KJV renders it simply as "throat," and the word's connection to swallowing keeps its meaning tightly focused on that physical passage.
caution: This word is a hapax legomenon, occurring only once in the OT, so its precise nuance cannot be confirmed through broader usage patterns.

definition: A small container or vessel, specifically used to hold salt in the one biblical passage where it appears.
article: This word appears only once in the Old Testament, in 2 Kings 2:20, where Elisha calls for a 'cruse' (KJV) to be brought to him filled with salt. Strong's connects it to a root suggesting something tall or elongated, describing it as a vial or salt-cellar. Interestingly, the ancient Greek translators (LXX) rendered the word simply as ἅλας, meaning 'salt' — focusing on the contents rather than the container itself. This suggests they understood the vessel primarily in terms of its function.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon, appearing only once in the entire Old Testament, which makes its precise shape or size impossible to determine with confidence.

definition: To grow weary or exhausted through hard toil, covering both the effort of labor and the fatigue that results from it.
article: יָגַע describes the experience of being worn out — either from strenuous work or from any draining effort — and it captures both the act of toiling and the resulting state of exhaustion. The word appears 26 times across 11 books, with a striking concentration in Isaiah (12 times), suggesting particular use in prophetic rhetoric about human limits and divine strength. The Septuagint consistently translates it with κοπιάω (11 times), the same Greek word the New Testament uses for laborious toil, showing ancient readers understood this as genuine, effortful weariness rather than mere idleness. The Hiphil stem, attested twice, carries a causative sense — to cause someone else to grow weary or to wear something out.
caution: Strong's proposes an underlying sense of 'to gasp,' but this root meaning is not directly visible in the attested OT uses, and the moderate confidence tier reflects some uncertainty about the word's precise core meaning.

definition: A proper name identifying one of David's mighty warriors listed in 1 Chronicles.
article: Yithmah (transliterated 'Ithmah' in most English Bibles) is a personal name appearing only once in the Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 11:46, where he is identified as a Moabite among David's elite warriors. The KJV and nearly all translations simply transliterate the name rather than translate it. Strong's connects the name to the root for 'orphan' (yathom), suggesting the name may carry a meaning like 'orphanage' or 'fatherlessness,' though personal names often preserve old meanings that were no longer semantically active.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon — appearing only once in the entire Old Testament — and the name's precise meaning and etymology cannot be established with confidence beyond the proposed connection to the orphan root.

definition: Something baked in an oven, referring to a batch of baked grain offerings.
article: This rare noun comes from the verb meaning 'to bake' and appears only once in the Old Testament, in Leviticus 2:4, where it describes grain offerings that are baked in an oven. The word captures the product of the baking process — a completed batch — rather than the act of baking itself. Its single appearance is in the context of priestly food-offering regulations, where specific baked forms of the grain offering are listed.
caution: This word occurs only once in the entire Old Testament (a hapax legomenon), so its full range of meaning cannot be confirmed beyond this single context.

definition: To pledge oneself as security for another, or to mix and intermingle with others — covering both financial guarantee and social blending.
article: This verb carries two distinct but related ideas: guaranteeing someone else's debt or safety (standing surety), and mixing or mingling with other people or groups. The surety sense dominates in Proverbs, which warns repeatedly against pledging yourself for a neighbor's obligations, while Genesis uses it of Judah personally guaranteeing Benjamin's safety. The social-mingling sense appears in Ezra, where it describes Israel intermarrying with foreign peoples. The LXX's choice of μίγνυμι ("to mix") for the blending sense and ἐκδέχομαι ("to take on oneself") for the pledge sense shows ancient readers recognized these as genuinely distinct uses of one root.
caution: The link between the "pledge" and "intermix" senses is not fully transparent, and scholars debate whether these represent one root or two; Strong's connects them through the idea of interweaving, but this remains uncertain.

definition: Public disgrace or humiliation brought by shameful treatment, scorn, or social disgrace from others or from circumstances.
article: חֶרְפָּה describes the experience of being publicly shamed, scorned, or reproached — often by enemies, but sometimes by one's own circumstances. It covers both the act of taunting and the resulting state of disgrace, which is why English translators move between 'reproach,' 'shame,' and 'rebuke' depending on context. The word appears 73 times across 17 books, concentrated heavily in Psalms (20×), Jeremiah (12×), and Ezekiel (7×), reflecting how central this concept was to Israel's lament and prophetic traditions. The LXX almost exclusively uses ὀνειδισμός and ὄνειδος — the same Greek word family that NT authors draw on when describing insults and public shame — confirming that ancient readers heard this word as social disgrace, not merely private embarrassment.
caution: Strong's notes the rare sense 'pudenda' (shameful body parts), but this is marginal and disputed; the overwhelming weight of the evidence points to social and relational disgrace as the core meaning.

definition: Achishar, a personal name referring to an official in Solomon's royal household.
article: Achishar appears exactly once in the Old Testament, in 1 Kings 4:6, where he is listed as the official in charge of Solomon's palace household. The name itself is treated as a proper noun throughout, and the KJV simply transliterates it as Ahishar. Notably, the Septuagint renders his role with the Greek word οἰκονόμος, meaning 'household manager' or 'steward,' giving us a clear picture of his administrative function at court.
caution: With only a single occurrence, nothing beyond the name and its bearer's basic role can be confidently established from the text.

definition: A personal name meaning 'the small one,' borne by an Israelite mentioned in Ezra.
article: Hakkatan is a proper name appearing once in the Old Testament, in Ezra 8:12, where it identifies the father of Johanan among those who returned from exile. The name is simply the common adjective קָטָן ('small') used as a personal name, with the definite article attached ('the small one'). The KJV renders it as 'Hakkatan,' preserving the Hebrew article as part of the transliterated name.
caution: This word occurs only once in the entire Old Testament, making it a hapax legomenon in its use as a proper name, with no additional context to clarify its significance.

definition: A seafaring vessel or ship, used for trade, travel, and naval expeditions.
article: אֳנִיָּה refers to a ship or seafaring vessel and appears 32 times across 12 books of the Old Testament. Its range spans practical narrative contexts — Solomon's trading fleet in 1 Kings, Jonah's flight by sea — as well as poetic and prophetic imagery in Psalms, Proverbs, and Isaiah. The LXX almost always renders it with the standard Greek word for ship, πλοῖον (23 times), confirming a straightforward and consistent meaning with very little semantic ambiguity.
caution: The two instances where the LXX uses λυτρόω ('to redeem') are unexpected for a word meaning 'ship' and likely reflect textual or translation anomalies that remain unexplained.

definition: A city or town, appearing almost exclusively in poetic and wisdom literature as a setting for public life.
article: קָ֫רֶת means 'city,' functioning as a poetic synonym for the more common Hebrew word for city. All five occurrences appear in wisdom literature — four in Proverbs and one in Job — suggesting this is an elevated, literary term rather than everyday prose vocabulary. In Proverbs, it often describes the city gates or heights where Wisdom calls out publicly (Proverbs 8–9), placing it at the center of civic and social life. The LXX rendered it once as ὄρθριος ('early morning'), which is puzzling and may reflect a translator struggling with an uncommon word.
caution: Confidence is rated low, the word is rare (only 5 occurrences), confined to poetry, and the LXX's unusual translation suggests even ancient scholars found it difficult — its precise relationship to the more common words for 'city' remains uncertain.

definition: A symbolic proper name meaning 'bitter,' chosen by Naomi to reflect her grief and loss.
article: Mara is the name Naomi gives herself in Ruth 1:20, declaring that the Almighty has dealt bitterly with her after losing her husband and sons. It appears only this once in the Old Testament, functioning less as a personal name and more as a public statement of grief. The ancient Greek translators rendered it with the verb πικραίνω, meaning 'to make bitter,' capturing the emotional weight Naomi intended rather than treating it as a neutral label.
caution: This word occurs only once in the entire Old Testament (a hapax legomenon), so its use is inseparable from this single narrative moment and cannot be verified against a broader range of contexts.

definition: The cardinal number ten, used for counting and in compound numbers like thirteen or fifteen.
article: עָ֫שֶׂר (ʿāśer) is the basic Hebrew word for the number ten, appearing 177 times across 26 books of the Old Testament. It functions primarily as an adjective modifying nouns in counting contexts, and also appears in compound forms that produce numbers like fifteen and seventeen. The ancient Greek translators of the Septuagint rendered it as δέκα ("ten") in 155 of its occurrences, confirming its consistent numerical meaning. Its heaviest use is in narrative and legal literature — 1 Kings, Numbers, and Ezekiel — where precise counting of people, objects, and measurements is frequent.

definition: An Aramaic demonstrative pronoun meaning 'these,' pointing to previously mentioned persons or things.
article: This is the Aramaic form of the Hebrew demonstrative pronoun 'these,' appearing just once in the entire Old Testament, at Jeremiah 10:11. That single verse is a striking anomaly — an Aramaic sentence embedded in the Hebrew book of Jeremiah, likely preserved as a spoken formula or public declaration. The word functions straightforwardly as a pointer: 'these gods' that did not make the heavens and earth.
caution: With only one occurrence in the OT, there is virtually no contextual range to analyze; all meaning rests on this single Aramaic verse in Jeremiah.

definition: To be laid down or set in place, used once of people settled at God's feet.
article: This rare verb appears only once in the Old Testament, in Deuteronomy 33:3, where it describes people sitting or settled at God's feet. The Pual stem indicates a passive sense — something like 'they are strewn' or 'they are set down' — which the KJV renders loosely as 'sit down.' Strong's connects the root to the idea of strewing or encamping, suggesting a picture of people spread out and resting in a place of safety.
caution: This word is a hapax legomenon, appearing only once in the entire Hebrew Old Testament, making its precise meaning very difficult to establish with confidence.

definition: To be grievous or distressing, describing something that causes severe pain or anguish.
article: This rare verb appears only 4 times across 4 books (1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, Job, and Isaiah), and the KJV renders it 'be grievous' only in Isaiah 15:4, with the other occurrences likely belonging to the related root רָעַע. The core idea seems to be a violent breaking or shattering that produces anguish. Because the evidence is so limited and the boundaries with a neighboring root are unclear, the full range of this word is difficult to pin down.
caution: Confidence is low: Strong's itself notes that only Isaiah 15:4 clearly belongs to this root, with the remaining three occurrences potentially misattributed to it rather than to the closely related root רָעַע.

definition: A fraudulent deception or delusion, used to describe something fundamentally false and misleading.
article: This rare noun appears only twice in the Old Testament, both times in the book of Jeremiah (10:15 and 51:18), and in identical contexts — both verses are nearly word-for-word the same, describing idols as works of delusion or fraud. The KJV renders it 'error,' but the underlying sense points to something actively deceptive, not merely mistaken. The narrow distribution in a single book, repeated in what appears to be a parallel passage, makes this one of the most contextually confined nouns in the Hebrew Bible.
caution: This word occurs only twice, both in near-duplicate verses in Jeremiah, making it extremely difficult to establish a full semantic range; its derivation from the root תָּעַע is itself debated, and confidence in the precise nuance is low.

definition: A type of dark stone or tile, likely black marble or a similar material used in decorative flooring or borders.
article: This word appears only once in the entire Old Testament, in Esther 1:6, describing the luxurious paving of the Persian royal court. Strong's connects it to a related root and defines it as a dark tile or tessera used for laying decorative borders. The KJV renders it simply as 'black marble,' which captures the likely sense of a prized, dark-colored stone used in ornate royal construction.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon with only one occurrence, making its precise meaning uncertain; the identification as black marble is plausible but not definitively established.

definition: A rare Hebrew verb meaning apparently to annihilate or destroy utterly, occurring only once in the Old Testament.
article: This word appears only once in the entire Hebrew Bible, in Ezekiel 39:2, making it an extremely rare term. Strong's identifies it as a primitive root meaning apparently to annihilate, though the KJV translators actually rendered it as 'leave but the sixth part,' a gloss that Strong's itself attributes to confusion with a different root (shashah). The single occurrence in Ezekiel falls within a prophetic passage about the devastation of Gog, which fits a sense of utter destruction contextually.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon with a disputed meaning — the KJV translation 'leave by the sixth part' is explicitly noted as a confusion with another root, leaving the true sense uncertain and the word's definition essentially unverified by translation tradition.

definition: To overpower or prevail against someone, implying forceful domination or overwhelming strength.
article: תָּקַף means to overpower or get the better of someone by force. It appears only 4 times in the Old Testament, confined entirely to Job and Ecclesiastes — both books that wrestle with human vulnerability and the limits of strength. The LXX evidence aligns with this forceful sense, and the KJV consistently renders it 'prevail against,' suggesting a narrow but clear meaning of one party decisively overwhelming another.
caution: With only 4 occurrences across 2 books, the semantic range is very limited, and confidence in capturing the word's full potential meaning remains low.

definition: An Aramaic adjective meaning beautiful or fair, used to describe something pleasing in appearance.
article: This Aramaic word appears only twice in the Old Testament, both times in Daniel 4 (verses 9 and 18), where it functions as an adjective. Its meaning is straightforward: beautiful or fair. The LXX evidence is puzzling — ancient translators rendered it as 'Δανιήλ' (the name Daniel) in one instance, which suggests the Greek translators may have handled this passage very differently rather than translating the adjective directly.
caution: Attestation is extremely sparse (only 2 occurrences, 1 book), the LXX rendering as a proper name rather than an adjective is unexplained, and the confidence tier is marked low, leaving the word's full semantic range uncertain.

definition: A resting place or lying-down spot, especially where animals settle and recline.
article: רֵ֫בֶץ refers to a place of repose — a spot where a creature lies down to rest. Its four occurrences appear in Isaiah (twice), Proverbs, and Jeremiah, and all fit a similar picture: a designated spot for reclining or settling, typically animals in pasture or lair contexts. Isaiah 65:10, for example, pictures flocks lying down in a restored land, and Jeremiah 50:6 mourns sheep who have forgotten their resting place. The word derives from the root רָבַץ, meaning to lie down, so it is essentially the noun form of that action.
caution: With only 4 occurrences across 3 books, the semantic range is narrow and the confidence tier is rated low, so nuances beyond 'resting place' should be held loosely.

definition: To chop or cut off a part of something, especially by severing a limb, branch, or edge completely.
article: קָצַץ means to cut or chop off, typically with a decisive, complete severing action. The word appears 14 times across 8 books, with concrete physical uses like cutting off thumbs and toes (Judges 1) or hands (2 Samuel 4), as well as cutting things into pieces (Exodus 39:3). The dominant LXX rendering ἀποκόπτω ('to cut off entirely') confirms that ancient translators understood this as a thorough, final severance rather than a partial cut.
caution: Confidence is rated low, and one surprising LXX rendering — ἱλασμός, meaning 'atonement' or 'propitiation' — is difficult to reconcile with the Hebrew root, suggesting possible manuscript variation or a highly unusual translation choice that scholars have not fully resolved.

definition: A bird of prey, likely a hawk or kite, listed among unclean birds in Mosaic law.
article: This word refers to a specific bird of prey, appearing only 3 times across Leviticus, Deuteronomy, and Job. In Leviticus and Deuteronomy it appears in the lists of birds forbidden for food, while in Job 28:7 it describes a creature with keen eyesight that cannot find wisdom's hidden path. The KJV renders it as both 'kite' and 'vulture,' reflecting genuine uncertainty about which raptor is meant, and the Septuagint's translation choices similarly vary.
caution: With only 3 occurrences and KJV translators themselves divided between 'kite' and 'vulture,' the precise species cannot be determined with confidence; Strong's derives it speculatively from a root meaning 'screamer.'

definition: An Aramaic word meaning the declaration or explanation of something hidden, used specifically for solving riddles or interpreting mysteries.
article: This Aramaic term appears only once in the Old Testament, in Daniel 5:12, where it describes the ability to explain or interpret difficult things — specifically the solving of riddles and mysteries. The KJV renders it simply as 'showing,' but Strong's indicates the core meaning is the declaration or solution of something obscure. Its single appearance in Daniel fits the book's consistent focus on supernatural interpretation of hidden knowledge.
caution: This word occurs only once in the entire Old Testament (a hapax legomenon in Aramaic), so its semantic range cannot be confirmed from internal biblical evidence alone.

definition: Describes grain that is unripe or late-growing, not yet mature at harvest time.
article: This word appears only once in the Old Testament, in Exodus 9:32, describing wheat and spelt that had not yet grown up when the plague of hail struck Egypt. The grain was unripe and therefore survived the hail damage that destroyed the more mature crops. The LXX translates it with ὄψιμος, meaning "late" or "late-ripening," which confirms the sense of grain that was behind in its growth cycle rather than simply damaged or weak.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon — appearing only once in the entire Old Testament — so its meaning rests on a single context plus the LXX rendering and Strong's connection to a related root meaning weakness or darkness.

definition: To flow or stream together, and also to shine or be radiant — two related senses sharing one root in Hebrew.
article: This rare root appears only 6 times across 4 books — Isaiah, Jeremiah, Psalms, and Micah — and carries two distinct but connected ideas: flowing like a river (nations streaming toward a place) and shining or being gladdened with radiance. In Isaiah 2:2 and Jeremiah 31:12, for example, peoples "flow" to a mountain or to God's goodness, while Psalm 34:6 uses the sense of a face being lit up or brightened. The LXX translators notably rendered the word as ἐμφανής ("visible, manifest") and ὑπεράνω ("above, prominent") in some passages, suggesting they read the shining or elevated sense rather than the flowing one — showing how ancient readers themselves felt the ambiguity.
caution: With only 6 occurrences and LXX renderings that diverge notably from the flowing sense, the precise meaning in each passage remains uncertain, and scholarly confidence in separating the two senses is low.

definition: A personal name borne by multiple Israelite men, meaning 'Yahweh has dwelt.'
article: Shecaniah (also spelled Shechaniah in some translations) is a proper name applied to several distinct Israelite individuals across the post-exilic period. Its 10 occurrences are spread across 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah — books that are themselves heavily focused on genealogy, temple service, and the return from exile. The name's two KJV spelling variants simply reflect different English transliterations of the same Hebrew form. Strong's counts at least nine different men bearing this name, making careful attention to context essential when identifying which Shecaniah is meant.
caution: The low confidence tier assigned to this entry suggests some uncertainty, possibly around distinguishing the individuals or the exact spelling tradition; readers should check context carefully when tracking a specific Shecaniah across books.

definition: To destroy or bring to ruin, attested only once in a passive-intensive form.
article: This verb appears a single time in the Old Testament, at Job 30:22, in the Pual stem — a passive-intensive form suggesting something is thoroughly destroyed or undone. The Strong's definition points to destruction as the core meaning, and the marginal KJV gloss 'substance' likely reflects an attempt to make sense of a difficult poetic context rather than a distinct meaning of the root itself. Its sole occurrence is in Job, one of the Bible's most linguistically challenging books, known for rare and obscure vocabulary.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon — appearing only once in the entire Old Testament — in a notoriously difficult poetic text, making its exact meaning highly uncertain; scholarly confidence is very low.

definition: A proper name referring to one of several distinct towns in ancient Palestine, most prominently the hometown of Samuel.
article: Ramah is a proper name shared by at least four different locations in ancient Palestine, which explains why it appears across so many different geographic and narrative contexts. It occurs 36 times in 11 books, with the heaviest concentration in 1 Samuel (15 times), where it is closely associated with the prophet Samuel — his hometown, his base of operations, and his burial place. The Septuagint consistently renders the word as Ῥαμᾶ (23 times), a simple transliteration, confirming that ancient readers treated this as a fixed place name rather than a common noun. The name is likely related to the Hebrew root for "height," which fits the hilly terrain typical of these settlements, though the digest does not elaborate on that connection.
caution: Moderate confidence reflects the fact that multiple distinct towns share this name, and identifying which Ramah is meant in any given verse requires careful attention to the surrounding geographic context.

definition: A specific place name referring to a campsite or settlement the Israelites stopped at during the wilderness journey from Egypt.
article: Hazeroth is a proper noun — a named stopping point on Israel's wilderness itinerary, appearing five times in Numbers and once in Deuteronomy. The underlying Hebrew word is the feminine plural of a common noun meaning yards or enclosures, suggesting the site may have been a settled area with compounds or courtyards. It is the place where Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses (Numbers 11–12), making it a narratively significant camp. The KJV consistently renders it as Hazeroth without translation, treating it purely as a place name.
caution: The exact geographical location of Hazeroth is unknown and debated; the site has not been identified with certainty, and the word appears almost entirely as a proper noun with very limited use as a common noun in this corpus.

definition: A personal name belonging to an Israelite mentioned in a genealogy in 1 Chronicles.
article: Ir is a proper name appearing once in the Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 7:12, where it occurs in a genealogical list. Strong's notes that the name is identical in form to the common Hebrew word for 'city,' though here it functions solely as a personal name. The KJV simply transliterates it as 'Ir' with no attempt at translation.
caution: This name appears only once in the OT, and Strong's notes it shares its form with another word, making its precise origin and meaning uncertain.

definition: A payment or gift given to a prostitute, specifically a bounty freely thrown out to attract lovers.
article: נֵדֶה appears only once in the Old Testament, in Ezekiel 16:33, where it describes the gifts or payments given to a prostitute. The word carries the specific sense of a bounty or inducement rather than a general gift, reflecting its root's idea of freely flinging or throwing money. The LXX renders it as μίσθωμα, meaning 'hire' or 'wages,' which confirms that ancient translators understood this as payment for sexual services rather than a gift in any ordinary sense.
caution: This word occurs only once in the entire Old Testament (a hapax legomenon), so its precise nuance rests almost entirely on its root derivation and the LXX translation choice rather than broad contextual evidence.

definition: To move slowly or glide, used once in the Old Testament in a context suggesting gentle, murmuring speech or quiet movement.
article: דָּבַב appears only once in the entire Old Testament, in Song of Solomon 7:10, making it a hapax legomenon. Strong's defines it as meaning to move slowly or glide, yet the KJV translates it 'cause to speak,' suggesting ancient translators may have connected it to murmuring or gentle, flowing speech. The LXX evidence for this word's translation is not supplied, leaving us dependent on context and classical lexicons alone. Given its sole appearance in the highly poetic Song of Solomon, the word likely carries an evocative, sensory quality — perhaps describing lips or words that flow smoothly and quietly.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon (occurring only once in the OT), and the gap between Strong's gloss ('glide') and the KJV rendering ('cause to speak') reflects genuine uncertainty about the word's precise meaning.

definition: A prisoner or captive, someone physically bound and held in confinement.
article: אָסִיר describes a person who is bound and imprisoned, derived from the root meaning to bind or restrain. The word appears 13 times across 7 books, with its most vivid narrative uses in Genesis (Joseph in prison) and Judges (Samson in Philistine captivity). The LXX most often renders it δέσμιος, meaning a bound prisoner — precisely the same word used in later Greek for prisoners in general — which confirms the concrete, physical sense of confinement as primary. The range is actually quite narrow for Hebrew: this word consistently means a literal prisoner rather than carrying broader metaphorical weight.
caution: Confidence is rated low, and one LXX rendering (ῥαπίζω, meaning 'to strike') is strikingly out of place, suggesting possible textual difficulty or mistranslation in at least one passage.

definition: A place name in the territory of Dan, appearing once in the Old Testament.
article: Yith-law appears only once in the entire Old Testament, in Joshua 19:42, as one of the towns listed within the allotment of the tribe of Dan. Strong's connects the name to the root meaning 'to hang' or 'be high,' suggesting a possible sense of elevation in the original place name. The KJV renders it as Jethlah, and no LXX translation evidence adds further clarity to its meaning or location.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon appearing solely as a proper noun, so its precise location and the reliability of the proposed root connection remain uncertain.

definition: A place name in Palestine, likely meaning 'fertile' or 'fatness,' referring to a town from which Asher failed to drive out the Canaanites.
article: Achlab (also spelled Ahlab) is a town mentioned once in Judges 1:31 as one of the cities whose Canaanite inhabitants the tribe of Asher failed to expel. The name appears to be derived from a root meaning 'fatness' or 'fertility,' suggesting it may have occupied agriculturally rich land. Because the KJV simply transliterates it as 'Ahlab,' no meaningful range of translation exists to analyze, and the LXX similarly treats it as a proper name.
caution: This word occurs only once in the entire Old Testament, making its meaning and precise location impossible to verify with confidence; its identification with any known archaeological site remains uncertain.

definition: Boastful lies or empty talk, often referring to proud, arrogant falsehoods spoken by a braggart or deceiver.
article: This rare word, appearing only 6 times across Job, Isaiah, and Jeremiah, refers to the kind of speech that is both false and arrogant — not just a mistake, but a proud brag that has no substance behind it. Isaiah uses it of Babylon's empty boasting, and Jeremiah applies it to Moab's pride, giving the word a consistent flavor of inflated, hollow claims. The KJV renders it simply as 'lie' or 'liar,' but the underlying sense carries the extra weight of bragging. The narrow distribution across three poetic-prophetic books suggests it belongs to a more elevated, rhetorical register rather than everyday prose.
caution: Confidence in this word's precise meaning is low — it is rare, its root is disputed, and the line between 'lie' and 'boastful empty talk' is not always clearly established by context alone.

definition: An Aramaic verb meaning to descend or bring something down, including depositing objects or removing someone from a position.
article: This Aramaic verb covers the movement of going down as well as the caused action of bringing something down to a place. In Ezra it appears in the context of temple vessels being deposited or placed in a location, while in Daniel it describes something coming down from a great height. The Hiphil stem shifts the meaning causatively — not merely descending but actively depositing or deposing — which explains the notably wide KJV gloss range of carry, come down, depose, lay up, and place from just six occurrences.
caution: Confidence is rated low, the word appears only 6 times across two Aramaic sections of the OT (Ezra and Daniel), making its full semantic range difficult to establish with certainty.

definition: A place name referring to a distant Mediterranean port, and by extension the large merchant ships that sailed to it, as well as a personal name used for both a Persian and an Israelite.
article: Tarshish appears 28 times across 10 books, most heavily in Isaiah (7×), 2 Chronicles (4×), and Jonah (4×). As a place, it represents a far-off, wealthy trading destination famous for silver, iron, and exotic goods — the kind of port Jonah famously tried to flee to. The phrase "ships of Tarshish" became a standing expression for large oceangoing merchant vessels, whether or not they literally sailed to that port, much as the LXX simply transliterates the name rather than translating it, reflecting that ancient readers treated it as a recognized proper noun. The name also appears as a personal name for a Persian official and an Israelite descendant of Benjamin.
caution: The exact location of Tarshish is disputed — candidates include Tartessos in Spain, Sardinia, and sites in the eastern Mediterranean — and confidence in identifying it is rated moderate.

definition: Laughter, whether joyful or mocking, depending on context.
article: This noun comes from the same root as Isaac's name and describes the act or experience of laughter, which Hebrew allows to span both genuine delight and contemptuous derision. Its two occurrences are spread across very different contexts: Genesis 21:6, where Sarah rejoices at Isaac's birth, and Ezekiel 23:32, where the image is of being made a laughingstock. The LXX reflects this same ambiguity, rendering it once as γέλως (laughter) and once as συγχαίρω (to rejoice together), showing ancient translators also wrestled with the word's tone.
caution: With only 2 occurrences across the entire Old Testament, the full semantic range of this noun is difficult to establish with confidence, and its precise nuance in any given passage depends heavily on context.

definition: A personal name belonging to an ancestor of temple servants (Nethinim) who returned from Babylonian exile.
article: Tabbaoth is a proper name appearing twice in the Old Testament, once in Ezra 2:43 and once in Nehemiah 7:46, both times in parallel lists of Nethinim — the dedicated temple servants — who returned from Babylon. The name is the plural form of a word meaning 'rings,' though in context it functions purely as a family or clan name. The KJV simply transliterates it as 'Tabaoth' in both occurrences, reflecting no attempt to render it as a common noun.
caution: With only 2 occurrences in parallel lists, nothing is known about the individual or family beyond the name itself, making any further interpretation speculative.

definition: A symbolic proper name meaning 'not pitied' or 'shown no mercy,' given to Hosea's daughter as a sign of divine judgment.
article: Lo-ruhamah is the name God commanded Hosea to give his daughter, carrying the meaning 'not pitied' — built from the Hebrew negative particle לֹא ('not') and the root רָחַם ('to show compassion or mercy'). All four occurrences are found exclusively in Hosea 1, where the name functions as a living prophetic sign of God's withdrawal of mercy from Israel. The LXX rendered the name with ἀντιτάσσομαι, meaning 'to set oneself against' or 'to oppose,' which suggests ancient translators interpreted the name as an active posture of divine rejection rather than merely the absence of pity.
caution: The LXX translation choice (ἀντιτάσσομαι, 'to oppose') diverges significantly from the Hebrew sense of the root רָחַם ('compassion/mercy'), making the ancient interpretive tradition somewhat uncertain and the Greek rendering difficult to reconcile with the Hebrew directly.

definition: A personal name referring to an Israelite man appearing in post-exilic records of Ezra and Nehemiah.
article: Binnui is a proper name borne by several Israelite men mentioned in the post-exilic books of Ezra and Nehemiah. The word appears all 7 of its occurrences across just these two books, fitting the narrow historical context of the return from Babylonian exile. The KJV translates it consistently as 'Binnui' without variation, and the name is likely related to the Hebrew root meaning 'built up.'
caution: Because this word functions solely as a proper name with only 7 occurrences in two closely related books, its underlying meaning is uncertain and the connection to its proposed root cannot be verified from usage alone.

definition: A proper name referring to both a man in Judah's genealogy and a place in Palestine, associated with the meaning 'sorrow' or 'grief.'
article: Jabez (יַעְבֵּץ) appears all 4 times in 1 Chronicles, making it a name confined to the genealogical and narrative material there. It refers both to a man notable for his prayer (1 Chr 4:9–10) and to a town associated with families of scribes (1 Chr 2:55). The name is explained within the text itself as connected to pain or sorrow at birth, and the Septuagint's rendering of the related explanation with γνῶσις ('knowledge') is a curious interpretive choice that suggests ancient translators understood some nuance in the passage differently than a straightforward 'grief' reading.
caution: The underlying root is listed as unused in Hebrew, so the proposed meaning 'sorrow' or 'grief' is reconstructed and not independently verifiable from other Hebrew usage.

definition: A personal name designating a son of Joktan, likely representing an ancient Arabian tribal ancestor.
article: Abimael appears exactly twice in the Old Testament — once in the Table of Nations in Genesis 10:28 and once in its parallel genealogy in 1 Chronicles 1:22 — always as a proper name. He is listed as a son of Joktan, whose descendants are generally associated with Arabian peoples. Strong's notes that the second element of the name is probably a foreign (non-Hebrew) word used nowhere else in the Old Testament, making the name's full meaning uncertain. The LXX transliterates the name rather than translating it, offering no additional insight into its meaning.
caution: The second element of this name comes from a word found nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible and is likely foreign in origin, so the traditional meaning 'father of Mael' remains uncertain and unverifiable.

definition: A proper name given to a disputed well, meaning 'strife' or 'contention' over water rights.
article: עֵשֶׂק is a proper noun appearing once in Genesis 26:20, where Isaac's herdsmen quarrel with local Philistine herdsmen over a well, prompting Isaac to name it Esek. The name is drawn from the root meaning strife or contention, and the KJV simply transliterates it as 'Esek' rather than translating it. The LXX renders the passage with words meaning 'to fight' and 'to claim,' both of which capture the sense of a disputed claim — exactly the kind of contention the well's name commemorates.
caution: This word occurs only once in the entire Old Testament, functioning as a place name whose underlying root meaning depends on a related verb that is itself relatively rare.

definition: A state of complete oblivion or forgetfulness, where one is utterly forgotten and beyond remembrance.
article: נְשִׁיָּה means oblivion or absolute forgetfulness — the condition of being entirely forgotten, as though one never existed. It appears only once in the entire Old Testament, in Psalm 88:12, where the psalmist asks whether God's wonders can be known "in the land of forgetfulness" (a poetic image for the realm of the dead). The LXX renders it with a Greek word for forgetfulness, confirming this sense of total erasure from memory. Its single occurrence in a deeply personal lament psalm gives it a haunting, poetic weight.
caution: This word is a hapax legomenon — appearing only once in the entire Hebrew Old Testament — so its precise nuance cannot be confirmed by comparison with other contexts.

definition: A term for the shameful disgrace or scornful whispering that arises from public mockery by hostile onlookers.
article: This rare word appears only once in the Old Testament, at Exodus 32:25, where Aaron's failure to restrain the people left them exposed to mockery among their enemies. Strong's connects it to scornful whispering by hostile spectators — the kind of shame that comes not just from wrongdoing but from being seen and ridiculed for it. The KJV simply renders it 'shame,' which captures the social disgrace but loses the nuance of contemptuous murmuring implied by the root.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon — occurring only once in the entire Old Testament — so its precise meaning and nuance cannot be confirmed by comparison with other biblical uses.

definition: A cover or concealed place, whether literal shelter, secret location, or hidden action done in secret.
article: סָ֫תֶר refers to anything covered, hidden, or secret — from a literal refuge or shelter to a covert deed done out of sight. Its 36 occurrences spread across poetry (Psalms, Job, Proverbs) and prose (Deuteronomy, Jeremiah, 1 Samuel), giving it both elevated metaphorical uses (God as a hiding place in Psalms) and practical legal ones (Deuteronomy's curses on those who act 'secretly'). The LXX most often renders it with κρυφῆ ('in secret, covertly') and λάθρα ('secretly, stealthily'), confirming that ancient readers understood the dominant sense as concealment or hidden action rather than mere physical shelter. The KJV range — from 'hiding place' and 'covert' to 'privily' and 'backbiting' — reflects this breadth well.
caution: The moderate confidence rating likely reflects a few difficult passages, including Deuteronomy 32:38 where the feminine form צִתְרָה appears, and one LXX rendering as αὔριον ('tomorrow') which is anomalous and may reflect a different Vorlage or scribal variant.

definition: Paruach, a personal name meaning 'blossomed,' borne by the father of one of Solomon's district officers.
article: Paruach is a proper name appearing once in the Old Testament, in 1 Kings 4:17, where it identifies the father of Jehoshaphat, one of Solomon's twelve administrative officers. The name derives from the root meaning 'to blossom or sprout,' so it carries the sense of 'blossomed one.' Because the word functions solely as a personal name in its single occurrence, its semantic range is effectively limited to that identification.
caution: With only one occurrence and no LXX translation evidence provided, nothing can be confirmed about this name beyond its single use as a patronym in 1 Kings 4:17.

definition: To do, make, or work something — especially as a sustained, deliberate, or habitual practice rather than a one-time act.
article: פָּעַל carries the sense of purposeful, ongoing action — doing or making something with intention and regularity. It appears 56 times across 11 books, but clusters heavily in poetry: Psalms alone accounts for 26 occurrences and Job adds 11, suggesting the word favors elevated, reflective contexts. The LXX most often renders it with ἐργάζομαι (15 times), the Greek word for working or laboring, which captures both the effortful and habitual dimensions of the Hebrew. The full KJV range — do, make, commit, work — confirms that the root covers both creative making and moral performing, so context must determine whether someone is crafting something or habitually committing an act, often evil.
caution: The moderate confidence rating likely reflects some difficulty distinguishing פָּעַל from synonyms like עָשָׂה (do/make) in specific contexts, though the core meaning is not seriously disputed.

definition: Zerubbabel, a Jewish leader who returned from Babylon and oversaw the rebuilding of the Jerusalem temple after the exile.
article: Zerubbabel is a personal name belonging to a prominent Jewish governor who led the first wave of exiles returning from Babylon to Jerusalem. He appears 21 times across 5 books, concentrated most heavily in Haggai (7×) and Ezra (5×), where he plays a central role in the temple reconstruction project. The LXX consistently renders his name as Ζοροβάβελ, showing that ancient Greek-speaking readers recognized him as a well-defined historical figure. Strong's connects the name to the idea of being born or descended in Babylon, reflecting his origins in the exile period.
caution: The etymology connecting the name to a Hebrew-Babylonian compound is plausible but not certain, and scholarly opinion on the precise derivation remains divided.

definition: A place name in ancient Canaan, referring to one or two locations associated with the cities of the plain.
article: Tseboim appears 8 times across Genesis, Deuteronomy, and Hosea, always as a proper place name. In Genesis 14 it refers to one of the cities of the plain destroyed along with Sodom and Gomorrah, while Deuteronomy and Hosea may reference a different settlement. The name appears to derive from a word meaning gazelles, though in the text it functions purely as a geographic identifier. The KJV renders it consistently as Zeboiim or Zeboim depending on the context.
caution: The low confidence tier and dual spellings suggest uncertainty about whether all occurrences refer to the same location, and scholarly opinion is divided on the precise identification of these sites.

definition: The grape, whether as a cluster on the vine or as harvested fruit used for wine and food.
