The LXX most often renders it with μήν, a Greek particle of strong affirmation, suggesting ancient readers heard its emphatic sense as primary.
caution: Confidence is rated low, and Strong's notes it is 'apparently a variation' of a related particle, meaning the root and precise semantic boundaries remain uncertain among scholars.

definition: A personal name referring to one or two Israelite men mentioned in the genealogies of Benjamin.
article: Rapha (or Raphah) is a proper name appearing twice in 1 Chronicles, both times within the genealogical records of the tribe of Benjamin. Strong's connects it to the Hebrew root meaning 'giant,' suggesting the name may carry that sense, though it functions here purely as a personal name. The word occurs in no other book of the Old Testament.
caution: Confidence is low: the name appears only twice, both in a single chapter cluster of Chronicles genealogies, and whether it refers to one individual or two distinct men named Rapha is unclear from the text.

definition: A fixed appointment — a set time, sacred festival, or the assembly that gathers at an appointed place — with emphasis on something officially designated in advance.
article: מוֹעֵד covers the idea of something deliberately scheduled: a date on the calendar, a recurring festival, or the community that convenes at a designated location. Its enormous frequency in Numbers, Leviticus, and Exodus reflects its technical role in Israel's worship calendar and the phrase 'tent of meeting' (אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד). The LXX's dominant choice, μαρτύριον ('testimony'), is striking — ancient translators apparently understood the meeting-tent as a place of witness or covenant encounter rather than simply a gathering spot, which shaped how the NT world read the concept. With 223 occurrences across 26 books, this is one of the most institutionally loaded terms in the Hebrew Bible.

definition: A proper name used for at least three different women and one place in the Old Testament narrative.
article: תָּמָר (Tamar) appears 25 times across 6 books, functioning as a proper name throughout. The most prominent bearers are the Tamar of Genesis 38 (Judah's daughter-in-law), and the Tamar who was David's daughter (heavily attested in 2 Samuel with 14 occurrences). A third Tamar appears as Absalom's daughter in 2 Samuel as well, and a place by this name is mentioned in Ezekiel. The LXX consistently renders the name as Θάμαρ, a straightforward transliteration, confirming that ancient readers understood it purely as a proper name with no attempt to translate an underlying meaning.
caution: The moderate confidence tier likely reflects uncertainty about whether all occurrences refer to distinct individuals or places; the Strong's definition notes the lemma is 'the same as' a common noun (meaning 'palm tree'), but the digest does not supply evidence for that underlying sense here.

definition: Adalia, one of the ten sons of Haman who were killed by the Jews in Persia.
article: Adalia is a Persian personal name appearing only once in the Old Testament, in Esther 9:8, as one of Haman's ten sons slain during the Jewish defense authorized by King Ahasuerus. The name is of Persian derivation, though its exact meaning is unknown. Because it is a proper name with a single occurrence, its only function is identification within the narrative of Esther.
caution: The Persian etymology is unresolved, and the name's original meaning cannot be determined from available evidence.

definition: Sharp points or spikes, referring to an extremely jagged or pointed surface.
article: This rare noun appears only once in the entire Old Testament, in Job 41:22, where it describes the sharp points on the underside of Leviathan — the fearsome creature whose body is portrayed as bristling with deadly spikes. The word derives from a root meaning sharpness or keenness, and the KJV simply renders it

definition: A personal name meaning 'captive of God' or 'returned to God,' borne by two Israelites in the Levitical genealogies.
article: Shebuel (also spelled Shubael) is a proper name appearing 6 times, all within the book of 1 Chronicles, where it identifies two different Levitical figures connected to David's organization of temple worship. One Shebuel was a descendant of Moses assigned over the temple treasuries, and another appears among the sons of Heman in the musical guilds. The KJV itself uses both spellings interchangeably, reflecting a genuine variation in the underlying Hebrew name.
caution: The root meaning is uncertain — the name may derive from a verb meaning 'to be taken captive' (שָׁבָה) or 'to return' (שׁוּב) combined with אֵל ('God'), giving two quite different senses, and scholars do not agree which root is original.

definition: A slender, swift-moving animal, exact species uncertain, mentioned once in a list of stately creatures in Proverbs 30.
article: This word appears only once in the entire Old Testament, in Proverbs 30:31, where it is listed among creatures that move with regal bearing. The KJV renders it 'greyhound,' following the idea of a tightly girt, slender creature built for speed, but the ancient Greek translators were themselves uncertain — the LXX offers 'rooster' (ἀλέκτωρ) as one rendering, suggesting even early translators were guessing. The root idea seems to point to something lean-waisted and swift, but no firm identification of the animal is possible from the text alone.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon — occurring only once in the OT — and both ancient and modern translators disagree significantly on which animal is meant, with proposals including greyhound, rooster, warhorse, and zebra.

definition: To cut or chop something into pieces, used specifically of splitting animal carcasses in two.
article: This rare verb appears only twice in the Old Testament, both occurrences in Genesis 15:10, describing Abram cutting the animals in half during the covenant-making ceremony. The Greek Septuagint consistently renders it with διαιρέω, meaning to divide or separate, confirming that the core idea is splitting something into distinct portions. The word is extremely narrow in its attested usage, functioning as a technical term for bisecting sacrificial animals.
caution: With only 2 occurrences in a single verse, the full semantic range of this root cannot be confidently established beyond this one specific ritual context.

definition: A personal name meaning 'ornament of God,' borne by three distinct Israelites in Chronicles.
article: Adiel (עֲדִיאֵל) is a proper name appearing all 3 of its Old Testament occurrences in the single book of 1 Chronicles. It identifies three different individuals: a leader from the tribe of Simeon (1 Chr 4:36), an ancestor of a priest who returned to Jerusalem (1 Chr 9:12), and the father of Azmaveth, who oversaw David's royal treasuries (1 Chr 27:25). The KJV consistently renders it simply as 'Adiel,' with no variation, as is typical for personal names.
caution: The name's meaning ('ornament of God') rests on a compound analysis of the root עֶדִי (ornament) and אֵל (God), but with only 3 occurrences all in one book, there is limited contextual evidence to confirm or nuance this etymology.

definition: A structural beam or girder that connects and supports parts of a building.
article: This word refers to a load-bearing timber or girder used in construction. It appears only once in the entire Old Testament, in Habakkuk 2:11, where the stone of a wall and the beam of a house's timber-work cry out against the violence of the one who built wrongly. The KJV renders it simply as 'beam,' which captures its architectural function well.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon — appearing only once in the entire Hebrew Bible — so its precise meaning rests on the word's root meaning ('to connect') and context rather than broad usage.

definition: A proper name referring to two distinct individuals — one Assyrian, one Israelite — both mentioned briefly in the Old Testament.
article: Sharezer is a personal name of foreign (likely Assyrian) origin, used for two different men in the Hebrew Bible. The first appears in 2 Kings 19:37 and Isaiah 37:38 as a son of the Assyrian king Sennacherib who, along with his brother Adrammelech, assassinated his father. The second appears in Zechariah 7:2 as someone sent to inquire of the priests in Jerusalem. The KJV consistently renders the name as 'Sharezer' across all four occurrences.
caution: The name is of foreign derivation and its precise linguistic origin is uncertain; Strong's labels it simply 'foreign' without further analysis, and scholarly reconstruction of the underlying Assyrian form carries some uncertainty.

definition: A fine white linen fabric, used for luxurious or royal textiles.
article: This noun refers to white linen, appearing only twice in the book of Esther — both times in descriptions of royal luxury (Est 1:6; 8:15). Its range is quite narrow: it denotes a specific fine textile associated with the Persian court. The LXX consistently renders it as βύσσινος, the Greek word for fine byssus linen, confirming that ancient translators understood it as a high-quality cloth rather than simply a color term.
caution: With only 2 occurrences confined to a single book and a low-confidence tier, the precise nuance of this word — whether it emphasizes the whiteness, the fineness of the weave, or both — cannot be determined with certainty.

definition: One who despises or shows contempt, used as a participle describing those who scorn with hostility.
article: שָׁאט appears only 3 times in the Old Testament, and all three occurrences are in the book of Ezekiel, always functioning as a participle meaning 'one who despises' or 'those who despise.' The word describes neighbors or surrounding peoples who treat Israel with open scorn and contempt. The Septuagint renders it with ἀτιμάζω in two instances, a Greek word meaning 'to dishonor' or 'to treat with contempt,' confirming that ancient translators understood the core sense as active, hostile disregard. Its concentration in Ezekiel's oracles of judgment gives it a sharp, confrontational tone.
caution: This word is extremely rare — only 3 occurrences in a single book — and Strong's notes it as related to the root סוּט, making its precise derivation uncertain; confidence in the exact lexical form is low.

definition: A small creeping reptile or creature, mentioned once in Leviticus among animals declared ritually unclean.
article: This word appears only once in the entire Old Testament, in Leviticus 11:30, within a list of small creatures declared ritually unclean. The KJV renders it 'snail,' but the root meaning suggests something that lies low or creeps, which points more toward a lizard than a snail. Identifying the precise species from this single occurrence is genuinely difficult, and modern translations vary widely on what creature is intended.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon with no LXX translation evidence provided, and the KJV gloss 'snail' is widely questioned — the exact creature cannot be identified with confidence.

definition: To shoot, as with arrows — a rare verb used in archaic and poetic contexts.
article: This verb appears only twice in the Old Testament, once in Genesis and once in Psalms, making it extremely rare. Its core meaning is to shoot, specifically in the context of archery, as in Genesis 49:23 where archers attack Joseph. The Septuagint translators struggled with this word, rendering it with four very different Greek words across its two occurrences — a sign that even ancient readers found it difficult to pin down.
caution: With only 2 occurrences and highly inconsistent LXX translations, the meaning is uncertain; Strong's notes it may overlap with a separate root רָבַב, and the confidence tier is explicitly marked low.

definition: To fasten a belt or girdle around oneself or another, especially to prepare for battle, work, or priestly service.
senseLabels: Girding on a belt or armor
article: חָגַר means to gird — to wrap or fasten a belt, sword, or armor around the waist, often as an act of preparation. It appears 44 times across 16 books, with concentration in narrative books like Samuel and Kings (where warriors gird on weapons) and in Leviticus and Exodus (where priests are girded with sashes as part of their ordination). The LXX almost exclusively uses forms of the Greek word περιζώννυμι, meaning 'to gird around,' which confirms the ancient translators understood the word as a concrete act of fastening something around the body. The KJV gloss 'be afraid' is an outlier that likely reflects an idiom rather than a separate root sense.
caution: The KJV gloss 'be afraid' is puzzling and its connection to this root is not fully explained by the digest, suggesting some uncertainty about at least one occurrence.

definition: A large, strong tree—likely an oak or terebinth—often used as a landmark or sacred site marker in narrative texts.
article: This word refers to a prominent, sturdy tree—most likely an oak or similar large tree—that served as a recognizable landmark in ancient Canaan. It appears all 9 times in narrative prose, never in poetry, and nearly always in connection with specific places: the plain or tree of Moreh, Mamre, and other named sites. The KJV translates it simply as
caution: ,which may reflect a flat clearing associated with a grove, but the Septuagint's use of ἔχω ("to have/hold") offers little help in clarifying the precise species, leaving the exact tree identification uncertain."caution":"The LXX translation with ἔχω is puzzling and unhelpful for identifying the tree species, and scholars continue to debate whether this word denotes an oak specifically or a broader category of large, sacred trees; confidence is low.

definition: Dyed or colored cloth, referring to fabric that has been dipped in coloring matter.
article: This rare noun appears only 3 times in the Old Testament, and all three occurrences are clustered in a single verse — Judges 5:30 — within the ancient victory song of Deborah. The context describes the spoils of war that enemy soldiers were expected to bring home, including embroidered or dyed garments. Strong's connects the word to an unused root meaning "to dip," which fits the ancient process of dyeing cloth by immersing it in coloring fluid. The word's restriction to this one poetic passage means its full semantic range cannot be established with confidence.
caution: With only 3 occurrences all in a single verse of archaic poetry, and the root itself marked as unused elsewhere, the precise meaning rests on limited evidence and the word should be treated as a near-hapax.

definition: A personal name identifying the father of the prophet Joel in the opening verse of that book.
article: Pethuel appears exactly once in the Old Testament, in Joel 1:1, solely to identify Joel's father. It is a proper noun and functions only as a patronymic. The name is rendered directly as 'Pethuel' in both the KJV and the LXX, with no interpretive translation attempted.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon — appearing only once in the entire OT — so nothing further can be said about the person or the name's usage beyond this single occurrence.

definition: To interlace or cross back and forth, describing a swift, winding movement or path.
article: This rare verb appears only once in the Old Testament, in Jeremiah 2:23, where it describes the swift darting movements of a young camel crossing the desert — capturing the image of a creature weaving and traversing unpredictably. The Piel stem suggests an intensive or repeated action, reinforcing the sense of back-and-forth interlacing motion rather than a single crossing. The KJV renders it 'traverse,' which catches the directional sense but loses the woven, interlacing quality that Strong's definition preserves.
caution: This word is a hapax legomenon, appearing only once in the entire Hebrew Bible, so its full semantic range cannot be confirmed and the precise nuance remains uncertain.

definition: A proper name referring to a chief or leader of Edom, listed in genealogical records.
article: Iram is a proper name appearing exactly twice in the Old Testament — once in Genesis 36:43 and once in its parallel in 1 Chronicles 1:54 — both in lists of Edomite chiefs descended from Esau. The KJV consistently renders it simply as 'Iram,' offering no translation. Strong's connects the name to the root for 'city,' suggesting a meaning like 'city-wise,' though this etymology is not reflected in any translation.
caution: With only 2 occurrences in parallel genealogical lists, this is effectively a hapax in terms of meaningful context, and the proposed etymology from the word for 'city' remains uncertain and unverifiable from usage alone.

definition: A personal name referring to an individual Israelite mentioned in a genealogical list in Chronicles.
article: Temeni is a proper name appearing once in the Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 4:6, as part of a genealogical record of the tribe of Judah. The KJV simply transliterates it as "Temeni," and it is never translated with a common noun. Strong's suggests it is probably a variant of the related name Temani, though the exact connection is uncertain.
caution: This word occurs only once in the entire Old Testament (a hapax legomenon in genealogical context), making its meaning and etymology difficult to verify with confidence.

definition: A water plant (rush or bulrush) growing in marshy ground, sometimes referring to a rope or hook made from such plants.
article: This rare word appears only 5 times, split between Isaiah (3×) and Job (2×), and its meaning is genuinely contested. The core sense seems to involve the rush plant that grows in marshy ground, and by extension products made from it — a twisted rope of rushes, or perhaps a hook or ring. Isaiah uses it in figurative contrasts between 'head and tail' or 'palm branch and rush,' suggesting a lowly plant, while Job's usage may point more toward a physical fastening. The KJV renders it four different ways — bulrush, caldron, hook, and rush — which itself signals how uncertain ancient translators were.
caution: Confidence is rated low: the word has only 5 occurrences, scholars disagree on whether the 'hook' and 'caldron' senses reflect the same root, and translation choices vary significantly even among ancient versions.

definition: An adjective describing vegetation as densely interwoven or thickly branched, used of leafy trees and branches.
article: עָבֹת describes something that is thickly intertwined or densely leafed — specifically applied to tree branches and boughs. It appears only 4 times across 3 books (Leviticus, Nehemiah, and Ezekiel), always as an adjective modifying vegetation. The KJV consistently renders it 'thick,' and the LXX mostly uses κλάδος ('branch' or 'bough'), confirming the word's tight connection to dense, leafy plant growth rather than any abstract sense of thickness.
caution: Confidence is rated low, and with only 4 occurrences the semantic range is very narrow; one LXX rendering (σημαίνω, 'to signal') is puzzling and may reflect a different Hebrew reading or a translator's interpretive choice, introducing some uncertainty.

definition: An Aramaic verb meaning to divide or split, used once in Daniel's vision of the statue.
article: This Aramaic verb appears only once in the Old Testament, in Daniel 2:41, where it describes the divided nature of the iron-and-clay kingdom in Nebuchadnezzar's dream. The KJV renders it simply as 'divided,' and the word carries no broader attested range in the Hebrew Bible beyond this single use. Its extreme rarity makes it impossible to establish a wider semantic profile from biblical evidence alone.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon in an Aramaic passage with only one attestation, so its full range of meaning cannot be reliably determined from biblical usage.

definition: To willingly consent or undertake something, agreeing to do or begin an action of one's own volition.
article: יָאַל describes the act of agreeing or willingly deciding to do something — the moment a person consents and steps forward to take action. All 12 verbal occurrences appear in the Hiphil stem, which here carries a causative-reflexive nuance best understood as 'bringing oneself to do' something. The KJV renders it in varied ways — 'be content,' 'please,' 'would,' 'willingly' — but the common thread is voluntary, self-motivated assent. Interestingly, the Septuagint most often chose ἄρχω, meaning 'to begin' or 'to take the lead,' suggesting ancient readers heard in this word not just consent but the decisive move to initiate action.
caution: The root's precise derivation is uncertain — Strong's notes it may be related to a root meaning mental weakness or yielding — and scholarly confidence in the etymology is low.

definition: An Aramaic verb meaning to be fragile or broken, used figuratively of weakness or division.
article: This is an Aramaic verb, not standard Biblical Hebrew, appearing only once in the Old Testament — in Daniel 2:42. There it describes the kingdom symbolized by the statue's feet of iron mixed with clay: partly strong, partly fragile or broken. The KJV renders it simply as 'broken,' capturing the figurative sense of structural weakness or division rather than physical shattering.
caution: This word appears only once in the entire Old Testament (a hapax in Aramaic Daniel), so its full semantic range cannot be established from biblical usage alone.

definition: An Aramaic word meaning 'the poor' or 'poor people,' used as a noun in the book of Daniel.
article: This Aramaic term appears only once in the Old Testament, in Daniel 4:24, where it refers to poor or needy people. The KJV consistently renders it as 'poor,' and its meaning in context is straightforward. The LXX evidence does not add significant nuance here, but the word fits naturally within the Aramaic sections of Daniel, where the language shifts from Hebrew to Aramaic for extended passages.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon in the Old Testament, appearing only in Daniel 4:24, and as an Aramaic loanword its Hebrew cognate connections are limited, leaving some uncertainty about its full semantic range.

definition: A proper name used for several different people and one place in the Old Testament.
article: Elah is a proper name appearing 16 times across five books — Genesis, 1 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, and 1 Chronicles. It refers to at least one Edomite chief, several Israelite individuals (including a king of Israel), and a valley in Palestine famously associated with David's battle with Goliath (1 Samuel 17). The KJV consistently renders it simply as 'Elah,' and the LXX similarly treats it as a transliterated proper noun, offering no interpretive Greek equivalent.
caution: Strong's links this name to the Hebrew word for a terebinth tree (also H424/H425), but the digest does not provide evidence to confirm or develop that connection, so the etymology must remain uncertain here.

definition: A personal name identifying the father of the prophet Ezekiel.
article: Buzi appears only once in the Old Testament, in Ezekiel 1:3, where Ezekiel is identified as 'the son of Buzi.' The name designates an Israelite man, almost certainly a priest given the context of that verse. Beyond serving as a paternal identifier for the prophet, nothing else is recorded about Buzi in the Hebrew Bible.
caution: Buzi appears only this single time in the OT, so virtually nothing can be known about the person or the name's meaning from biblical evidence alone.

definition: A covering or cloth used to wrap and protect sacred objects during transport.
article: כְּסוּי refers to a covering used to protect objects, appearing only twice in the Old Testament, both in Numbers 4 where the Israelites are given instructions for transporting the tabernacle's sacred items. The word is a passive participle of the root כָּסָה (to cover), so it literally means 'that which is covered' or 'a covering.' Interestingly, the LXX renders it with πορφυροῦς, meaning 'purple,' suggesting the translators focused on the specific color of the cloth rather than the abstract function — a reminder that these coverings were richly colored materials.
caution: With only 2 occurrences in a single book, the full semantic range of this word is difficult to establish with confidence.

definition: A personal name belonging to one of David's mighty warriors, a man from Hushah.
article: Sibbecai (also spelled Sibbechai in some English Bibles) is the name of an Israelite warrior who served under King David. He appears 4 times across 2 Samuel and 1 Chronicles, consistently identified as a member of David's elite fighters known as the Mighty Men. He is notably credited with killing a Philistine giant, and in 1 Chronicles 27 he is listed as a military commander. The KJV renders the name as both 'Sibbecai' and 'Sibbechai,' reflecting a minor spelling variation across manuscripts.
caution: Strong's links this name to the root סָבַך meaning a thicket or copse, but name etymologies in Hebrew are often uncertain and the connection carries low confidence.

definition: A person who has escaped from battle, disaster, or destruction — a survivor or refugee who got away.
article: פָּלִיט describes someone who has fled and survived a catastrophic event, most often a military defeat or massacre. The word appears 24 times across 11 books, with its heaviest use in Jeremiah (6×) and Ezekiel (7×), where it frequently describes the handful of survivors left after God's judgment falls on a nation. The LXX most often renders it with διασώζω, meaning

definition: A proper name identifying a king of Judah and, once, a Levite in the Old Testament.
article: Asa is a personal name used 58 times across 4 books, referring almost entirely to Asa king of Judah, whose reign is chronicled extensively in both 1 Kings (26 times) and 2 Chronicles (29 times). A single occurrence in 1 Chronicles refers to a Levite. The LXX consistently renders the name as Ἀσά, a straightforward transliteration, confirming it was treated as a proper name rather than a meaningful Hebrew word by ancient translators.
caution: The derivation and original meaning of the name are uncertain, as Strong's notes, so no underlying Hebrew sense can be confidently assigned.

definition: A choice or principal grapevine, used once in a poetic lament over a vine-rich region.
article: שְׂרוּקֵּי appears only once in the Old Testament, in Isaiah 16:8, within a lament over the destruction of Moab's famous vineyards. It is a passive participle form related to the root behind שֹׂרֵק, which denotes a choice or high-quality vine. The KJV renders it 'principal plant,' capturing the sense of a prized, cultivated grapevine. Its single occurrence in a poetic, elegiac passage suggests it carries an elevated register fitting the lament genre.
caution: This word occurs only once in the entire Old Testament (a hapax legomenon), making its precise meaning difficult to confirm independently; the definition relies heavily on its relationship to the related root שֹׂרֵק.

definition: To cry out or wail loudly, as in an anguished or desperate outcry.
article: יָבַב means to cry out with a loud, anguished voice. It appears only once in the Old Testament, in Judges 5:28, where it describes the crying out associated with desperate waiting and anxiety. The LXX renders it with μεταστρέφω, which normally means 'to turn around,' a surprisingly different choice that suggests ancient translators may have understood the gesture of turning in distress as part of the scene.
caution: This word is a hapax legomenon, occurring only once in the entire Hebrew Bible, so its precise meaning rests on very thin evidence.

definition: A personal name meaning 'formative' or 'creative,' belonging to an Israelite musician in David's temple organization.
article: Yitsri is a proper name appearing once in the Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 25:11, where it designates one of the Levitical musicians appointed by David for temple worship. The name derives from the root יָצַר, meaning to form or shape, giving it the sense of 'formative' or 'one who forms.' Because it occurs only in a genealogical-musical list, nothing further about the individual's life or role is recorded beyond this single mention.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon appearing only once in a genealogical list, so nothing can be confirmed about the name's usage beyond this single occurrence.

definition: To move away or withdraw from a place or position, whether departing, ceasing, or being removed by another.
article: מוּשׁ means to withdraw or move away — the core idea is separation from a location or state. In the Qal stem (15 occurrences) it is typically intransitive: something or someone departs or ceases, as when the pillar of cloud did not depart from Israel (Exo 13:22) or the book of the law should not depart from one's mouth (Jos 1:8). The Hiphil stem (4 occurrences) shifts to a causative sense — someone actively removes or takes something away. The LXX most often chose κινέω, 'to move or set in motion,' which captures the physical displacement at the heart of the word, though a couple of unusual renderings suggest the translators occasionally struggled to find the right Greek equivalent.
caution: The moderate confidence tier and Strong's note that this root may overlap with another identical-looking root (also מוּשׁ) suggest some uncertainty about whether all 21 occurrences truly belong to a single root.

definition: To scatter or disperse something, whether spreading it out generously or breaking it apart in a hostile sense.
article: פָּזַר describes the act of scattering, and its tone depends entirely on context — it can picture someone generously distributing gifts (Psalm 112:9, where a righteous person scatters to the poor) or the violent breaking apart of enemies (Psalm 89:11). The word appears 10 times and is concentrated heavily in poetry, especially Psalms (5 times), which suggests an elevated or vivid register rather than plain administrative language. The Piel stem, the most active and intensive form, accounts for 6 of the 9 verbal uses, emphasizing that this is not a gentle dispersal but a deliberate, forceful scattering in either direction. The LXX translation choices are unusually varied and do not map neatly to a single Greek concept, which reflects genuine breadth in the Hebrew root.
caution: Confidence is rated low, and the LXX renders this word with three unrelated Greek terms across just a few instances, suggesting ancient translators themselves found the word's range difficult to pin down consistently.

definition: A state of being taken captive, or collectively the people and goods seized in war — covering both the condition of exile and the captives or plunder itself.
article: שֶׁבִי refers to the condition of captivity, the captives themselves, or the spoil taken in war — a breadth typical of Hebrew nouns that cover an entire situation rather than one slice of it. It appears 48 times across 16 books, with the heaviest concentration in Jeremiah (10×), reflecting that prophet's intense focus on Babylon's deportation of Israel. The LXX translators rendered it as αἰχμαλωσία ('captivity') 31 times out of 34 renderings, showing that ancient readers heard the dominant sense as the condition or collective experience of being taken prisoner rather than physical plunder.
caution: The extension to 'booty' is attested in KJV glosses and Strong's but is a secondary sense, and the boundary between 'captives' and 'plunder' is not always sharp in the text, leaving some passages mildly ambiguous.

definition: Deep darkness or thick gloom, used both of literal blackness and of misfortune and hopeless confusion.
article: This word describes an especially dense or oppressive darkness — not just the absence of light but a heavy, enveloping blackness. It appears in vivid contexts like the Egyptian plague of darkness (Exodus 10:22) and the proverbial 'way of the wicked' being like deep darkness where one stumbles without knowing why (Proverbs 4:19). The LXX translators reached for two different Greek words — σκότος (ordinary darkness) and γνόφος (thick, stormy gloom) — suggesting ancient readers felt the word carried extra weight beyond simple nighttime dark. Its concentration in prophetic and wisdom literature gives it a distinctly elevated, often threatening tone.
caution: The low confidence tier and the LXX rendering τότε ('then') in two instances — apparently reading the word differently or working from a variant text — introduces genuine uncertainty about the word's precise form or meaning in those passages.

definition: To weigh or measure by suspending in a balance, used once in a context of comparison or evaluation.
article: סָלָא appears only once in the entire Old Testament, in Lamentations 4:2, where it describes an act of weighing or comparing — much like placing something on a scale to assess its worth. Strong's connects it to the idea of suspending something in a balance, which fits a context of valuing or reckoning. Interestingly, the Septuagint translators chose the Greek word κεραμεύς, meaning 'potter,' which suggests they may have read the passage quite differently — pointing to real uncertainty in how ancient readers understood this rare word. The KJV rendered it simply as 'compare,' capturing the evaluative sense without the literal weighing imagery.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon — occurring only once in the OT — and the LXX's divergent rendering (κεραμεύς, 'potter') signals that even ancient translators were uncertain about its meaning, making any definition provisional.

definition: To hide or conceal something, and in its stronger uses, to destroy or cut off completely.
article: כָּחַד covers two related ideas: keeping something secret or hidden, and — especially in the intensive Piel stem — wiping something out entirely. The Niphal (passive) form typically means 'to be hidden' or 'to be concealed,' while the Piel pushes toward destruction or complete removal. The word appears 32 times across 13 books, with its heaviest concentration in Job (7×) and Psalms (5×), suggesting it carries some weight in poetic and wisdom contexts. The LXX translators struggled to find a single Greek equivalent, which itself signals how broad the Hebrew root's range is.
caution: The LXX renderings here are unusually scattered and do not clearly map to the Hebrew senses, making the ancient translators' understanding difficult to assess with confidence.

definition: To drip or leak through, used of a dripping roof and of a soul dissolving in grief.
article: This verb describes the slow, persistent dripping of liquid — most concretely, a roof leaking in Ecclesiastes 10:18, where laziness leads to a house that 'drops through.' In Psalm 119:28 the same word describes a soul 'melting' or 'dropping' with sorrow, showing how naturally Hebrew extends a physical image into emotional language. All three occurrences are in the Qal stem and appear in poetic or wisdom literature, which fits the word's vivid, image-driven quality.
caution: With only 3 occurrences across the entire Old Testament and no strong LXX translation pattern provided, the precise nuance in each context carries genuine uncertainty.

definition: A Hebrew personal name meaning 'Yahweh has promised' or 'Yahweh has said,' borne by several Israelite men in the Old Testament.
article: Amariah is a personal name appearing 16 times across 5 books, concentrated heavily in 1 Chronicles (7 times) and Nehemiah (4 times), where genealogical and post-exilic community lists are common. The name combines the Hebrew root for 'said' or 'promised' with the divine name Yah, giving it the sense 'Yahweh has said' or 'Yahweh has promised.' It belongs to at least nine different individuals in the Old Testament, including priests, Levites, and community members mentioned in Ezra and Nehemiah. The KJV consistently renders it simply as Amariah, with no variation.
caution: The confidence tier for this entry is marked low, and the exact nuance of the name's meaning — whether 'Yahweh has said' or 'Yahweh has promised' — cannot be determined with certainty from the root alone.

definition: A foul stench or putrid smell, typically from rotting corpses or decaying matter.
article: בְּאֹשׁ refers to a powerful, offensive odor associated with decay and death. It appears only 3 times in the Old Testament, each time in a prophetic book — Isaiah, Joel, and Amos — and always in contexts of divine judgment involving masses of unburied dead. The KJV consistently renders it 'stink,' and its use is limited to these vivid prophetic scenes of catastrophe. Notably, the LXX translators chose βρέχω (meaning 'to rain' or 'to wet') in one instance, an unusual choice that suggests some ancient uncertainty about the word's precise sense.
caution: This word occurs only 3 times and solely in prophetic literature, its root derivation is uncertain, and the unexpected LXX rendering of βρέχω points to genuine ambiguity in the ancient transmission — confidence in the exact nuance is low.

definition: A Geshurite — a member or the collective people of Geshur, a territory bordering Israel.
article: Geshurite refers to the inhabitants of Geshur, a region that appears in boundary descriptions and conquest accounts. The word appears 6 times across Deuteronomy, Joshua, and 1 Samuel, mostly in Joshua's territorial lists. Notably, the Septuagint twice renders this word as Χανααναῖος ("Canaanite"), suggesting ancient translators sometimes grouped the Geshurites broadly among Canaan's peoples rather than treating them as a wholly distinct nation.
caution: Confidence is low, likely because the location of Geshur itself is debated — the name may refer to more than one distinct region in the Old Testament, making precise identification of the people uncertain.

definition: A joining point or coupling edge where two sections of the tabernacle curtains were fastened together.
article: This word appears all 4 times in a single context: the construction instructions for the tabernacle in Exodus 26 and 36, describing where curtain panels were joined together at their edges. As a feminine active participle of the root meaning 'to join or couple,' it refers to the physical edge or junction of one curtain set that meets and connects to another. The LXX translations are notably inconsistent — rendering the word as 'outer,' 'sardius,' and 'topaz' across its occurrences — suggesting the ancient Greek translators themselves struggled with this technical architectural term.
caution: Confidence is low: the LXX translations are wildly inconsistent and unhelpful, indicating even ancient readers were uncertain about this specialized tabernacle-construction term.

definition: Ceasing or destitute — describing someone who has stopped, is failing, or is utterly lacking in vitality or standing.
article: This adjective comes from the root meaning to cease or stop, and it describes someone who is vacant or destitute — drained of life, ignored, or cut off. Its three occurrences span poetry and prophecy: Psalm 39 uses it of human frailty, Isaiah 53 applies it to the suffering servant as one despised and rejected, and Ezekiel 3 uses it of those who refuse to hear. The LXX renders it with widely varying Greek words — including one meaning 'disobedience' and one meaning 'madness' — suggesting ancient translators found the word genuinely difficult to pin down.
caution: With only 3 occurrences and a notably inconsistent LXX rendering, the precise nuance of this adjective is uncertain and scholarly confidence is low.

definition: The moon, named for its whiteness or brightness, appearing in poetic and prophetic contexts.
article: לְבָנָה means 'the moon,' derived from the root meaning 'white' — a fitting name for the moon's pale glow. It appears only 3 times in the Old Testament, all in poetic or prophetic passages: once in Song of Solomon and twice in Isaiah. The LXX consistently renders it as σελήνη, the standard Greek word for the moon, confirming there was no ambiguity for ancient translators. Isaiah uses it in striking cosmic imagery, such as the moon being put to shame when God's glory surpasses it (Isa 24:23) and the moon shining seven times brighter in the age of restoration (Isa 30:26).
caution: With only 3 occurrences, all in elevated literary contexts, the full range of this word's usage is difficult to assess with confidence.

definition: A town in the territory of Naphtali, listed among its fortified cities in Joshua 19.
article: Adamah is a proper noun referring to a specific settlement assigned to the tribe of Naphtali, mentioned once in the Old Testament at Joshua 19:36. The word shares its spelling with the common Hebrew noun for 'ground' or 'earth,' but here it functions purely as a geographic name. The LXX simply transliterates or renders it as a place name, offering no additional semantic information.
caution: Appears only once in the OT, making it a hapax in its proper-noun usage; its exact ancient location remains unidentified with certainty.

definition: A place name referring to the town of Abel-Beth-Maacah in northern Israel, associated with the rebellion of Sheba son of Bichri.
article: Beth-maacah is a proper place name meaning 'house of Maacah,' identifying a specific town in northern Israel. All 4 of its Old Testament occurrences are concentrated in 2 Samuel 20, in the account of Joab's pursuit of the rebel Sheba. The LXX rendering καταβάλλω ('to throw down') in one instance likely reflects a translator working with a difficult text rather than a distinct meaning of the place name itself.
caution: Confidence is low; the extremely narrow occurrence range (4 times, one book) and the unusual LXX translation choice suggest textual uncertainty around this name.

definition: A Persian personal name belonging to two different officials mentioned in the book of Ezra.
article: Mithredath is a Persian personal name appearing twice in the Old Testament, both times in the book of Ezra. The first occurrence (Ezra 1:8) refers to the treasurer of King Cyrus who handed over the temple vessels to Sheshbazzar, and the second (Ezra 4:7) refers to an official who co-signed a letter opposing the rebuilding of Jerusalem. The KJV consistently renders it as "Mithredath" with no attempt at translation, confirming it is treated purely as a proper name throughout.
caution: The name is of Persian origin and appears only twice in the Old Testament, both in a single book, making any broader analysis of its meaning or usage impossible from the Hebrew text alone.

definition: A skilled craftsman or expert artisan, used once in the Old Testament to describe mastery in a craft.
article: This rare noun appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Song of Solomon 7:2, where it describes the work of a skilled artisan. It derives from the same root as the word for faithfulness and firmness (אָמַן), here applied in the sense of training and expertise. The KJV renders it "cunning workman," using "cunning" in its older English sense of craftsmanship rather than trickery. The LXX evidence for this term is limited, reflecting its extreme rarity in the text.
caution: This word is a hapax legomenon, appearing only once in the entire Old Testament, which makes its precise semantic range difficult to pin down with certainty.

definition: The finest or most select of a group — whatever has been chosen as the choicest or best specimen available.
article: מִבְחָר comes from the root meaning 'to choose' and consistently points to the cream of the crop — the finest men, the best burial sites, the choicest cedars. Its range is narrow: it always singles out whatever stands at the top of a category. The LXX most often renders it ἐκλεκτός ('select, chosen'), which is the same Greek word used for 'the elect' in the New Testament, showing ancient readers heard strong connotations of deliberate selection and high quality. Its 13 occurrences are spread across prophetic and narrative literature, with Ezekiel using it most (4×), typically of elite warriors or prized possessions.
caution: The confidence tier for this word is marked low, and two LXX renderings as νεκρός ('dead/corpse') are puzzling and may reflect a difficult or corrupt Hebrew text in those passages, suggesting the meaning is not entirely settled in every context.

definition: A personal name referring to a single Israelite mentioned as the father of Jedaiah in Nehemiah's account of the wall rebuilding.
article: Charumaph (also spelled Harumaph in the KJV) is a personal name appearing exactly once in the Old Testament, in Nehemiah 3:10, where Jedaiah son of Harumaph is listed among those who repaired the Jerusalem wall. The name itself appears to be a compound meaning something like 'snub-nosed,' according to Strong's, though its bearer is otherwise completely unknown to us beyond this single mention. Because it occurs only as a proper name in one verse, its semantic content matters less than its function as an identifier within Nehemiah's careful record of the builders.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon appearing only once, and virtually nothing is known about this individual beyond the single reference in Nehemiah 3:10.

definition: A unit of measurement or proportion, used once to describe a hundredfold agricultural yield.
article: This word appears only once in the Old Testament, in Genesis 26:12, where Isaac reaps a hundredfold harvest. It derives from a root related to measuring or sectioning off a quantity. Strikingly, the ancient Greek translators (LXX) rendered it as κριθή, meaning "barley," suggesting they may have understood the passage differently — reading it as a grain type rather than a measure — which highlights genuine ambiguity in the text.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon (one occurrence only), and the LXX's divergent translation as 'barley' rather than 'measure' indicates real uncertainty about the word's precise meaning.

definition: An Aramaic word for a brief, fleeting moment of time, equivalent to what we would call an 'hour' or instant.
article: This Aramaic term appears all 5 of its Old Testament occurrences in the book of Daniel, reflecting the Aramaic sections of that book. It conveys a short, defined unit of time — translated consistently as 'hour' in the KJV — but its root meaning suggests something closer to 'a look' or a fleeting glance of time. The word's restriction to a single book and its Aramaic character set it apart from the standard Hebrew vocabulary for time.
caution: Confidence is low due to sparse attestation (only 5 occurrences in 1 book) and the reconstructed connection to a root meaning 'a look,' making the precise semantic range uncertain.

definition: A feminine noun meaning youthfulness or the state of being the youngest, referring to smallness in age.
article: This rare word appears only once in the Old Testament, in Genesis 43:33, where Joseph's brothers are seated in order from firstborn to youngest. It conveys the idea of smallness in age — essentially the quality of being young or junior in birth order. The ancient Greek translators rendered it as νεότης, meaning "youth" or "youthfulness," confirming that the sense is about age and relative youth rather than physical smallness.
caution: This word occurs only once in the entire Old Testament, making it a hapax legomenon; its meaning relies heavily on context and the LXX translation rather than broader usage patterns.

definition: An Aramaic adjective meaning 'new,' used once in the Old Testament in an Aramaic passage of Ezra.
article: This Aramaic word simply means 'new' and corresponds directly to the Hebrew adjective for the same concept. It appears only once in the entire Old Testament, in Ezra 6:4, within an Aramaic section describing building instructions for the Jerusalem temple. Because it occurs in an Aramaic administrative context rather than Hebrew poetry or prose, it carries a straightforward, practical sense with no apparent metaphorical or theological extension in the text.
caution: This word appears only once in the Old Testament (a hapax in the Aramaic portions of Ezra), so its full semantic range cannot be established from biblical usage alone.

definition: A passive participle meaning 'prepared' or 'made ready,' describing something put in a state of readiness.
article: עֲתוּדִים is the passive participle of the root עָתַד, meaning 'prepared' or 'ready.' Its single appearance in the Old Testament comes in Esther 8:13, where it describes Jews being made ready — put in a state of preparation — to defend themselves. The LXX evidence is not available for nuancing this specific form, but the underlying root carries the straightforward sense of something having been set in order in advance. The word functions as an adjective, modifying a noun to indicate a condition of readiness.
caution: This word appears only once in the entire Old Testament (a near-hapax), so its full semantic range cannot be confirmed from Hebrew usage alone.

definition: To form a marriage alliance, whether by giving a daughter in marriage or by becoming related through marriage as an in-law.
article: חָתַן covers both the act of forming a marriage bond and the resulting family relationship — it can describe the action of intermarrying as well as the status of being a son-in-law, father-in-law, or mother-in-law. The word is heavily concentrated in Exodus (15 of its 33 occurrences), largely because of the recurring relationship between Moses and his father-in-law Jethro. The Hithpael stem, used 4 times, carries a reflexive sense of entering into a marriage alliance for oneself, and Deuteronomy uses it in warnings against intermarrying with Canaanite peoples. The LXX most often chose ἐπιγαμβρεύω, a Greek word specifically meaning 'to become a son-in-law,' showing that ancient readers understood the relational bond as central.
caution: The same root serves as both a verb and the basis for multiple kinship titles (son-in-law, father-in-law, mother-in-law), which can make individual occurrences ambiguous in parsing; confidence is rated moderate.

definition: A proper name meaning 'horn of eye-paint,' given to one of Job's daughters after his restoration.
article: Keren-happuch is the name of the third daughter born to Job after God restored his fortunes (Job 42:14). The name combines the word for 'horn' (a vessel used to hold cosmetics) with a word for dark eye-paint or antimony, suggesting beauty and adornment. Both occurrences appear in the same verse, where all three daughters are named together — a literary moment emphasizing Job's full restoration. The name itself paints a vivid picture of feminine beauty in the ancient Near East.
caution: Because this is a proper name appearing only once in the narrative (twice only due to the verse's phrasing), its precise nuance is uncertain and its meaning relies on the component words rather than independent attestation.

definition: To spy out or reconnoiter a place, or to go about slandering and tale-bearing against a person.
article: רָגַל covers two related but distinct activities: secretly scouting enemy territory and maliciously spreading reports about a person. The reconnaissance sense dominates the Old Testament, appearing prominently in Genesis 42 (where Joseph's brothers are accused of being spies seven times) and in the spy narratives of Joshua and Judges. The LXX almost always renders it with κατασκοπέω or κατάσκοπος — words meaning 'to spy' or 'a spy' — confirming that ancient readers saw this as the core meaning, while the slander sense is the rarer but still attested strand behind glosses like 'backbite' and 'slander.'
caution: Confidence is moderate because the root is thought to derive from רֶגֶל ('foot'), suggesting 'going about on foot,' but the connection between the spy sense and the slander sense is not fully transparent, and scholarly discussion of whether these are one root or two remains unsettled.

definition: An Aramaic word for an official decree, order, or judicial decision issued by a royal authority.
article: This Aramaic term appears only 5 times in the Old Testament, confined to Ezra (4 times) and Daniel (1 time), always in contexts of Persian royal administration. Its core meaning is an official command or decision handed down by a king or governing authority. The Greek translators of the LXX consistently rendered it as γνώμη, meaning 'judgment' or 'opinion,' signaling that ancient readers understood it as a formal authoritative ruling rather than a mere suggestion. The KJV renders it variously as 'commandment,' 'account,' and 'matter,' reflecting how the word can describe both the act of commanding and the substance of what is decided.
caution: Confidence is rated low, likely due to the word's sparse attestation (only 5 occurrences) and its Aramaic rather than Hebrew nature, which introduces additional uncertainty about precise nuance in each context.

definition: A designated position or standing, whether a physical post of duty or an official role or office.
article: מַעֲמָד comes from the root עָמַד, meaning 'to stand,' and refers to where or how someone stands in a formal sense — either a physical post (where attendants are stationed) or an official position of responsibility. In 1 Kings 10:5 and 2 Chronicles 9:4, it describes the orderly attendance of Solomon's servants, while in 1 Chronicles 23:28 and 2 Chronicles 35:15 it points to the assigned stations of Levites in temple service. The LXX most often uses στάσις ('standing, station'), which confirms the sense of a fixed, formal post, while one instance uses οἰκονομία ('administration'), nudging toward the idea of an official office.
caution: With only 5 occurrences across 4 books, the word's full semantic range is difficult to establish with confidence, and the single LXX rendering as οἰκονομία in Isaiah 22:19 introduces some uncertainty about whether that instance carries a meaningfully different sense.

definition: A personal name belonging to a man in the genealogies of Judah in 1 Chronicles 4.
article: Eshton is a proper name appearing twice in 1 Chronicles 4 (verses 11 and 12) as part of the tribal genealogy of Judah. The KJV translates it consistently as 'Eshton' with no variation, and it appears nowhere else in the Old Testament. The name's meaning is uncertain, though Strong's tentatively connects it to a root suggesting rest or restfulness.
caution: This name appears only in a single genealogical passage in 1 Chronicles, making its meaning and background very difficult to establish with confidence.

definition: A place name meaning 'double city,' referring to two distinct locations in ancient Israel and Transjordan.
article: Kiriathaim (also spelled Kirjathaim) is a dual-form proper noun literally meaning 'double city,' appearing 8 times across 6 books. It refers to two different settlements: one in Transjordan associated with Reuben (Numbers, Joshua, 1 Chronicles) and one in Moab mentioned in prophetic oracles against that nation (Jeremiah, Ezekiel). The word's dual grammatical form — marking a pair — is built into the name itself, making the meaning transparent to Hebrew readers.
caution: Confidence is low; the precise locations of both sites remain uncertain in historical geography, and scholarly identification of the ruins is disputed.

definition: A town in the lowland territory of Judah, mentioned once in a boundary list.
article: Dilan (also spelled Dilean in older translations) appears exactly once in the Old Testament, in Joshua 15:38, as part of a list of towns in the Shephelah — the low foothills of Judah. It functions purely as a proper geographical name with no narrative description attached. Its location has not been identified with certainty by archaeologists, and the word's derivation is unknown.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon appearing only in a place-name list; its meaning, etymology, and precise location are all uncertain.

definition: The hollow or cupped part of the hand, foot, or similar concave surface, extended to mean power or control in figurative use.
article: כָּף refers primarily to the cupped, hollow part of the hand — the palm — but its range extends naturally to the sole of the foot, the paw of an animal, and even concave objects like a dish, sling-bowl, or door handle. With 195 occurrences across 30 books, it is one of the more versatile body-part words in Hebrew. The LXX most often renders it with χείρ (the ordinary Greek word for "hand," 95 times), showing that ancient translators read it as a general hand-word, though the eight renderings as ἴχνος ("footprint" or "track") confirm the sole-of-the-foot sense was also well recognized. Figuratively, the outstretched or raised palm became a natural image for power and control, much as English speakers still talk about holding something "in the palm of one's hand."

definition: A proper name referring to Javan, son of Japheth, and the people and territory associated with him, understood as the Greeks (Ionians).
article: יָוָן (Yavan) appears 11 times across 6 books, always translated in the KJV as 'Javan.' In Genesis and 1 Chronicles it names a son of Japheth in the Table of Nations, while in Ezekiel, Isaiah, and Zechariah it refers collectively to the Greeks or their territory as a trading partner or distant nation. The LXX translators rendered it as Ἕλλην ('Greek/Hellene') 4 times, which is strong evidence that ancient readers understood this as a direct reference to the Greeks — the same people Paul addresses in the New Testament as Ἕλληνες. Its appearance in Daniel (3 times) likely refers to the Greek empire, fitting the book's prophetic focus on world powers.
caution: Confidence is rated low, possibly because one LXX rendering is διαμάχομαι ('to fight against'), which is strikingly different and may reflect a variant text or a disputed passage; scholarly agreement on every occurrence is not complete.

definition: A personal name meaning 'father of goodness,' belonging to a Benjaminite man listed in a genealogy.
article: Abitub is a proper name appearing exactly once in the Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 8:11, where he is listed as a son of Shaharaim in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin. The name is composed of two elements meaning 'father' and 'goodness,' making it a typical Hebrew compound name expressing a positive quality. Because it occurs only in a genealogical list, nothing is known about the person beyond his family connections.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon — appearing only once in the entire Old Testament — so no broader usage pattern can be established.

definition: A multiplicative adverb or intensifier meaning seven times over, often expressing extreme or complete measure of punishment or return.
article: This word is a dual or intensified form of the number seven, used to express that something happens or is repaid seven times over. It appears only 6 times across 4 books — Genesis, Psalms, Proverbs, and Isaiah — and carries the force of extreme amplification, especially in contexts of vengeance or recompense. The LXX is inconsistent: it renders the word as ἑπτάκις ('seven times') in some places but elsewhere uses surprisingly divergent Greek words, including κλῆμα ('vine branch') and παραλύω ('to disable'), suggesting ancient translators occasionally struggled with its force or context. Its small cluster of uses in both narrative (Genesis 4) and poetry (Psalms, Proverbs) shows it functioned as a vivid intensifier across different literary registers.
caution: The low confidence tier and the strikingly inconsistent LXX renderings — including two Greek words unrelated to 'seven' — suggest real uncertainty about the word's meaning or text in at least some of its occurrences.

definition: A personal name belonging to at least three different Israelite men mentioned in genealogical records.
article: Jamin is a proper name appearing 6 times across 5 books, used for at least three distinct Israelite individuals. It occurs in genealogical lists in Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Chronicles, and Nehemiah. The KJV consistently renders it as 'Jamin' without variation, and Strong's notes the name shares its form with the common Hebrew word for 'right hand' or 'south.'
caution: Because this is a proper name derived from a common noun, its precise meaning as a name and whether bearers of the name are always distinct individuals can be difficult to confirm from the sparse genealogical context alone.

definition: A person or group of people from the ancient city of Erech (Uruk), mentioned as settlers in the region of Samaria.
article: This Aramaic term refers collectively to people originating from Erech, the ancient Mesopotamian city known elsewhere in the Bible as one of Nimrod's cities. It appears only twice in Ezra 4:9, within a list of ethnic groups who wrote a letter opposing the rebuilding of Jerusalem. The LXX evidence is not noted in the digest, leaving ancient Greek translation choices unclear for this term.
caution: This is a rare Aramaic gentillic term appearing only in a single verse (Ezra 4:9), with low confidence in its precise referent; scholarly identification of the exact population group is uncertain.

definition: The base or foundation of something, most often the bottom of an altar where sacrificial blood was poured out.
article: יְסוֹד refers to the lowest supporting part of a structure or object — its base or foundation. The word appears 20 times across 10 books, but its heaviest concentration is in Leviticus (8 occurrences), where it consistently describes the base of the altar where priests were to pour out sacrificial blood. The LXX translators used βάσις ("base") 9 times and θεμέλιος ("foundation") 5 times, confirming that ancient readers understood the word's core meaning as a supporting bottom structure, whether ritual or architectural. In Job, Psalms, and Proverbs, the word stretches into broader figurative territory, describing the foundational underpinning of things in a more metaphorical sense.
caution: The moderate confidence tier likely reflects uncertainty in a small number of occurrences where the grammatical role or precise referent is ambiguous, including the two instances the LXX unusually renders as ἐκχέω ("to pour out"), suggesting translators occasionally interpreted the altar-base context through the pouring action rather than the structure itself.

definition: A personal name referring primarily to David's son Absalom, whose rebellion against his father is narrated extensively in Samuel.
article: Abishalom (or Absalom in its shortened form) is almost entirely a proper name for a specific individual — David's son whose dramatic revolt and tragic death dominate large sections of 2 Samuel. Of its 111 occurrences, 102 appear in 2 Samuel alone, making it one of the most concentrated proper-name distributions in the Old Testament. The name's components suggest the meaning "father of peace," though his story is defined by anything but peace. The single Psalms occurrence (Psalm 3's superscription) connects directly to the same narrative, when David fled from Absalom's rebellion.

definition: A rare word of uncertain meaning, possibly indicating repetition, multiplicity, or a great number in a military or heavenly context.
article: This word appears only once in the Old Testament, at Psalm 68:18, where the KJV translates it as 'angels' — though that gloss is interpretive rather than literal. Strong's connects it to a root meaning 'change' or 'repetition,' suggesting the idea of a vast, repeated, or innumerable host. The LXX rendered it as ταχύ, meaning 'quickly' or 'swiftly,' which points in yet a different direction and shows that ancient translators themselves were uncertain how to handle it.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon with no scholarly consensus on its meaning; the KJV gloss 'angels,' the root sense of 'repetition,' and the LXX rendering 'swiftly' all point in different directions, leaving the word's true meaning genuinely unresolved.

definition: To lift or carry a burden, often implying something imposed or taken up with weight.
article: נָטַל means to lift or take up, with a sense of bearing something heavy or imposed. Its four occurrences span Isaiah, 2 Samuel, and Lamentations, appearing in both prophetic poetry and lament — contexts where weight and burden carry emotional force. Notably in Isaiah 40:15, it describes God lifting the islands like fine dust, a use that stresses effortless divine power against the word's usual connotation of heavy bearing. The KJV renders it as 'bear,' 'offer,' and 'take up,' reflecting this range from physical lifting to presenting something formally.
caution: With only 4 occurrences across 3 books, the semantic range is narrow and confidence in precise nuance is low; the root may carry meanings not fully visible in such sparse attestation.

definition: A priest or official who performs sacred duties and mediates between the people and God.
article: כֹּהֵן is the standard Hebrew word for a priest — someone who officiates in religious duties, offers sacrifices, and serves at a sanctuary. It appears 750 times across 29 books, with the heaviest concentration in Leviticus (194×) and 2 Chronicles (89×), reflecting how central priestly matters are to those books. The ancient Greek translators rendered it as ἱερεύς (the standard Greek word for a priest) an overwhelming 716 out of 750 times, showing that ancient readers understood this word almost exclusively in its priestly sense. In a handful of cases it applies to royal or civic officials rather than religious ones, as when Genesis uses it of Egyptian court figures.

definition: Fine powder or dust, used in the context of perfumed or scented powder.
article: This rare feminine noun appears only once in the Old Testament, in Song of Solomon 3:6, where it describes fragrant powders — likely perfumed dust or spice powder associated with incense and exotic trade goods. Its sole occurrence is in a poetic context, lending it an elevated, sensory register. The LXX renders the passage with language related to fragrant spices, confirming the aromatic nuance. As the feminine form of the root for dust or powder, it narrows that broader concept specifically toward fine, scented material.
caution: This word is a hapax legomenon, occurring only once in the entire Hebrew Bible, so its precise nuance cannot be confirmed from additional contexts.

definition: A type of shield or protective weapon used by soldiers and displayed as a symbol of military power.
article: The word שְׁלָטִים refers to a kind of shield, appearing 7 times spread across narrative, prophetic, and poetic books. It shows up in contexts of royal armories and military display — notably in 2 Samuel 8:7 and 2 Kings 11:10, where shields are taken as war trophies or stored in the temple. The romantic imagery in Song of Solomon 4:4 uses shields hung on a tower as a decorative or symbolic image, suggesting the word carried associations of prestige and power beyond mere battlefield equipment.
caution: Confidence in the precise meaning is low — the LXX translations for this word are surprisingly inconsistent, rendering it as a military officer and even proper names rather than 'shield,' which raises genuine uncertainty about the word's exact referent or whether all occurrences share the same meaning.

definition: To be or make deep, whether physically or in terms of hidden, obscure, or corrupt intention.
article: עָמַק means to be deep or to make something deep, and its range covers both literal depth and the idea of going deep into concealment or corruption. Strikingly, 7 of its 9 occurrences appear in the Hiphil stem, meaning the word most often describes a causative action — someone deliberately making something deep or pushing something further into hiddenness. The prophets Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Hosea use it predominantly in moral contexts, describing people who 'go deep' in their scheming or corruption, while the LXX renders it with βαθύς ('deep') in 3 instances, confirming that ancient readers heard a genuine sense of depth, not just a metaphor.
caution: With only 9 occurrences spread across 4 books and a low confidence tier, the precise boundary between literal and figurative uses is difficult to draw with certainty.

definition: To rain or cause rain to fall, often describing God sending rain — whether life-giving or destructive — upon the earth.
article: מָטַר is a verb meaning to rain or to make it rain. It appears 17 times across 7 books, most often in the Hiphil stem (9 times), which is the causative form — so the focus is typically on God actively causing rain to fall rather than rain simply falling on its own. This fits the contexts well: Genesis and Exodus use it for both divine provision and catastrophic judgment (the flood, the plagues), while Amos and Psalms use it for agricultural blessing or its withdrawal. The LXX almost always renders it with βρέχω, the standard Greek word for raining, though one instance is rendered κτίζω (to create), which is puzzling and likely reflects a difficult or variant Hebrew text.
caution: The low confidence tier and the single anomalous LXX rendering as κτίζω ("to create") suggest at least one textual instance is uncertain or disputed in meaning.

definition: A deep, consuming grief or sorrow that wastes the spirit away through prolonged distress.
article: דַּאֲבוֹן describes an inner anguish of soul, the kind of sorrow that slowly drains a person. It appears only once in the Old Testament, in Deuteronomy 28:65, where Moses warns of the devastating consequences of covenant unfaithfulness — God will give an anxious mind, failing eyes, and a despairing heart. The KJV renders it simply as "sorrow," but the underlying root דָּאַב carries the sense of pining or wasting away, suggesting grief that lingers and consumes rather than a momentary sadness.
caution: This word is a hapax legomenon, occurring only once in the entire Old Testament, so its precise nuance cannot be confirmed by comparing multiple contexts.

definition: A watchtower or sentinel post, a place from which a guard keeps watch.
article: This word appears only once in the Old Testament, at Isaiah 21:5, where it describes a watchman's post in a dramatic vision of Babylon's fall. It derives from the root צָפָה, meaning to look out or spy, and carries the sense of a fixed station for keeping watch. The KJV renders it 'watchtower,' which captures the structural idea, though the underlying root emphasizes the act of watching rather than the physical tower itself.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon — occurring only once in the entire Hebrew Bible — so its precise meaning rests on a single context and its relationship to the root צָפָה, leaving some uncertainty about its exact semantic nuance.

definition: An adjective meaning 'eastern,' referring to direction toward the east.
article: קַדְמוֹנָה appears only once in the Old Testament, in Ezekiel 47:8, where it describes the direction of a river flowing eastward in Ezekiel's vision of the restored temple. The word derives from the root קָדַם, which relates to what is 'in front' or 'before,' since east was understood as the direction one faces. The KJV consistently renders it 'east,' and the term functions as an adjective modifying direction. Its single occurrence makes it a hapax legomenon with a straightforward geographic meaning.
caution: This word occurs only once in the entire Old Testament, making contextual comparison impossible, though its derivation from the well-attested root קָדַם strongly supports the 'eastern' meaning.

definition: A Levitical city in the territory of Naphtali, identified by its hot springs near Dor.
article: Chammath-Dor (also spelled Hamath-Dor in the KJV) appears only twice in the Old Testament, both occurrences in Joshua 21:32, where it is listed among the cities assigned to the Levites from the tribe of Naphtali. The name combines a word meaning 'hot springs' with the place name Dor, suggesting the site was known for thermal springs. Its extremely limited occurrence — just one verse in one book — means almost nothing is known about its history or significance beyond this single administrative list.
caution: The site's exact location is uncertain and unconfirmed archaeologically, and the doubled occurrence in Joshua 21:32 likely reflects a textual feature of the list rather than two distinct references.

definition: A Hebrew term appearing only in psalm titles, likely denoting a specific literary or musical category whose exact meaning remains unknown.
article: Michtam appears exactly 6 times in the Old Testament, all as a title heading in the Psalms (Psalms 16, 56–60). Strong's connects it to a root meaning 'engraving,' suggesting a polished or carefully crafted poem, but this is speculative. The ancient Greek translators were clearly uncertain too — the LXX renders it with wildly inconsistent Greek words, including 'prayer,' 'corrupt/destroy,' and even the proper name 'Saul,' which tells us they were essentially guessing. Because every modern English translation simply transliterates it as 'Michtam,' readers are left with an untranslated label whose function remains a mystery.
caution: The meaning of miktam is genuinely unknown; scholarly proposals range from 'golden poem' to 'atonement psalm' to 'inscription,' and the chaotic LXX evidence confirms ancient uncertainty as well.

definition: A place name referring to a town in Palestine, assigned to the tribe of Reuben and given to the Levites.
article: Mephaath is a proper geographical name referring to a specific town in Palestine. It appears 5 times across Joshua, Jeremiah, and 1 Chronicles, consistently as a place name with no other semantic range — the KJV always renders it simply as 'Mephaath.' In Jeremiah 48:21 it appears among a list of Moabite towns facing judgment, suggesting it had passed into Moabite territory by that period, which adds an interesting historical dimension to its Reubenite and Levitical assignments in Joshua and Chronicles.
caution: Confidence is low; the spelling varies (Mophaath, Meyphaath, Mephaath) across manuscripts and editions, and the connection to the root יָפַע meaning 'to shine' is a lexical proposal, not a certainty.

definition: To be fully satisfied or filled to the point of having enough, whether with food, drink, or other experiences.
article: שָׂבַע describes the state of being completely filled or satisfied — most commonly after eating, but also with other experiences to the point of having more than enough. Its range runs from positive contentment (eating and being full, Deuteronomy 8:10) to negative surfeit (being so glutted as to grow weary). The Septuagint consistently renders it with ἐμπίπλημι (40 times), meaning 'to fill up completely,' confirming that ancient readers understood this as genuine fullness, not mere adequacy. The word appears most heavily in Psalms and Proverbs, where it often carries a reflective or wisdom-oriented tone about sufficiency and desire.
caution: The 'weary of' sense (from the KJV gloss range) pushes the word into unusual figurative territory that is not uniformly attested, so the negative excess meaning should be applied cautiously in any given passage.

definition: A people or nation viewed as a unified community, ranging from a single tribe to all humanity's peoples to military forces.
article: עָם (am) is one of the most common nouns in the Hebrew Bible, appearing 1,870 times across all 39 books, with especially heavy use in Exodus, Jeremiah, and Isaiah — books deeply concerned with Israel's identity and destiny as a community. The word describes a people bound together by shared identity, whether ethnic, tribal, or national, and can extend to military troops or attendants. The LXX translators overwhelmingly chose λαός (1,487 times) over ἔθνος (44 times), a meaningful distinction: λαός in Greek tends to emphasize a people in relationship with their leadership or deity, while ἔθνος stresses ethnic or national identity — suggesting ancient readers heard עָם as a word about belonging and communal bond, not merely ethnicity.

definition: Greatness or majesty, referring to elevated dignity, high rank, or sovereign splendor.
article: This Aramaic word appears only 5 times, all in the book of Daniel, where it describes the imposing dignity and splendor belonging to kings and kingdoms. Its range covers both concrete royal greatness and the more abstract sense of elevated status or majesty. Interestingly, the LXX renders it with ὑπόνοια, a Greek word more commonly meaning 'suspicion' or 'conjecture,' which is an unusual and somewhat puzzling choice that may reflect translator uncertainty about the term.
caution: Confidence is rated low: this is a rare Aramaic term attested in only 5 verses, the LXX translation choice is unexpected and may signal ancient uncertainty, and the root relationship is reconstructed rather than fully transparent.

definition: A word meaning inaccessible or lofty, appearing once in the Old Testament, likely describing something unreachably high or fortified.
article: This rare Hebrew word appears only once, in Zechariah 11:2, and derives from a root associated with fortification or being cut off from access. Its core sense is something elevated and unreachable. Notably, the KJV translated it as 'vintage' — almost certainly a confusion with the similar-looking word bātsîyr — suggesting even early translators found this term difficult. The word's single occurrence makes its precise meaning depend heavily on context and root analysis rather than a broad pattern of biblical usage.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon (occurring only once), and the KJV's mistranslation as 'vintage' reflects genuine ancient confusion with a near-identical word; the actual meaning rests entirely on root derivation, not usage patterns.

definition: A proper name: the king of Sodom mentioned in the battle of the five kings in Genesis 14.
article: Bera is a proper name appearing exactly once in the Old Testament, in Genesis 14:2, as the king of Sodom who joined a coalition of five kings against Chedorlaomer. The KJV simply transliterates the name as 'Bera,' and there is no meaningful LXX translation choice to analyze — the Greek also renders it as a proper name. Because it occurs only this single time, nothing can be said about a broader semantic range.
caution: The root and meaning of the name are explicitly uncertain, and as a hapax legomenon with no known reliable etymology, no further interpretation is possible.

definition: A proper name identifying one of Job's three friends who comes to comfort and later debate him.
article: Bildad is a personal name found exclusively in the book of Job, appearing all 5 times in that single book. He is one of the three companions who visit Job in his suffering, and he speaks in three of the book's dialogues (chapters 8, 18, and 25). The LXX's use of ὑπολαμβάνω — meaning "to take up" or "to reply" — in connection with Bildad reflects his role as one who responds and argues against Job's position rather than being a translation of the name itself.
caution: The meaning and derivation of the name Bildad are uncertain, as Strong's notes explicitly, and no reliable etymology can be established from the available evidence.

definition: A female blood relative; a woman who is close kin by family relationship.
article: This noun refers to a female blood relative or kinswoman. It appears only once in the Old Testament, in Leviticus 18:17, within the laws governing forbidden sexual relationships.
