Its concentration in Ecclesiastes fits that book's reflective, philosophical register.
caution: With only 3 occurrences all in one book, the full semantic range is difficult to establish with confidence, and the precise nuance between 'reason,' 'device,' and 'account' remains somewhat uncertain.

definition: A particle asserting existence — 'there is/are' — used wherever English needs any form of 'to be' to state that something exists or is present.
article: יֵשׁ is Hebrew's primary word for asserting that something exists or is on hand, covering the full range of what English expresses with 'there is,' 'there are,' 'have,' or 'has.' It appears 138 times across 25 books, with heavy use in Genesis, Ecclesiastes, Proverbs, and Job — books that frequently reason about what does or does not exist in the world. The LXX translators overwhelmingly rendered it with εἰμί (the Greek verb 'to be'), confirming that ancient readers heard it as a straightforward existence claim. One common construction uses יֵשׁ with a possessive sense, so 'יֵשׁ לְ' (yesh + lamed) means 'X has' something — a function English handles with a completely different verb.

definition: Rain or a heavy shower of rain, especially the seasonal rainfall that sustains crops and life.
article: גֶּשֶׁם refers to rain, particularly the kind of substantial shower that matters for agriculture and survival. Its range is narrow — the KJV translates it only as 'rain' or 'shower' — but its significance is wide, appearing across narrative, prophecy, poetry, and wisdom literature in 17 books. The Septuagint almost exclusively renders it as ὑετός (25 out of 35 occurrences), the standard Greek word for rain, confirming that ancient readers saw little ambiguity here. Its heaviest use is in Ezekiel (6×) and 1 Kings (5×), the latter driven by the famous drought-and-rain narrative of Elijah.
caution: The moderate confidence tier likely reflects minor uncertainty about distinguishing this root from related forms, but the word's core meaning as 'rain' is not in serious dispute.

definition: To carry or bear a heavy burden, whether a physical load or the weight of toil and hardship.
article: סָבַל conveys the idea of bearing something weighty — a physical load carried on the body, or the grinding labor and hardship a person endures. Its five occurrences in Isaiah include God declaring that he has carried and will continue to carry his people, giving the word a powerful relational dimension. The Pual stem (passive-intensive) appears once, suggesting something being heavily borne. With only 9 occurrences spread across 5 books, this is a relatively rare verb, and the single LXX rendering ὑπέχω ("to hold under, to sustain") confirms the sense of bearing weight from beneath.
caution: The low confidence tier and sparse attestation (9 occurrences total) mean the full semantic range is difficult to pin down with certainty, and some glosses like "be gravid" (pregnant with young) rest on very limited evidence.

definition: An Aramaic noun meaning fire or flame, used in Daniel's vision of divine judgment.
article: This is the Aramaic form of the common Hebrew word for fire, appearing just once in the Old Testament, in Daniel 7:11, where it describes the flaming destruction of a beast in a vision. Its single occurrence reflects the Aramaic sections of Daniel rather than standard Biblical Hebrew prose. The word carries the same vivid, consuming sense as its Hebrew counterpart, here deployed in an apocalyptic scene of divine judgment.
caution: With only one occurrence in the entire Old Testament, this Aramaic entry has extremely limited attestation, and its full range of usage can only be inferred from the broader Aramaic cognate tradition rather than Biblical evidence alone.

definition: A musing or deep inner meditation, describing the focused activity of reflective thought.
article: הָגוּת is a noun derived from the verb הָגָה, which carries the sense of murmuring, pondering, or meditating. It occurs only once in the Old Testament, in Psalm 49:4, where the psalmist describes opening a riddle accompanied by this kind of reflective musing. The LXX renders the concept in a way consistent with deep contemplative thought, and the word's sole appearance in a wisdom psalm places it squarely in the elevated, reflective register of Hebrew poetry.
caution: This word is a hapax legomenon, appearing only once in the entire Old Testament, so its precise nuance cannot be confirmed by comparing multiple contexts.

definition: A rare word covering both abundance or satiety and the stroke or blow of punishment.
article: This word appears only twice in the Old Testament, both in the book of Job, making its meaning difficult to pin down with confidence. The two KJV renderings — 'sufficiency' (Job 20:22) and 'stroke' (Job 36:18) — point to two quite different senses: one of having more than enough, the other of a chastising blow. Strong's connects both senses to the same root, suggesting the underlying idea may involve something forceful or overwhelming, whether abundance or punishment.
caution: With only 2 occurrences, both in Job, and two seemingly unrelated English glosses ('sufficiency' and 'stroke'), the precise meaning in each context remains genuinely uncertain and is disputed among scholars.

definition: An adjective meaning 'right' or 'on the right side,' referring to the right hand or right side of the body or an object.
article: יְמָנִי is a straightforward adjective meaning 'right' as in the right-hand side, used consistently across its 33 occurrences. It appears most heavily in Leviticus (20 times), where it describes specific body parts in priestly ritual — the right ear, right thumb, and right big toe — as locations for applying blood or oil in consecration ceremonies. The LXX translates it uniformly as δεξιός, the standard Greek word for 'right,' confirming that ancient readers understood this word with no ambiguity. Its concentration in ritual legal texts gives it a precise, technical flavor rather than a poetic or metaphorical one.
caution: The moderate confidence tier may reflect uncertainty about the exact derivation from the root יָמַן, but the word's meaning in context is not disputed.

definition: To divide into sixths or give a sixth part of something as a portion or offering.
article: This rare verb appears only once in the Old Testament, in Ezekiel 45:13, where it describes the proportional division of grain offerings into sixth-parts. It is a denominative verb, meaning it was formed directly from the Hebrew word for "six" (shesh), functioning much like coining an English verb "to sixth" something. Because it occurs only in this single technical, priestly context, its meaning is precise and narrow rather than broad.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon — appearing only once in the entire Old Testament — so its full semantic range cannot be independently verified beyond this single ritual-measurement context.

definition: The right time or occasion; a fitting turn or season when something is said or done appropriately.
article: אֹפֶן appears only once in the Old Testament, in Proverbs 25:11, where it describes words spoken at the right moment — like apples of gold in settings of silver. Strong's connects it to an unused root meaning 'to revolve,' suggesting the idea of a wheel turning to the right point, a fitting season or occasion. The KJV renders it as part of the phrase 'fitly spoken,' capturing the sense of perfect timing. Its single appearance in proverbial wisdom poetry gives it a distinctly elevated, metaphorical flavor.
caution: This word is a hapax legomenon, appearing only once in the entire Old Testament, so its precise meaning depends heavily on context and root reconstruction rather than broad attestation.

definition: A personal name belonging to an Israelite man listed in the genealogies of Judah.
article: Rinnah is a proper name appearing once in the Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 4:20, where it is listed among the descendants of Judah. It shares its form with the common Hebrew noun meaning joyful singing or a cry of joy, but here it functions purely as a personal name. Because it appears only in a genealogical list, no further context about this individual is provided.
caution: This name appears only once in the entire Old Testament, making it a hapax in terms of narrative context, with no additional detail available about the person named.

definition: A memorial stone named 'Ezel' (meaning departure), used as a location marker in one narrative passage.
article: Ezel is a proper name for a specific stone or landmark mentioned only once in the Old Testament, in 1 Samuel 20:19, where it serves as a meeting point for David and Jonathan. The name itself derives from a root meaning departure, which fits its narrative role as the site of their fateful farewell. Because the KJV simply transliterates the word as 'Ezel' without translation, ancient versions including the LXX offer limited help in clarifying its exact nature.
caution: This word appears only once in the entire Old Testament, making it a hapax legomenon as a proper noun; its precise identification as a stone, monument, or place remains uncertain.

definition: A proper name identifying one of the ten sons of Haman who was killed in Persia.
article: Arisai is a proper name of Persian origin appearing once in the Old Testament, in Esther 9:9, as one of the ten sons of Haman who were slain by the Jewish people in Susa. The KJV simply transliterates the name as "Arisai," and the word carries no broader semantic range beyond this single identification. Its sole occurrence in the book of Esther fits the narrative list of Haman's fallen household.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon of likely Persian origin, and its precise etymology and meaning in Persian remain uncertain.

definition: A round or bowl-shaped object, used of water springs, decorative bowls, and rounded architectural features.
article: גֻּלָּה refers to something round or globe-like, covering a surprisingly wide range: the bowls on top of the Jerusalem temple pillars in 1 Kings and 2 Chronicles, the ornamental 'pommels' of sacred architecture, and natural water springs in Joshua and Judges — all linked by their rounded shape. The word appears 15 times across 6 books, clustering in architectural and geographical contexts. The LXX renders it with συγκαλύπτω ('to cover over') in two places and τετράγωνος ('four-cornered') in one, which is a puzzling mismatch and suggests the ancient translators themselves were uncertain how to handle it.
caution: The LXX translations are inconsistent with each other and with the Hebrew sense of roundness, indicating genuine ancient uncertainty; the confidence tier for this word is rated low.

definition: Serious illness or disease, often referring to severe, debilitating sickness sent as a consequence of wrongdoing.
article: This rare word, appearing only 5 times across 4 books, refers to serious bodily disease or malady. Its most memorable appearance is in Psalm 103:3, where God is praised as the one who heals 'all your diseases.' The word appears in Deuteronomy and Jeremiah in contexts of divine judgment, suggesting the sicknesses in view are severe and consequential. The LXX most often renders it as νόσος, the standard Greek word for disease or illness, though one puzzling rendering as νέφος ('cloud') and another as ὑπερῷον ('upper room') suggest ancient translators occasionally struggled with the term.
caution: Confidence is rated low, likely because the word is rare and at least two LXX renderings are difficult to explain, hinting at genuine uncertainty about the word's precise meaning in certain contexts.

definition: To escape or slip away from danger, and in active stems to rescue or deliver someone else to safety.
article: מָלַט covers the full arc of deliverance — both the experience of escaping and the act of rescuing another. Strong's traces it to a root idea of being smooth or slippery, which fits the sense of slipping out of danger's grip. The Niphal stem (40×), the passive-reflexive form, naturally handles self-escape, while the Piel (14×) is used when someone actively delivers another. Ancient translators reached for σώζω (35×) and διασώζω (20×) — the standard Greek words for salvation — signaling that Hebrew readers heard genuine rescue and deliverance in this word, not mere lucky escape. The word appears most heavily in 1 Samuel, Jeremiah, and Job, books saturated with life-or-death crises, which fits its core urgency.
caution: Strong's also lists specialized senses — 'bring forth young' and 'emit sparks' — that are rare and contextually specific; scholars are not fully agreed on whether these represent the same root or a homonym.

definition: To shatter or crush violently, and by extension to oppress or harass with crushing force.
article: רָעַץ describes an act of breaking something apart with great force, and it can extend to the relentless crushing of people through oppression. Its two occurrences span Exodus and Judges — one in the victory song of Exodus 15:6, where God's right hand dashes the enemy to pieces, and one in Judges 10:8, describing how the Philistines crushed Israel. The Greek translators chose θραύω, a word meaning to shatter or smash, confirming the core sense of violent, destructive force.
caution: With only 2 occurrences across the entire Old Testament and a low confidence rating, the precise semantic range of this root is difficult to establish with certainty.

definition: A Babylonian deity associated with fortune or luck, named alongside other foreign gods in a context of apostasy.
article: גַּד (Gad) appears only once in the Old Testament, in Isaiah 65:11, where it refers to a pagan deity of fortune worshipped by Israelites who had abandoned God. The KJV translates it as 'that troop,' obscuring the divine name, but the LXX renders it as δαίμων ('demon' or 'spirit'), making clear that ancient translators understood this as a reference to a foreign god. Strong's identifies it as a variation of the common noun גָּד meaning fortune or luck, here serving as the proper name of a Babylonian divine being.
caution: This word occurs only once in the entire Old Testament (a hapax legomenon in this sense), and the KJV's rendering 'that troop' suggests translators were uncertain whether it was a divine name or a common noun, reflecting genuine ambiguity in the text.

definition: A small, shy rock-dwelling animal (most likely the hyrax) that hides in rocky terrain, listed among unclean animals in the law of Moses.
article: The word refers to a small creature associated with rocky habitats, translated consistently as 'coney' in the KJV. It appears in Leviticus and Deuteronomy as an unclean animal — it chews the cud but does not have split hooves — and memorably in Psalms and Proverbs as an example of a creature that finds refuge in the rocks. The most likely identification is the hyrax (rock badger), a small mammal native to the Levant. Interestingly, the LXX translators rendered this word as ἀναγινώσκω ('to read') and φωνή ('voice') in various contexts, which strongly suggests those Greek renderings reflect scribal name confusion rather than the animal term — pointing to a different lemma sharing this form in the narrative books of Kings, Chronicles, and Jeremiah.
caution: The LXX evidence (rendered as 'read' and 'voice') almost certainly reflects a different word — likely a personal name (Shaphan, a royal scribe) — sharing the same spelling, meaning the 34 occurrences span two distinct Hebrew words that modern readers and scholars carefully distinguish.

definition: Pleasure, delight, or sensuous luxury — the experience of physical and emotional enjoyment or well-being.
article: This word conveys a rich sense of pleasure or delightful enjoyment, covering both physical comfort and deeper emotional satisfaction. Its five occurrences are spread across very different contexts: Sarah's private musing about physical pleasure in Genesis, the luxuries enjoyed by women in 2 Samuel, a river of God's delights in Psalm 36, and place-name references in Jeremiah and Amos. The KJV renders it as 'pleasure,' 'delight,' and 'delicate,' showing its range from inner enjoyment to outward luxury. Notably, the LXX translators chose different Greek words across occurrences, suggesting they found this Hebrew word difficult to pin down with a single equivalent.
caution: Confidence is rated low, and with only 5 occurrences spread across widely different contexts, the precise nuance in each case remains uncertain; some grammatical roles in the digest are ambiguous.

definition: A personal name belonging to an Israelite man mentioned in genealogical lists in Chronicles.
article: Ashchur (also rendered 'Ashur' in the KJV) is a proper name appearing only twice in the Old Testament, both times in 1 Chronicles in genealogical contexts. Strong's connects the name to the root meaning 'black,' but this is a tentative etymology, not a demonstrated meaning. Because both occurrences function as a personal name in a list, the word carries no broader semantic range to explore.
caution: This name appears only twice in a single book, the etymology ('black') is speculative, and scholarly confidence in the root derivation is low.

definition: To prepare or make ready something for future use or purpose.
article: עָתַד means to prepare or make ready, covering the idea of getting something fit and in order for what lies ahead. Its range is narrow — the evidence points consistently to a single core idea of preparation. The word appears only twice in the Old Testament, once in Job and once in Proverbs, both poetic books, suggesting it carries a somewhat elevated register. The LXX translators chose παρασκευάζω, a straightforward Greek word for making preparations, confirming that ancient readers understood it as practical readiness.
caution: With only 2 occurrences across the entire Old Testament and a low confidence tier, the full semantic range of this root is difficult to establish with certainty.

definition: To fly or move swiftly through the air, and by extension to grow faint or exhausted, covering a range from literal flight to physical collapse.
article: This verb covers two distinct but connected ideas: the physical act of flying (like birds) and the experience of growing faint or weary, possibly linked by the shared idea of dimness or swooning. The Qal stem appears 11 times in straightforward flying contexts, while fainting or weariness shows up notably in narrative passages like 1 Samuel 14, where troops are exhausted after battle. The LXX translators most often chose πέτομαι ("to fly"), confirming that flight was the dominant sense ancient readers recognized, though they also used ἐκλύω ("to grow faint/weak") to capture the exhaustion meaning. The word appears most heavily in Isaiah, Proverbs, and Psalms, suggesting it carried some poetic and metaphorical weight beyond plain prose usage.
caution: The connection between the "flying" and "fainting" senses is debated — some scholars treat them as two separate roots that happen to share the same spelling, so the unified entry carries moderate uncertainty.

definition: To cry out urgently — whether a desperate plea for help, a shout in distress, or a public summons to assemble.
article: זָעַק describes raising one's voice with urgency, covering both the anguished cry of someone in danger or pain and the loud public call that gathers people together. Its 73 occurrences spread across 22 books, with the heaviest concentration in Judges and 1 Samuel — narrative books full of battles, oppression, and desperate appeals to God. The LXX most often uses βοάω and κράζω, both Greek words for loud, forceful shouting, confirming that ancient readers heard this as a strong, even raw, vocal act rather than a quiet request.
caution: The confidence tier for this word is marked moderate, likely because the same root carries both the emotional cry of distress and the more administrative sense of publicly convening people, and distinguishing the two in any given context requires careful attention.

definition: A collective term for the descendants of Jishvi, a clan within the tribe of Asher.
article: Yish-vee refers to the Jishvites, the family group descended from Jishvi son of Asher. The word appears only once in the Old Testament, in the tribal census of Numbers 26:44, where it functions as a gentillic (group-membership) label. The KJV renders it 'Jesuites,' reflecting an older English transliteration style. As a patronymic clan name, its meaning is entirely bound to its ancestral referent and carries no broader semantic range.
caution: This word occurs only once in the entire Old Testament, making it a hapax in usage context; its meaning is certain only because it functions as a standard patronymic form.

definition: To marry or become master over someone, especially as a husband taking a wife.
article: This verb carries two closely related ideas: the act of marrying and the exercise of authority or ownership that marriage implied in the ancient world. It appears 16 times across 7 books, with the heaviest concentration in Isaiah (7×) and Deuteronomy (3×), where it often describes a man marrying or 'being husband to' a woman. The Niphal stem (passive) adds the nuance of a woman 'being married.' The LXX most often renders it with συνοικέω, meaning 'to live together with,' which suggests ancient translators foregrounded the relational and domestic dimension over the idea of raw mastery.
caution: Confidence is rated low, possibly because the verb overlaps substantially with the noun בַּעַל (lord, master, Baal) and it is not always clear whether a given form should be read as this verb or as a related nominal form; the one LXX rendering as ὀπώρα ('autumn fruit') is particularly puzzling and may reflect a textual difficulty.

definition: Parvaim, an unidentified foreign region mentioned as the source of gold used in Solomon's temple.
article: Parvaim appears only once in the Old Testament, in 2 Chronicles 3:6, where it names the source of gold used to decorate Solomon's temple. Strong's identifies it as a word of foreign origin referring to an Oriental region, and the single KJV translation is simply the transliterated name 'Parvaim.' Interestingly, the LXX rendered the passage using the Greek word κοσμέω, meaning 'to adorn' or 'to decorate,' suggesting ancient translators may not have recognized it as a place name at all.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon of uncertain foreign origin, and its exact geographical location remains unidentified; even ancient translators appear to have been unsure how to handle the word.

definition: A small tied bundle, bag, or bound-up packet — also something as tiny as a pebble or grain.
article: This noun describes something wrapped or bound together, ranging from a money bag (as in Genesis 42, where the brothers find their silver in their bundles) to a small stone or grain. The same word covers both the container and the tiny object it might hold, reflecting Hebrew's tolerance for semantic breadth. Ancient translators (LXX) rendered it mainly as δεσμόν, 'a binding or bundle,' confirming the core sense of something tied up, though one occurrence was rendered quite differently, hinting at interpretive uncertainty. Its most memorable use is in 1 Samuel 25:29, where being 'bound up in the bundle of the living' became a beloved image of divine protection.
caution: Confidence is rated low, the range from 'bag' to 'small stone' is genuinely broad and some occurrences are disputed, so the precise sense in a given verse may be uncertain.

definition: To scoff or mock with contempt; also to interpret or mediate between parties speaking different languages.
article: This root covers two surprisingly different ideas: contemptuous mockery and linguistic interpretation. The 'scorner' or 'mocker' sense dominates the Old Testament, appearing 18 times in Proverbs alone, where the scorner (לֵץ) is a stock figure of foolish arrogance set against the wise. The interpreter sense shows up in Genesis 42:23 and a few other places, likely because making exaggerated mouth movements to speak a foreign language looked like mocking — the same physical gesture underlies both ideas. The LXX translators frequently chose λοιμός ('pestilent fellow, plague') and κακός ('evil, bad'), confirming that ancient readers felt the scorn sense most strongly.
caution: The connection between the 'mocker' and 'interpreter' senses rests on an uncertain etymology, and some scholars treat them as distinct roots that merged; the moderate confidence rating reflects this unresolved debate.

definition: A personal name belonging to a son of Judah, also carried by a later ancestor in Israel's genealogies.
article: Shelah is used exclusively as a personal name in the Old Testament, appearing 8 times across Genesis, Numbers, and 1 Chronicles. The most prominent use is in Genesis 38, where Shelah is Judah's youngest son, whose withholding from Tamar drives a key episode in the patriarchal narrative. The LXX sometimes renders the name with κάθημαι (
caution: )sitting/remaining," suggesting the translators may have detected a wordplay on Judah keeping Shelah back from Tamar. Strong's notes a possible connection to the word for "request," but this etymology plays no role in the biblical text itself."}{"caution":"The confidence tier is rated low, and the LXX's unexpected rendering of the name with κάθημαι rather than a transliterated proper name raises unresolved questions about the text tradition and whether a pun or alternate reading was intended."}

definition: To sling a stone as a weapon, or to carve decorative designs into wood or stone surfaces.
article: This verb covers two distinct physical actions that Strong's links to a shared idea of circular or shaping motion: hurling a stone with a sling and cutting decorative patterns into a surface. The slinging sense appears in the famous David-and-Goliath account (1 Samuel 17) and in the reference to seven hundred left-handed Benjaminite slingers in Judges 20. The carving sense appears in 1 Kings 6, describing the engraved decorations inside Solomon's Temple. Curiously, the one LXX rendering translates the word as περικεφαλαία ("helmet"), which is puzzling and suggests the ancient translators may have struggled with the same ambiguity.
caution: Confidence is rated low, the two senses (slinging and carving) are quite different from each other, and with only 7 occurrences the root's full range is difficult to establish with certainty.

definition: A proper name used for both a person and a place in ancient Israel.
article: Shual appears twice in the Old Testament — once as a place name in 1 Samuel 13:17, referring to a region associated with Philistine military movements, and once as a personal name in 1 Chronicles 7:36, identifying an Israelite individual. The KJV renders it simply as 'Shual' in both cases, with no variation. The name shares its spelling with the common Hebrew word for 'fox' or 'jackal,' though in these two verses it functions purely as a proper noun.
caution: Because both occurrences are proper names and the underlying common noun meaning is not activated in context, the connection to any animal word is uncertain and cannot be pressed from this digest alone.

definition: Foolishness or moral folly, especially the senseless, self-destructive behavior of a person who rejects wisdom.
article: אּוֶּ֫לֶת refers to foolishness in a deeply practical and moral sense — not mere intellectual dullness, but the reckless, undisciplined conduct that brings ruin. Its range is fairly narrow: all 25 occurrences fall in just two poetic books, with 23 of those in Proverbs alone, marking it as a term central to wisdom literature's ethical vocabulary. The LXX most often renders it ἀφροσύνη, meaning senselessness or lack of good judgment, but also uses ἄνοια (mindlessness) and, strikingly, ἀπαίδευτος (uneducated, unteachable) — suggesting ancient readers heard in the word not just bad behavior but a refusal to be instructed.
caution: The confidence tier is marked moderate, and the LXX rendering varies enough (including the unexpected πανοῦργος, meaning cunning or sly) to suggest some translational uncertainty about the word's precise shade of meaning in context.

definition: A snare, trap, or lure — anything that catches, entangles, or leads someone into ruin, whether literal or figurative.
article: מוֹקֵשׁ refers to a device for catching animals — a noose or snare — but the vast majority of its 27 occurrences use this image figuratively for anything that draws people into disaster. Idolatry, wicked rulers, foolish speech, and enemy nations are all called מוֹקֵשׁ in contexts ranging from Exodus to Proverbs. The word appears most heavily in Proverbs (8×) and Psalms (6×), the books most concerned with wisdom and the dangers of moral failure. The LXX splits its translation between παγίς (a physical trap) and σκάνδαλον (a stumbling block or offense) — the same Greek word the NT uses — revealing that ancient readers saw both the trapping and the stumbling dimensions as real parts of this word's meaning.
caution: The moderate confidence rating reflects some uncertainty about the precise nuance in a handful of poetic passages where the line between literal trapping and metaphor is difficult to draw.

definition: Dominion or rule over others, possibly also carrying a sense of likeness or comparison, depending on the root.
article: This rare noun appears only 3 times in the Hebrew Bible, spread across Job, Daniel, and Zechariah. It likely derives from the verb מָשַׁל, but that root has two distinct meanings — 'to rule' and 'to be like' — and the noun may draw on either, making context decisive. In Daniel 11:4 and Zechariah 9:10 the sense of political dominion or empire fits clearly, while Job 41:25 is less straightforward. The KJV translates it as both 'dominion' and 'like,' reflecting genuine ambiguity in the underlying root.
caution: With only 3 occurrences and a root that carries two unrelated meanings (rule and likeness), the correct sense in any given passage is disputed and confidence is low.

definition: A son of Noah and ancestor of Abraham, also referring to the territory associated with his descendants.
article: Arphaxad is a proper name appearing 9 times across Genesis and 1 Chronicles, consistently in genealogical contexts tracing the line from Noah to Abraham. The name refers both to an individual — one of Shem's sons — and apparently to the region settled by his descendants, though that territory's exact location remains unidentified. The LXX renders the name as Ἀρφαξάδ but also introduces Καϊνάν as an additional ancestor in the same lineage, which is why Luke's genealogy in the New Testament includes a generation that the Hebrew text does not.
caution: The name is almost certainly of foreign origin with no agreed Hebrew etymology, and its precise geographic referent is unknown; confidence in any deeper meaning is low.

definition: A fugitive or one who flees, escaping from danger or destruction.
article: נָיס means a fugitive — someone who has fled or is fleeing from danger. It appears only once in the Old Testament, in Jeremiah 48:44, within a poem of judgment against Moab describing inescapable doom: whoever flees one disaster falls into another. The word is derived from the common root נוּס (to flee), but this particular noun form occurs nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible.
caution: This word is a hapax legomenon, appearing only in Jeremiah 48:44, so its full semantic range cannot be confirmed from biblical usage alone.

definition: To reign or rule as a monarch, or to make someone king; covers both holding royal power and the act of enthroning.
article: This verb is the standard Hebrew word for royal rule, appearing 351 times across 22 books with the heaviest concentration in Kings and Chronicles — the historical books most focused on Israelite and Judahite monarchy. The Qal stem (145 occurrences) describes simply reigning, while the Hiphil stem (7 occurrences) carries the causative sense of making or installing someone as king. The LXX renders it with the Greek βασιλεύω an overwhelming 313 times, confirming that ancient translators saw this as a tightly focused royal-rule word with very little ambiguity. The range of KJV glosses — from 'reign' to 'make king' to 'set up' — reflects not a vague word, but a verb whose core meaning shifts predictably depending on the grammatical stem.

definition: To be of profit or benefit; to help, avail, or do any good for someone or something.
article: יָעַל means to profit, benefit, or be of use to someone, and it appears almost exclusively in the Hiphil stem (19 of 19 verbal occurrences), meaning it is nearly always used in a causative sense: 'to cause benefit' or 'to do good for.' Its 23 occurrences cluster heavily in prophetic literature — Isaiah (8×) and Jeremiah (7×) — where it frequently appears in negative form to deny that idols or false refuges can profit anyone. The LXX consistently renders it with ὠφελέω (11×) and related forms, the ordinary Greek word for 'benefit' or 'profit,' confirming that ancient readers understood its core meaning as practical usefulness rather than mere moral goodness.
caution: Strong's suggests an underlying root meaning 'to ascend,' but this etymology does not visibly shape any attested usage, and confidence in the root derivation is only moderate.

definition: The outward form or appearance of a person, especially their physical looks or attractiveness.
article: תֹּאַר refers to the visible shape and overall appearance of a person — what someone looks like at a glance. In practice it nearly always describes physical attractiveness, whether striking beauty (Rachel, Joseph) or the lack of it (Isaiah's suffering servant). The KJV varies widely — 'form,' 'countenance,' 'favoured,' 'comely' — but the LXX translator consistently chose εἶδος ('outward form, visible appearance') in 14 of its 15 occurrences, showing ancient readers understood it as a straightforward term for physical aspect. All 15 occurrences attach to people, never objects or landscapes, which keeps its range tighter than a fully general word for 'form.'
caution: Confidence is rated low, likely because the underlying root תָּאַר is poorly attested as a verb, making the word's derivation uncertain and leaving its precise semantic boundaries somewhat disputed.

definition: An upright, elevated posture — standing tall and unashamed as a picture of freedom and dignity.
article: This word appears only once in the Old Testament, at Leviticus 26:13, where God promises he broke Israel's bonds so they could walk 'upright' — heads held high rather than stooped under a yoke. It comes from the root meaning 'to rise or stand,' and its ancient Greek translators (LXX) chose παῤῥησία, a word meaning boldness or confidence, suggesting they understood it as dignity and unashamed freedom rather than just physical posture. The word functions adverbially, describing the manner of walking, so its force is something like 'with your head held high.'
caution: This is a hapax legomenon — appearing only once in the Hebrew Bible — so its precise nuance rests on a single context and the LXX's interpretive translation choice.

definition: A razor used for cutting hair, especially in Nazirite vow contexts where its use is forbidden.
article: This rare word appears only 3 times across 2 books — Judges and 1 Samuel — and in every case it refers to a razor that must not touch the head of someone under a Nazirite vow (Samson in Judges 13 and 16, and the promised Samuel in 1 Samuel 1). The KJV consistently translates it as 'razor,' and the word's meaning is quite narrow. Interestingly, the LXX most often renders it as σίδηρος, meaning 'iron' or 'iron tool,' which suggests the ancient translators understood it broadly as a metal cutting instrument rather than specifying a razor per se.
caution: Confidence is low given only 3 occurrences, and the LXX's use of σίδηρος ('iron') rather than a specific word for razor introduces some uncertainty about the precise referent.

definition: A large, strong tree — likely an oak or terebinth — used as a landmark and gathering place in ancient Israel.
article: The word אֵלָה refers to a large, sturdy tree, most likely an oak or terebinth, appearing 13 times across 8 books. It shows up prominently in narrative contexts — notably under such a tree that Gideon met the angel of the Lord (Judges 6:11), and Absalom's hair caught in a tree described with this word (2 Samuel 18:9). The KJV renders it variously as 'oak,' 'elm,' and 'teil-tree,' reflecting real uncertainty about the exact species. Intriguingly, the LXX most often translates it with the preposition ὑπό ('under'), suggesting the translators focused on the shade or shelter the tree provided rather than identifying the species precisely.
caution: The exact species is genuinely uncertain — 'oak,' 'terebinth,' and 'elm' have all been proposed — and the low confidence tier reflects unresolved scholarly disagreement about which tree this word consistently identifies.

definition: A formal testimony or witness, most often referring to the sacred covenant documents housed in the tabernacle's ark.
article: עֵדוּת carries the sense of an authoritative, binding testimony — evidence of an agreement or command that must be honored. In the Old Testament its 59 occurrences cluster heavily in Exodus (21×) and Numbers (12×), where it almost always refers to the stone tablets or the ark that contained them, called 'the ark of the testimony.' The LXX overwhelmingly renders it μαρτύριον (44 times), the standard Greek word for witness or testimony, confirming that ancient readers understood it as formal, legally binding witness — a usage the New Testament authors inherited when they spoke of the 'tabernacle of testimony' in Acts 7:44.
caution: The moderate confidence tier reflects some uncertainty about the full range of the word, including three unusual LXX renderings as ἐμβάλλω ('to throw in') that scholars have not fully explained.

definition: A demonstrative pronoun pointing to something near or just mentioned, meaning 'this' or 'this one.'
article: זֶה is the basic masculine demonstrative pronoun in Hebrew, used to point to a specific person, thing, or idea — usually something nearby or just introduced. With 1,178 occurrences across 34 books, it is one of the most common words in the Old Testament. The LXX translators rendered it as οὗτος ("this one") an overwhelming 932 times, confirming that ancient readers understood it straightforwardly as a near-pointing demonstrative. Its grammatical roles split between functioning as a determiner modifying a noun and standing alone as an independent pronoun.

definition: A Canaanite king of Admah, named as one of the five kings who fought in the battle of the Siddim Valley.
article: Shinab appears only once in the Old Testament, in Genesis 14:2, as the king of Admah who joined the coalition of five kings against Chedorlaomer and his allies. Because it is a proper name, its meaning in Hebrew cannot be established with certainty from usage alone. The LXX simply transliterates the name, offering no interpretive Greek translation that might shed light on its sense.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon (occurring only once), and the proposed meaning 'a father has turned' is speculative etymology from Strong's — not verifiable from any broader usage or ancient translation tradition.

definition: A large house or pavilion, likely referring to a royal garden hall or banquet space within a palace complex.
article: This rare word appears only 3 times, all in the book of Esther, where it describes a space associated with royal feasting and the Persian court. Strong's connects it to the common word for 'house,' suggesting a large, impressive structure. The LXX translators rendered it inconsistently — once as γάμος (wedding feast), once as συμπόσιον (banquet), and once as παραιτέομαι (to excuse oneself) — showing that even ancient translators were uncertain what precisely it described. The KJV consistently renders it 'palace,' but the feast contexts in Esther suggest a garden pavilion or banquet hall may be more accurate.
caution: This word is extremely rare (only 3 occurrences, all in Esther), the LXX renderings are inconsistent and one is clearly contextual rather than translational, and the precise meaning remains uncertain — the confidence tier is explicitly marked low.

definition: A personal name identifying the father of Amasa, described as an Israelite or Ishmaelite in 2 Samuel 17:25.
article: יִתְרָא is a proper name appearing only once in the Old Testament, in 2 Samuel 17:25, where it identifies the man who fathered Amasa by Abigail. The KJV renders it as "Ithra." Strong's notes it as a variant form of the related name יִתְרָה, suggesting the two spellings refer to the same individual.
caution: The text itself is uncertain about whether Ithra was an Israelite or an Ishmaelite — a discrepancy also noted in the parallel passage in 1 Chronicles 2:17 — reflecting a genuine textual ambiguity in the manuscript tradition.

definition: To become dull or blunted — of a blade losing its edge or teeth set on edge by sour food.
article: This rare verb appears only 4 times across 3 books, describing something losing its sharpness or edge. In Ecclesiastes 10:10, a blunted iron blade makes work harder. In Jeremiah 31:29–30 and Ezekiel 18:2, the vivid idiom of children's teeth being 'set on edge' because their parents ate sour grapes carries a strong sense of inherited consequence — a proverb that both prophets cite and challenge. The Piel stem appears once, suggesting an intensified or causative form of the dulling action.
caution: With only 4 occurrences and a low confidence tier, the precise nuance of the root — especially whether 'bluntness' and 'teeth on edge' share a single underlying sense or represent two distinct metaphors — remains uncertain.

definition: A humble, modest disposition toward others and before God, ranging from personal meekness to gentle condescension.
article: This noun describes an inward quality of lowliness or modesty, the disposition of someone who does not assert themselves above others or before God. Its four occurrences cluster almost entirely in Proverbs, where it appears alongside wisdom and the fear of the LORD as a companion virtue (PRO 15:33, 18:12, 22:4), giving it a strongly proverbial, instructional register. The lone appearance in Zephaniah (2:3) calls the humble of the land to seek this quality as shelter before judgment. Strong's notes both a human side (personal modesty) and a divine side (clemency), but the OT evidence leans toward the human virtue of humble self-positioning.
caution: With only 4 occurrences across 2 books, the full semantic range is difficult to establish with confidence, and the distinction between the human and divine senses remains somewhat speculative.

definition: Compassionate sparing of someone from harm, driven by pity or merciful feeling toward them.
article: חֶמְלַת denotes a deep feeling of compassion that moves someone to spare another from harm. It appears only twice in the Old Testament — once in Genesis 19:16, where angels mercifully take Lot by the hand, and once in Isaiah 63:9, describing God's compassion toward Israel. The LXX consistently renders it with φείδομαι, a Greek verb meaning 'to spare,' which suggests ancient translators understood the word as active mercy expressed through protective restraint, not merely an emotion.
caution: With only 2 occurrences across the entire Old Testament, the full semantic range of this word cannot be established with confidence.

definition: To refuse or be unwilling to do something, consistently expressing firm rejection of a request or command.
article: מָאֵן means to refuse — to decline or reject what is asked, commanded, or expected. It appears 41 times across 17 books, with its heaviest concentration in Jeremiah (10×) and Exodus (6×), often in contexts of stubborn resistance to divine commands, as when Pharaoh repeatedly refuses to let Israel go. All 26 verbal uses occur in the Piel stem, which gives the action a sense of deliberate, emphatic refusal rather than a casual or accidental one. Interestingly, the LXX most often renders it with θέλω (13×) — meaning 'to will' or 'to want' — framing the refusal as a matter of the will, which aligns with the Piel's connotation of purposeful, volitional rejection.
caution: The moderate confidence tier and the LXX's varied renderings (including εἰσακούω, meaning 'to listen/obey,' three times) suggest the word's nuance in a few passages is not entirely settled.

definition: To bring to an end or completion — whether finishing a task, consuming something entirely, or ceasing altogether.
article: כָּלָה covers the full arc from purposeful completion to total exhaustion or destruction. In the Qal stem it often means simply to end or cease; in the Piel it tends toward actively finishing or consuming something — a distinction that matters when the object is a building project versus an enemy. The word appears 205 times across 29 books, with a broad spread from Genesis to the Psalms to the prophets, showing it belongs to everyday Hebrew prose as much as poetry. The LXX overwhelmingly chooses συντελέω (

definition: To cover or shelter someone, used of protective covering in a blessing context.
article: חָפַף appears only once in the entire Old Testament, in Moses's blessing of Benjamin in Deuteronomy 33:12, where God is said to cover or shield Benjamin all day long. The word carries a sense of sheltering protection, similar to the way a parent might cover a child. Strong's connects it to related roots meaning to cover or to be barefoot, but in its single attested use the protective sense is unmistakable.
caution: This word occurs only once in the entire Hebrew Bible (a hapax legomenon), making its precise nuance difficult to confirm with certainty.

definition: A wind instrument made of reeds, likely a pipe or flute, used in music and worship contexts.
article: The word refers to a reed-based musical instrument, appearing only 4 times across Genesis, Job, and Psalms. Its root suggests breathing or blowing, consistent with a pipe or flute rather than a stringed instrument. Interestingly, the LXX twice renders it as κιθάρα (a stringed lyre), which suggests ancient translators were not entirely certain of its precise nature either. The KJV uniformly translates it as 'organ,' but that rendering reflects older English usage for any wind instrument, not the modern pipe organ.
caution: This word appears only 4 times and the LXX's inconsistent translation (once even rendering it as πάθος, meaning 'passion') signals genuine ancient uncertainty about its exact meaning; scholars debate whether it was a pipe, flute, or another reed instrument entirely.

definition: A specific rock or cliff city in Edom (Idumaea), referred to by name or as a literal rocky stronghold.
article: Sela was a notable rock-city associated with Edom (Idumaea), appearing only 3 times across Isaiah and 2 Kings. The word sits on the boundary between proper name and common noun, sometimes functioning as a place name and sometimes as a descriptive term for a rocky location. The Septuagint consistently renders it as πέτρα, the ordinary Greek word for rock, suggesting ancient translators sometimes read it as a common noun rather than a fixed place name.
caution: With only 3 occurrences and mixed grammatical roles, it is genuinely uncertain in some passages whether Sela refers to the specific Edomite city or simply to a rocky cliff, and the confidence tier for this entry is rated low.

definition: To be or become hot or warm, whether from the sun, body heat, or fire — literal heat in nearly all uses.
article: חָמַם means to be hot or to become warm, covering the full range from sunlight warming the ground (manna melting in Exodus 16) to a person warming an elderly king with body heat in 1 Kings 1. The word appears 13 times across 8 books, with the heaviest concentration in Isaiah (5×). The LXX translators rendered it as θερμαίνω (
caution: The confidence tier for this entry is rated low, and the relatively rare attestation (13 occurrences) means some contextual nuances — especially where the line between literal and figurative heat is drawn — remain uncertain.

definition: An Aramaic verb meaning to terrify or alarm someone, often expressed as acting in haste or urgent distress.
article: This is the Aramaic form of the root בָּהַל, found exclusively in the book of Daniel across all 11 of its Old Testament occurrences. It captures a blend of emotional alarm and the urgent rushing that fear produces — the KJV renders it both 'in haste' and 'trouble,' reflecting how terror and hurried action appear together in Daniel's narratives of royal crises. Strong's connects it directly to its Hebrew counterpart, which similarly spans the ideas of being terrified and acting in panicked haste.
caution: Confidence is low due to the word being confined to Aramaic Daniel with sparse attestation; the single attested verb stem (M stem) and mixed grammatical roles make its full semantic range difficult to pin down precisely.

definition: Hebron, a prominent city in Canaan and the name of at least two Israelites in the Old Testament.
article: Hebron is overwhelmingly used as a place name referring to the well-known city in the hill country of Canaan, appearing 71 times across 10 books. It figures most heavily in 2 Samuel (23 times) and Joshua (15 times), reflecting its importance as David's early capital and as a major city in the tribal allotments. Genesis introduces it early as the location near where Abraham settled and where Sarah was buried. The KJV translates the word consistently as Hebron every single time, and the name likely carries the sense of
caution: The confidence tier is marked moderate, possibly because Strong's notes it applies to two individuals as well as the city, making the referent occasionally ambiguous in context.

definition: A clan name referring to the Tirathites, a family of scribes living at Jabez, mentioned in Judah's genealogy.
article: Tirathites (תִּרְעָתִים) is a proper gentillic noun — a name identifying members of a particular group — appearing only once in the Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 2:55. There it names one of three scribal families living at Jabez, descended from or associated with the Kenites. Strong's notes the name derives from an unused root likely meaning 'gate,' but the actual settlement called Tirah is otherwise unknown to us.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon tied to an unidentified place name, so both the location and the precise meaning of the root remain uncertain.

definition: To be strong or mighty, especially in the sense of overpowering, prevailing, or surging beyond normal limits.
article: גָּבַר describes strength that asserts itself over something — not just being strong in a static sense, but strength that wins out, overwhelms, or surpasses. Its most vivid uses are in Genesis 7, where floodwaters "prevailed" and "surged greatly" over the earth, covering the mountains — a sense the LXX captures well with κατισχύω ("to overpower") used 5 times. The Hithpael stem, a reflexive-iterative form, adds a nuance of actively making oneself strong or exerting one's force, while the Piel and Hiphil forms carry causative weight. With only 25 occurrences across 13 books, the word is concentrated but not rare, appearing in narrative prose (Genesis, Exodus) and poetry (Psalms, Job) alike.
caution: The confidence tier is marked moderate, and there is some scholarly discussion about the precise distinction between this root and related strength-words like חָזַק and עָזַז; the exact nuance in a given context can be uncertain.

definition: A personal name referring to a specific Israelite official, one of Solomon's secretaries.
article: Elichoreph is a proper name appearing only once in the Old Testament, in 1 Kings 4:3, where he is listed as one of Solomon's scribes or secretaries. The name is generally understood to mean something like 'God of autumn,' combining the elements for God and the Hebrew word for harvest season. The LXX rendering reflects the translators working with the name contextually rather than translating it as a common noun.
caution: This word occurs only once in the entire Old Testament, making it a hapax legomenon as a proper name, and the precise meaning of its component parts remains uncertain.

definition: A building or constructed structure, referring to the physical form or frame of an edifice.
article: מִבְנֵה means a building or structural form, derived from the root בָּנָה ("to build"). It appears only once in the Old Testament, in Ezekiel 40:2, where it describes the visionary structure — likely the idealized temple — that Ezekiel sees in his prophetic vision. The KJV renders it simply as "frame," capturing the sense of a constructed outline or architectural form. Its single occurrence makes it difficult to establish a broader semantic range beyond this architectural context.
caution: This word is a hapax legomenon, appearing only once in the entire Old Testament, so its precise nuance rests entirely on a single context in Ezekiel's temple vision.

definition: A boundary line or border that marks the edge or full extent of a territory or region.
article: גְּבוּל refers to a boundary or border — the line that defines where one territory ends and another begins — and by extension the land enclosed within those borders. Its range is broad enough to cover anything from a property edge to a national frontier. The word appears 241 times across 25 books, with Joshua alone accounting for 84 occurrences, reflecting that book's detailed land-allotment surveys. The ancient Greek translators were remarkably consistent, rendering it as ὅριον ("boundary") 232 out of 241 times, confirming that territorial demarcation was understood as the word's clear core meaning.

definition: To press upon or urge compellingly, as a burden curves or bends a person toward action.
article: אָכַף appears only once in the Old Testament, in Proverbs 16:26, where it describes the driving force of hunger upon a laborer. The root suggests a physical image of being bent or curved under pressure, which then extends to the inner urge or craving that compels action. The LXX rendered it with μέντοι, a Greek particle meaning 'indeed' or 'however,' suggesting the ancient translators understood it as emphasizing the reality of this compulsion rather than translating the verb directly.
caution: This word is a hapax legomenon, appearing only once in the entire Hebrew Bible, making its precise meaning and root very difficult to establish with confidence.

definition: A specific gate of the Jerusalem temple, named 'Sur,' appearing only once in the Old Testament.
article: Sur is a proper name referring to a gate of the temple in Jerusalem, mentioned once in 2 Kings 11:6 in the context of the guard assignments during Athaliah's reign. Because it is treated as a proper name, the KJV simply transliterates it as 'Sur' rather than translating it. The underlying root may connect to a common Hebrew word, but in this single occurrence it functions purely as a place name identifying a specific architectural feature of the temple complex.
caution: This word occurs only once in the entire Old Testament (a hapax legomenon), and its exact location or identification as a gate is uncertain; some scholars think it may be the same gate called 'Foundation' in the parallel account in 2 Chronicles 23:5.

definition: A cattle-tender or herdsman who looks after oxen and livestock.
article: בּוֹקֵר means a herdsman, specifically one who tends cattle. It appears only once in the entire Old Testament, in Amos 7:14, where the prophet Amos famously identifies himself as 'a herdsman' before insisting he was not a professional prophet. The KJV consistently renders it 'herdman,' and the word derives from the same root as בָּקָר, the common Hebrew word for cattle or oxen.
caution: This word is a hapax legomenon, occurring only once in the OT, which limits certainty about its full semantic range.

definition: A natural channel, fissure, or cavern used as a hiding place in rocky terrain.
article: This word appears only once in the Old Testament, in Judges 6:2, where the Israelites hide from the Midianites in dens and strongholds. It describes a natural hollow in the rock — whether a channel, fissure, or full cave. The Greek translators chose τρυμαλιά, meaning a hole or opening, which confirms the sense of a narrow rocky cleft rather than a large open chamber. The KJV simply renders it 'den,' which captures the hiding-place function but slightly underplays the geological imagery of the original.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon — appearing only once in the entire Hebrew Old Testament — so its precise nuance cannot be confirmed by cross-referencing other contexts.

definition: To totter, slip, or give way — describing anything that loses stability and risks collapsing or falling.
article: מוֹט describes the loss of firm footing or stable support, whether physical (a foot slipping, a land shaking) or figurative (a nation, person, or institution on the verge of collapse). It appears 39 times and is heavily concentrated in Psalms (25 of those occurrences), which means the word carries a distinctly poetic and often theological weight — frequently describing what happens to the righteous or wicked when divine support is present or withdrawn. The Niphal stem dominates (23×), casting the subject as the one being moved or made to totter, while the Hiphil (2×) shifts the picture to an agent who causes something to slip. The LXX translations are unusually scattered — rendering it with words for "sinner," "cup," and "distress" in different passages — which reflects real interpretive difficulty in specific contexts.
caution: The confidence tier is moderate, and the LXX rendering choices are strikingly inconsistent, suggesting some contextual uses were genuinely puzzling to ancient translators and may remain uncertain today.

definition: A restraining device for an animal's head — a halter or bridle that controls by checking movement.
article: This rare word (only 4 times in the Old Testament, spread across Job, Psalms, and Isaiah) refers to a piece of equipment used to restrain or guide an animal, much like a halter or bridle. The core idea is physical control through checking movement, and by extension it can suggest the jaw or muzzle as the point of restraint. Psalm 32:9 uses it to warn against being like a horse or mule that needs such a device to be controlled — giving the word a clear metaphorical, moral edge in poetry. The LXX translators were notably inconsistent, rendering it as 'clothing' (ἔνδυσις), 'breastplate' (θώραξ), and 'bridle' (χαλινός), suggesting the ancient translators themselves were uncertain about its precise meaning.
caution: Confidence is rated low, the LXX offers three incompatible translations across four occurrences, and the root is otherwise unused in Hebrew, making the word's exact sense genuinely uncertain.

definition: An Aramaic preposition or conjunction meaning 'until,' 'up to,' or 'as far as,' marking a limit in time or extent.
senseLabels: As far as / to a point
article: This Aramaic word functions as a temporal or spatial limit marker, most often meaning 'until' or 'up to.' It appears 35 times, confined entirely to the Aramaic sections of Daniel (26×) and Ezra (9×), reflecting its Aramaic rather than Hebrew character. The LXX translators rendered it as ἕως ('until,' 'as far as') in 24 of those instances, confirming that ancient readers consistently understood it as a boundary or limit word. Its grammatical role as a relative pronoun in many occurrences also allows it to introduce clauses meaning 'to the point that' or 'so that.'
caution: Confidence is moderate because this is an Aramaic loanword with a limited OT footprint, and its grammatical classification as a 'relative pronoun' in some contexts sits alongside its prepositional uses, leaving the precise boundaries of each function somewhat debated.

definition: Zilpah is a personal name: the maidservant of Leah who became a secondary wife of Jacob and mother of Gad and Asher.
article: Zilpah is exclusively a proper name in the Old Testament, appearing all 7 times in Genesis as the handmaid given to Leah and later given by Leah to Jacob as a wife. All occurrences are concentrated in the patriarchal narratives of Genesis 29–35. Interestingly, the LXX does not simply transliterate the name in every case but occasionally renders surrounding narrative with verbs like συλλαμβάνω ("to conceive"), reflecting the translators' focus on the childbearing episodes associated with her.
caution: Strong's connects the name to an unused root possibly meaning "to trickle" or "fragrant dropping," but this etymology is unverified and the name's meaning remains uncertain.

definition: To cover or overlay a surface, used specifically of skin forming over bones in a vision.
article: קָרַם means to cover, and its two occurrences are both found in Ezekiel 37, the famous vision of the valley of dry bones. In both verses the word describes skin spreading over the bones as they come back to life. Because it appears only in this single passage, the full semantic range of the word is difficult to determine — it may have been a more common term whose other uses simply did not survive in the text we have.
caution: With only 2 occurrences in a single chapter, this word is effectively a near-hapax, making it nearly impossible to establish a broader semantic range with confidence.

definition: Ekron, a Philistine city in Canaan associated with territorial boundaries, conflict, and prophetic judgment.
article: Ekron is one of the five major cities of the Philistines, appearing 22 times across 8 books of the Old Testament. It features prominently in Joshua as a boundary marker for tribal territories, in 1 Samuel in connection with the ark of the covenant and battles with Israel, and the prophets Jeremiah, Amos, Zephaniah, and Zechariah all single it out as a target of divine judgment. The LXX consistently renders it as Akkaron, confirming it was understood purely as a place name throughout the ancient tradition.
caution: Strong's links the name to a root meaning 'eradication,' but place-name etymologies are frequently uncertain, and this connection should not be pressed.

definition: A cutting implement or blade, likely an axe or similar tool used for cutting.
article: This word appears only once in the Old Testament, at 2 Samuel 12:31, in the context of David subjecting the Ammonites to forced labor with iron tools. It derives from the root גָּזַר, meaning to cut, and Strong's defines it as a cutting implement or blade. The KJV renders it as 'axe,' and the LXX is notably split — one translator used διάγω (to pass through) and another used τρίβολος (a thorny or spiked object) — suggesting ancient uncertainty about the exact tool being described.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon appearing only once in the OT, and the divergent LXX translations indicate that even ancient scholars were unsure precisely what kind of cutting implement it refers to.

definition: A city or fortified town, used as a general term for a settled urban community.
article: קִרְיָה means a city or town, functioning as a standard Hebrew noun for an urban settlement. Its range is straightforward and narrow — the KJV translates it as 'city' every single time. The ancient Greek translators (LXX) rendered it consistently as πόλις, the ordinary Greek word for city, confirming that no special nuance was intended beyond a settled urban place. The word appears 29 times, concentrated especially in Isaiah (10×) and Proverbs (5×), giving it a slight lean toward poetic and prophetic contexts.
caution: The confidence tier is marked moderate, likely because the root derivation is somewhat uncertain, though the meaning itself is consistently attested as 'city' across all occurrences.

definition: A place name referring to a town in southern Judah, meaning 'settlement of the fox.'
article: Hazar-shual is a town name appearing 8 times across three books: Joshua, 1 Chronicles, and Nehemiah. In Joshua it appears in boundary lists for both Judah and Simeon, while Chronicles and Nehemiah place it in settlement records. The KJV consistently renders it as 'Hazar-shual,' simply transliterating the Hebrew rather than translating it, which reflects how firmly it functioned as a fixed proper name.
caution: The exact location of this site is uncertain, and confidence in identifying it archaeologically remains low.

definition: A person who is morally perverse and stubbornly foolish, rejecting wisdom and acting to their own ruin.
article: אֱוִיל describes someone who is not merely unintelligent but willfully and perversely foolish — a person who rejects wisdom and behaves ruinously. The word appears 26 times in the Old Testament, concentrated heavily in Proverbs (19 of 26 occurrences), which signals that this is a wisdom-literature term carrying real moral weight, not just a casual insult. The Septuagint most often renders it ἄφρων (11×), a Greek word meaning 'senseless' or 'mindless,' confirming that ancient readers heard in this word a failure of both mind and character. Psalm 107:17 captures the moral dimension well, linking the אֱוִיל's foolishness directly to suffering caused by their own rebellion.
caution: The root is listed as unused in Strong's, making the precise etymology uncertain and contributing to the moderate confidence rating for this word's core sense.

definition: A sudden, unexpected moment — used adverbially to mean instantly or without warning.
article: פֶּ֫תַע describes a moment of abrupt action, conveying both the brevity of an instant and the element of surprise. It appears 7 times across just 4 books — Numbers, Proverbs, Isaiah, and Habakkuk — mostly in contexts of sudden disaster or judgment. The LXX translators most often chose παραχρῆμα (meaning 'immediately') and ἐξάπινα ('suddenly'), confirming that ancient readers heard both speed and unexpectedness in the word. It functions adverbially throughout, often in phrases like 'at an instant' describing swift, irreversible calamity.
caution: The root is listed in Strong's as unused, meaning the word's derivation is reconstructed rather than directly attested, which introduces some uncertainty about its core meaning.

definition: A personal name of a Levitical musician appointed by David in 1 Chronicles 25.
article: Asarelah is a proper name appearing exactly once in the Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 25:2, where he is listed as a son of Asaph appointed to prophetic music in the temple service. Strong's notes a connection to the name Jesarelah (יְשַׂרְאֵ֫לָה), which may be a variant form of the same individual in verse 14. Because the name occurs only as a personal name, its semantic content is simply its identification of this particular musician in David's organized worship roster.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon appearing only once, and the relationship between this spelling and the variant Jesarelah (1 Chr 25:14) is uncertain — they may refer to the same person under different name forms.

definition: To say, speak, tell, or command — the basic Aramaic verb for verbal communication in all its forms.
article: This is the Aramaic equivalent of the common Hebrew verb for speech, used 71 times across just three books: Daniel (65 times), Ezra (5 times), and Jeremiah (once). It covers the full range of verbal communication, from ordinary conversation to royal commands, which reflects the Aramaic diplomatic and administrative contexts found in Daniel and Ezra. All attested occurrences are in the Qal stem, the basic active form, keeping its meaning straightforward. The concentration in Daniel is especially notable, where it frequently introduces the speech of kings and officials in the Babylonian and Persian court narratives.
caution: This is an Aramaic entry, not Hebrew, and its single occurrence in Jeremiah (a predominantly Hebrew book) may reflect an isolated Aramaic passage or scribal variation; the moderate confidence tier suggests some uncertainty in classification.

definition: A crossing-place or ford where people pass over a body of water.
article: This rare Hebrew noun refers to a place for crossing over water — essentially a ford or ferry point. It appears only twice in the Old Testament, both in 2 Samuel, in narratives connected to David's flight and return during Absalom's rebellion. The LXX renders it with διαβαίνω, a verb meaning 'to cross over,' which confirms the sense of a physical crossing-place rather than anything abstract.
caution: With only 2 occurrences in a single book and a low confidence tier, the precise nuance — whether a natural ford or an operated ferry crossing — remains uncertain.

definition: A large desert bird, most likely an ostrich or a species of owl, associated with desolate and ruined places.
article: This word appears 8 times across 6 books, consistently in contexts of desolation and ruin — waste places, cursed lands, and barren wilderness. The KJV translates it as 'owl,' but its appearance alongside other creatures of the desert in passages like Isaiah 13:21 and 34:13 has led many translators to favor 'ostrich' as the intended bird. The LXX evidence and the word's distribution in prophetic literature (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Micah) suggest it carries a strong literary association with divine judgment and abandonment of once-inhabited places.
caution: The exact species is genuinely uncertain — scholars debate whether this refers to an owl or an ostrich, and Strong's simply defines it as the feminine form of a related word without resolving the identification.

definition: A fixed food ration or regular allowance of provisions granted by an authority to a dependent person.
article: אֲרֻחָה refers to a set, appointed portion of food — the kind officially allocated rather than freely chosen. It appears 6 times across Jeremiah, 2 Kings, and Proverbs. Its most vivid uses are in 2 Kings 25:30 and Jeremiah 52:34, where the exiled king Jehoiachin receives a regular daily allowance from the Babylonian king — a striking picture of provision under captivity. Proverbs 15:17 contrasts a simple meal eaten in love with a lavish feast eaten in hatred, where the word carries the sense of an everyday dinner.
caution: The root אָרַח in the sense of 'appointing' behind this noun is itself uncertain, and the word's sparse attestation (only 6 occurrences in 3 books) limits confidence in fully mapping its semantic range.

definition: A personal name — the youngest son of Ishmael, listed among the twelve Ishmaelite tribal leaders.
article: Kedemah is the name of the youngest of Ishmael's twelve sons, appearing in the genealogical lists of Genesis 25:15 and its parallel in 1 Chronicles 1:31. The KJV renders it consistently as 'Kedemah' in both occurrences, and the name appears only in these two parallel passages. Strong's connects the name to the root meaning 'precedence' or 'eastward,' but in the text it functions purely as a proper name for a tribal ancestor.
caution: With only 2 occurrences, both in parallel genealogical lists, virtually nothing can be said about this figure beyond the name itself; any meaning drawn from the underlying root remains speculative.

definition: The olive tree, its fruit, or the oil it produces — a central agricultural and symbolic plant of ancient Israel.
article: זַיִת refers to the olive in its several forms: the tree itself, its fruit, and by extension the groves where it grew. Its 38 occurrences spread across 21 books reflect how central the olive was to Israelite life — providing oil for lamps (Exodus 27:20), anointing oil (Exodus 30:24), and food. The LXX translators used ἐλαία (26×) for the tree or fruit and ἐλαιών (7×) for olive groves, showing that ancient readers recognized the word could point to either the individual plant or an entire orchard. Zechariah's five uses are especially striking, where olive trees appear in visionary imagery alongside lampstands.
caution: The precise root is uncertain — Strong's notes it derives from an unused root — but the word's meaning as 'olive' is not in dispute across any of its occurrences.

definition: Fragments or broken pieces resulting from something shattered to ruin.
article: שְׁבָבִים refers to the broken pieces or fragments left after something is smashed apart, derived from a root meaning to break up. It appears only once in the Old Testament, in Hosea 8:6, where the prophet declares that the calf-idol of Samaria will be broken to pieces — a vivid image of total destruction. The KJV renders it 'broken in pieces,' which captures the concrete physical sense well. Because the root itself is not otherwise attested in Hebrew, the word's full range rests entirely on this single occurrence.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon (occurring only once, in Hosea 8:6), and its root is listed as unused, so the meaning relies almost entirely on context and cognate inference rather than broad attestation.

definition: A narrow fissure or cleft in rock, used as a natural hiding place or shelter.
article: נִקְרַת refers to a crack or hollow split in rock. It appears only twice in the Old Testament — once in Exodus 33:22, where God hides Moses in a cleft of the rock, and once in Isaiah 2:21, where people flee into rock crevices in fear. The Greek translators rendered it with ὀπή, meaning a hole or opening, confirming the sense of a narrow, enclosed gap in stone rather than a broad cave.
caution: With only 2 occurrences across the entire Old Testament, the precise nuance of the word's shape or size cannot be determined with confidence.

definition: A Persian royal title used in the Old Testament to refer to a specific Persian king, most likely Xerxes I, appearing almost entirely in the book of Esther.
article: Ahasuerus is a Hebrew rendering of a Persian royal title, which Strong's notes likely refers to Xerxes I (reigning circa 486–465 BC), though it is sometimes linked to Artaxerxes. Of its 32 occurrences, 30 are concentrated in Esther, with single appearances in Ezra and Daniel. The LXX evidence is notably unusual: instead of consistently transliterating the name, ancient Greek translators rendered it with common Greek words like πολύς (
caution: The LXX's failure to consistently transliterate this name — using ordinary Greek words rather than a proper name — raises genuine uncertainty about how the Greek translators understood the text, and scholars continue to debate whether Ahasuerus always refers to the same historical figure across Esther, Ezra, and Daniel.

definition: Hail or hailstones, frozen precipitation falling as a destructive weather event.
article: בָּרָד refers to hail or hailstones, the frozen precipitation that falls as a destructive force from the sky. Its range is quite narrow — this word means hail and essentially nothing else. The heavy concentration in Exodus (17 of 29 occurrences) reflects the seventh plague on Egypt, while appearances in Psalms, Isaiah, and Job show it also serves as a poetic image of divine judgment and power. The LXX overwhelmingly renders it as χάλαζα (25 of 29 times), the standard Greek word for hail, confirming that ancient readers understood it with no ambiguity.
caution: The three non-standard LXX renderings (ὄψις, ὑετός, φλογίζω) are unusual enough to suggest possible textual or translation irregularities in a handful of passages, though the word's overall meaning is not in dispute.

definition: To stumble, totter, or collapse through weakness — ranging from a physical trip to moral failure, defeat, or ruin.
article: כָּשַׁל covers the full arc from a literal stumble — weak legs giving way underfoot — to the collapse of armies, nations, and individuals under pressure. The Qal stem describes the basic act of stumbling or faltering, while the Hiphil carries the causative sense of making someone else fall or fail. The word's concentration in Isaiah, Jeremiah, Hosea, and Daniel suggests it is especially at home in prophetic warnings about national ruin. The LXX's dominant choice, ἀσθενέω (
caution: to be weak or sick,

definition: A personal name meaning 'heard by Yah,' belonging to an Israelite mentioned in Nehemiah.
article: Azaniah is a proper name appearing once in the Old Testament, in Nehemiah 10:10, where it identifies the father of Jeshua, one of the Levites who sealed the covenant. The name combines a verb meaning 'to hear' or 'to give ear' with the divine name Yah, suggesting the meaning 'Yah has heard.' Because it is a personal name with a single occurrence, its semantic range is entirely confined to identifying this one individual.
caution: This word occurs only once in the entire Old Testament, making any analysis beyond its function as a proper name impossible to verify.

definition: A personal name belonging to a descendant of Seir the Horite, listed in Edomite genealogy.
article: Chemdan (also spelled Hemdan in the KJV) is a proper name appearing once in the Old Testament, in the genealogy of the Horites of Edom in Genesis 36:26. Strong's notes the name likely carries the sense of 'pleasant,' connecting it to the root for desirability or delight, though as a proper name its meaning would not have been felt actively by readers. Interestingly, the Septuagint renders the name as Charrhan, suggesting the ancient Greek translators either had a variant textual tradition or adapted the name according to their own conventions.
caution: This word occurs only once in the entire Old Testament, making it a hapax in terms of context; as a proper name with only one attestation, nothing beyond its genealogical placement can be confidently established.

definition: A whisperer or talebearer who spreads damaging talk and stirs up division among people.
article: This word describes someone who spreads harmful rumors or whispers — the kind of person whose words quietly destroy relationships and trust. All four occurrences appear exclusively in Proverbs, which fits its elevated, moralistic register: the book uses it to warn that such a person fuels conflict the way fuel feeds a fire (Proverbs 26:20). The KJV translates it as both 'talebearer' and 'whisperer,' capturing the sneaky, behind-the-back quality of the behavior. The word functions as both a verb (Niphal stem, suggesting the action of being or acting as a whisperer) and a noun describing the person themselves.
caution: Confidence is low: the root is listed as unused, meaning the word's precise etymology is uncertain, and with only 4 occurrences confined to one book, the full semantic range is difficult to establish with certainty.

definition: A personal name for a king of Judah; the name itself means 'the LORD will raise up.'
article: Jehoiakim was a king of Judah, originally named Eliakim, whose name was changed by Pharaoh Necho when he was installed as a vassal ruler (2 Kings 23:34). The name appears 37 times across 5 books, with the heaviest concentration in Jeremiah (23 times), reflecting that prophet's extensive engagement with Jehoiakim's reign and its consequences. The LXX evidence here is unusual — the Greek equivalents listed (Babylon, send, innocent, blood, Chaldean) are almost certainly surrounding context words rather than translations of the name itself, which ancient translators would have simply transliterated, consistent with standard practice for proper names.
