definition: A rare word for brilliant, radiant brightness or luminous splendor.
article: זֹהַר refers to intense, shining brilliance — the kind of dazzling luminosity associated with celestial or divine glory. It appears only twice in the Old Testament, once in Ezekiel and once in Daniel, both visionary or apocalyptic contexts. The LXX renders it with φωστήρ, meaning 'luminary' or 'light-bearer,' suggesting ancient readers understood it as something close to a glowing celestial body rather than mere reflected light.
caution: With only 2 occurrences, both in late prophetic-visionary texts, the full semantic range of this word cannot be established with confidence, and its precise nuance remains uncertain.

definition: A personal name identifying one or two Nethinim (temple servants) mentioned in post-exilic lists.
article: Tsiha (also spelled Ziha in most English Bibles) is a proper name appearing all 3 of its times in the post-exilic books of Ezra and Nehemiah, specifically in lists of Nethinim — the hereditary temple servants who returned from Babylon. The name may refer to two different individuals: one whose descendants are listed among the returning exiles, and one who was an overseer of the Nethinim at Ophel. Because the KJV always renders it simply as 'Ziha,' there is no meaningful range of translation to discuss.
caution: With only 3 occurrences all in list contexts, and Strong's suggesting the name may derive from a root meaning 'drought,' the etymology and whether one or two distinct individuals are intended remains genuinely uncertain.

definition: A first-ripe fig, referring to the earliest and choicest figs of the season.
article: This word refers to a first-ripe fig, the earliest fruit to ripen on the fig tree, considered especially desirable. It appears only once in the Old Testament, in Jeremiah 24:2, where it describes a basket of exceptionally good figs. The LXX renders it with both σῦκον (fig) and πρώϊμος (early/first), together capturing both the fruit itself and its quality as the season's first and best. Strong's identifies it as a spelling variant of the related Hebrew word בִּכּוּרָה, meaning the same thing.
caution: This word occurs only once in the entire Old Testament (a hapax legomenon), so its range of meaning rests on a single passage and its relationship to a closely related form.

definition: Something possessed or inherited; a holding that belongs to someone, occasionally used for cherished thoughts or desires.
article: This rare noun comes from the root meaning to possess or inherit, and its core sense is a thing that belongs to someone — land, territory, or an inherited holding. Its three occurrences spread across Job, Isaiah, and Obadiah suggest it appeared in elevated or poetic contexts rather than everyday prose. In Job 17:11 it is rendered as 'thoughts' in the KJV, showing the word could extend metaphorically to things a person holds close internally, much as one holds property. The LXX evidence does not narrow the range further, so both the concrete and figurative senses should be kept in view.
caution: With only 3 occurrences across the entire Old Testament and a KJV gloss as unusual as 'thought,' the exact semantic range is uncertain and confidence in the figurative sense is low.

definition: A noun meaning abundance or majority, used of large numbers, great quantities, or interest charged on a loan.
article: מַרְבִּית refers to something that is large in amount or proportion — a multitude, the greatest part of a group, or growth of some kind. Its range spans from numerical majority (the bulk of a crowd or army) to financial increase (interest charged on capital), showing how Hebrew uses one root to cover what English splits into separate ideas. The LXX twice chose πλεῖστος, meaning 'very many' or 'most,' which confirms that the dominant sense ancient readers recognized was sheer quantity or majority. With only 5 occurrences spread across Leviticus, Samuel, and Chronicles, the word is rare enough that context must do heavy work in pinning down which shade of meaning is intended.
caution: With only 5 occurrences and a confidence tier rated low, the precise boundaries between its senses — majority, offspring, and financial interest — are difficult to establish firmly, and translators have disagreed on several of the individual verses.

definition: A rare adjective describing something twisted, bent, or coiling in shape — used of a serpent.
article: This adjective appears only once in the entire Old Testament, in Isaiah 27:1, where it describes Leviathan as the 'crooked' or 'coiling' serpent. It comes from a root meaning tortuous or twisted, vividly picturing the sinuous movement of a great serpent. The LXX renders the passage with imagery of a fleeing and coiling dragon, reinforcing the sense of writhing, unpredictable motion.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon — appearing only once in the Hebrew Bible — so its precise nuance cannot be confirmed by comparison with other contexts.

definition: A garment or piece of clothing, measured or cut to a specific length or extent.
article: מַדְוֵי refers to a garment or item of clothing. It appears only twice in the Old Testament, both times in parallel accounts of the same incident — the humiliation of David's servants by the Ammonites, whose garments were cut short (2 Samuel 10:4 and 1 Chronicles 19:4). The word's root suggests the idea of measured extent, which may reflect how garments were understood as cloth measured and cut to a fitting length. The KJV consistently renders it simply as "garment," and the LXX similarly uses standard Greek clothing vocabulary, offering no additional nuance.
caution: This word occurs only twice, both in parallel passages describing the same event, making it nearly a hapax in terms of distinct context; its precise meaning depends on an otherwise unattested root, keeping confidence low.

definition: An enclosure or pen where flocks of sheep or cattle are kept.
article: This rare word appears only 3 times in the Old Testament, twice in Psalms and once in Habakkuk, always referring to a livestock enclosure or fold. The KJV consistently renders it as 'fold' or 'sheepfold,' and the root connects to the idea of confining or shutting in animals. The LXX translations are strikingly inconsistent — using Greek words meaning 'to whiten,' 'to sprinkle,' 'hyssop,' and 'snow' — suggesting the ancient Greek translators were uncertain about its meaning in context.
caution: Confidence is low: with only 3 occurrences and widely scattered LXX renderings that do not point to a single consistent understanding, the precise meaning remains uncertain and scholarly agreement is limited.

definition: A personal name meaning 'known of God,' belonging to a leader of the tribe of Gad in the wilderness period.
article: Deuel is a proper name appearing all 4 times in the book of Numbers, always identifying the same individual: the father of Eliasaph, who was the appointed leader representing the tribe of Gad. The name combines the Hebrew roots for 'to know' and 'God,' suggesting the meaning 'known of God.' Because it is a personal name, the KJV simply transliterates it as Deuel in every instance.
caution: The confidence tier is flagged as low, and some manuscripts and translations read 'Reuel' instead of 'Deuel' in at least one passage, suggesting possible scribal variation in the transmission of this name.

definition: A solemn, binding agreement or covenant between two parties, often sealed by ritual and carrying lasting obligations.

definition: Upbringing or tutelage; the training and nurture received under a guardian's care.
article: אָמְנָה refers to the care and training a child receives from a guardian or foster-parent — essentially one's upbringing. It appears only once in the Old Testament, in Esther 2:20, where it describes how Esther had been raised under Mordecai's guardianship. The LXX renders it with three different Greek words across manuscript traditions, including πατρίς (homeland/origin) and ἀγωγή (upbringing/conduct), showing ancient translators understood it as pointing to Esther's background and formation. This single occurrence makes it a hapax legomenon, but its meaning fits naturally within the broader Hebrew root related to faithfulness, firmness, and trustworthy care.
caution: This word occurs only once in the entire Old Testament, making it a hapax legomenon; its precise nuance relies heavily on context and the related root rather than broad attestation.

definition: An adjective meaning dark or swarthy in complexion, describing a deeply sun-darkened skin tone.
article: This word appears only once in the entire Old Testament, in Song of Solomon 1:6, where the beloved describes herself as darkened by the sun. It is an intensified or reduplicated form related to the root for 'black' or 'dark,' conveying a deep, swarthy brownness rather than absolute blackness. The KJV simply renders it 'black,' but the form suggests an intensified or nuanced shade — more like 'very dark' or 'swarthy.' Its single appearance in the love poetry of Song of Solomon fits the elevated, descriptive register of that book.
caution: This word occurs only once in the Old Testament (a hapax legomenon), so its precise shade of meaning cannot be confirmed through broader usage patterns.

definition: To flow, pour out, or run down — liquid spilling, trickling, or being poured away — sometimes with the sense of being delivered over or stretched out.
article: נָגַר describes the motion of liquid moving downward — trickling, running, or being poured out — and by extension the idea of something being given over or discharged entirely. The range runs from literal flowing water to figurative images of life or fate draining away. It appears most often in poetic books (Psalms accounts for 3 of the 10 occurrences), which fits the word's frequent use in vivid imagery of dissolution and loss. The Septuagint renders it with καταφέρω, a Greek word meaning 'to bring or carry down,' confirming that ancient readers heard a strong sense of downward movement in this root.
caution: With only 10 occurrences across 7 books and a low confidence tier, the precise semantic boundaries — especially the figurative sense of 'delivering over' — remain uncertain and are not always clearly supported by context.

definition: To strip bare or expose something — whether uncovering a body in disgrace, baring an arm for action, or draining away water.
article: חָשַׂף describes the act of making something naked or bare, with a range spanning human disgrace, dramatic divine action, and physical removal of water. It appears 11 times across 6 books, concentrated heavily in the prophets — especially Isaiah with 4 occurrences. The most striking usage is Isaiah 52:10, where God 'bares his holy arm' before the nations, a gesture of readiness for powerful action. The Septuagint twice renders it with ἀποκαλύπτω, the same Greek word used for 'revelation' or 'uncovering,' confirming that ancient readers understood the word as a broad act of exposure or disclosure.
caution: Confidence is rated low, and the word's sense of 'draining or bailing out liquid' (attested in Isaiah 30:14) sits somewhat awkwardly alongside the 'stripping bare' sense, suggesting the root may cover more ground than surviving examples clearly establish.

definition: A high-ranking military officer or official, though the word can also refer to a three-fold measure or a three-stringed musical instrument.
article: The dominant use of שָׁלִישׁ across the Old Testament is as a title for a senior military officer — appearing 8 times in 2 Kings alone, often alongside chariots and armies. The KJV renders it variously as 'captain,' 'lord,' and 'prince,' reflecting genuine uncertainty about the precise rank, though it clearly denotes someone near the top of a military or royal hierarchy. Less frequently, the word seems to refer to a three-fold unit of dry measure, and in one or two poetic or musical contexts it may indicate a stringed instrument. The LXX translators used different Greek words depending on context, which confirms that ancient readers recognized this word's range of meaning rather than locking it to a single sense.
caution: The precise meaning in any given context — military rank, measure, or instrument — is genuinely disputed, and scholars disagree about whether these are related senses of one root or effectively different words that share a form; confidence is only moderate.

definition: To bristle or stand on end, as hair does in response to fear or awe.
article: סָמַר describes the physical sensation of hair standing on end, specifically in moments of terror or overwhelming reverence. It appears only twice in the Old Testament — once in Job 4:15, where a spirit passing by causes the speaker's hair to bristle, and once in Psalm 119:120, where the psalmist's flesh bristles in fear of God. Both occurrences sit in poetic contexts, fitting the elevated register typical of Job and Psalms. The KJV renders it both 'stand up' and 'tremble,' capturing the physical and emotional dimensions of the experience.
caution: With only 2 occurrences across the entire Old Testament, this is a very rare word, and confidence in its precise semantic range is low.

definition: A stinging insect, most likely a hornet or wasp, used in the Old Testament as a divine weapon to drive out Israel's enemies.
article: This word appears only 3 times in the Old Testament, always in the same narrative context: God promises to send the hornet ahead of Israel to drive out the Canaanites (Exodus 23:28, Deuteronomy 7:20, Joshua 24:12). All major English translations consistently render it 'hornet.' Interestingly, the Septuagint chose the Greek word πρότερος ('the one going before') rather than a word for an insect, suggesting some ancient translators understood the term more figuratively — perhaps as a vanguard force — rather than literally as a wasp or hornet.
caution: The LXX's choice of πρότερος instead of a Greek insect word raises genuine uncertainty about whether the Hebrew term referred to a literal hornet, a metaphor for a terror-striking advance force, or something else entirely, and scholarly opinion remains divided.

definition: A man or strong person, used as a poetic term for a human being.
article: גְּבַר is a rare poetic noun meaning 'man' or 'person,' appearing only once in the Old Testament, in Psalm 18:26. It is closely related to the more common גֶּבֶר, and Strong's connects both to the root גָּבַר, which carries the sense of strength or might. The Septuagint renders the surrounding verse in ways that emphasize moral character, reflecting how this term fits into a poetic context about how God deals with different kinds of people.
caution: This word appears only once in the entire Old Testament (a near-hapax), making its precise nuance difficult to establish with confidence beyond its clear relationship to the common root for 'man.'

definition: A Hebrew personal name meaning 'Yahweh has built,' borne by multiple distinct individuals in the Old Testament.
article: Benaiah is a proper name appearing 42 times across 6 books, with the heaviest concentration in 1 Kings (15×) and 1 Chronicles (14×). The most prominent bearer is Benaiah son of Jehoiada, a celebrated warrior under David and Solomon who commanded the royal bodyguard. The KJV consistently renders the name as 'Benaiah,' and Strong's identifies at least twelve different individuals who carried this name in the Hebrew Bible.
caution: The LXX translation evidence is puzzling — Greek words meaning 'thousand,' 'sea,' 'greatly,' 'wise,' and 'sand' appear, which almost certainly reflects transliteration inconsistencies or textual confusion in the LXX manuscript tradition rather than genuine semantic range, so LXX evidence is unreliable for this entry.

definition: To spin thread or fiber, as in preparing textile material by twisting raw fibers together.
article: This verb appears only twice in the Old Testament, both in Exodus 35, describing skilled women who spun yarn for the tabernacle. The Qal stem is used in both cases, carrying the straightforward sense of spinning raw material into usable thread. The LXX evidence is mixed but includes νήθω, the standard Greek word for spinning, confirming the core meaning, alongside αἴγειος and θρίξ (referring to goat hair), which reflects the specific material being spun in context rather than the verb's meaning itself.
caution: With only 2 occurrences in a single chapter, this is nearly a hapax legomenon, and the low confidence tier signals limited grounds for expanding its meaning beyond basic spinning.

definition: To flow over or flood, describing water that overflows, sweeps away, or causes something to float or swim.
article: צוּף means to overflow or flow over, with the Qal stem describing water in motion and the Hiphil (causative) stem meaning to make something float — as when Elisha caused an iron axe head to float in 2 Kings 6:6. The word appears only 3 times across 3 books, spanning law, narrative, and poetry. Its most striking use is in Lamentations 3:54, where waters flowing over the speaker's head becomes a vivid image of near-death despair. The KJV renders it both "flow" and "swim," reflecting this dual sense of flooding and floating.
caution: With only 3 occurrences across the entire Old Testament, the full semantic range is difficult to establish with confidence, and this low-frequency root should be interpreted cautiously in any given context.

definition: An encampment or camp, especially of troops or travelers, and by extension the army or company itself that occupies it.
article: מַחֲנֶה refers to a camp as a physical site and, by extension, to the group gathered there — most often soldiers, but also traveling caravans, angels, and even livestock. With 216 occurrences spread across narrative and legal literature, it is one of the most common nouns in the Hebrew Bible, appearing most densely in Numbers (49×), Judges (28×), and 1 Samuel (22×), reflecting its strong association with Israel's wilderness wandering and military history. The Septuagint renders it almost exclusively as παρεμβολή (218×), a Greek military term for an encampment or fortified position, confirming that ancient readers understood its core sense as a structured, organized gathering rather than a loose assembly. The KJV range — camp, host, army, company, drove, tents — reflects how naturally Hebrew shifts between the place and the people in it.

definition: A place name referring to a location near the wilderness, mentioned as one of the geographical markers in Moses' farewell address.
article: תֹּפֶל (Tophel) appears only once in the Old Testament, in Deuteronomy 1:1, as part of a list of locations used to identify where Moses delivered his final speeches to Israel. Its exact geographical location remains unidentified by modern archaeology. The KJV simply transliterates the Hebrew as "Tophel," and the word appears to share a root with a term meaning quagmire or muddy ground, though in context it functions purely as a proper place name.
caution: The site of Tophel is archaeologically unconfirmed, and the word occurs only once in the entire Old Testament, making its meaning and location highly uncertain.

definition: The act of searching out or investigating something, often used to describe the limits of what can be discovered or understood.
article: חֵקֶר refers to the process of thorough examination or searching, but it appears most often in contexts that stress the impossibility of such searching — things beyond human reach or comprehension. Its heavy concentration in Job (7 of its 12 occurrences) fits that book's central preoccupation with the limits of human knowledge before God's wisdom. The LXX translators split notably between ἀνεξιχνίαστος (

definition: Fine white linen fabric, and occasionally marble, both valued for their bright, bleached appearance.
article: This word refers primarily to high-quality white linen fabric, the kind used extensively in the tabernacle's curtains, screens, and priestly garments as described in Exodus, where it appears 33 of its 42 times. The LXX translators rendered it βύσσος — the standard Greek word for fine linen — 22 times, confirming that ancient readers understood it as a prestigious textile. Outside of Exodus, it describes luxury fabrics in Esther's royal palace and the beloved's appearance in Song of Solomon, and Ezekiel uses it for costly trade goods. In a small number of contexts it appears to refer to white marble rather than cloth, both meanings sharing the idea of something brilliantly white and refined.
caution: Confidence is moderate because the KJV occasionally renders this word as 'silk' or 'blue,' and the precise material — whether Egyptian linen, another fine fiber, or marble — can be difficult to determine in specific contexts.

definition: A Gileadite — a person belonging to or descended from the clan or region of Gilead.
article: Gileadite refers to someone identified with Gilead, whether by descent from the man Gilead or by connection to the Transjordanian region his clan settled. The KJV translates it the same way every time — 'Gileadite' — and the 11 occurrences are spread across historical and administrative books, appearing most often in Judges where figures like Jephthah are specifically identified by this designation. Its use is almost entirely as a gentillic (a descriptor of ethnic or regional belonging), which explains why 10 of 11 occurrences are tagged as such rather than as a common noun.
caution: Confidence is rated low, likely because the word straddles both genealogical descent and regional geography, making it unclear in individual cases whether 'Gileadite' signals tribal lineage or simply place of origin.

definition: To pull or draw someone out, especially from water or a dangerous situation.
article: מָשָׁה means to pull or draw something out, with all three occurrences involving rescue from peril. Its most famous use is in Exodus 2:10, where it provides the folk etymology for the name Moses — he was drawn out of the water. The same imagery appears in 2 Samuel 22:17 and Psalm 18:17, where God is pictured reaching down to draw the psalmist out of deep waters. The LXX renders it with ἑλκύω, meaning to drag or pull, confirming the physical sense of forceful extraction.
caution: This root occurs only 3 times in the OT, making its full semantic range difficult to establish with confidence; confidence tier is rated low.

definition: A violently wronged person; someone who has been oppressed or robbed by force.
article: חָמוֹץ appears only once in the Old Testament, in Isaiah 1:17, where it is translated 'oppressed' in the KJV. The word comes from the root חָמֵץ and carries the sense of someone subjected to violent, forceful wrongdoing — essentially a victim of robbery or brutal mistreatment. Its sole occurrence in Isaiah's call to justice ('relieve the oppressed') places it in a powerful ethical and legal context, where caring for the wronged is a core moral demand.
caution: This word occurs only once in the entire Old Testament (a hapax legomenon), so its precise meaning rests heavily on its root derivation and context rather than broad usage evidence.

definition: Household idols or figurines used for divination and family religion, apparently associated with healing or oracular guidance.
article: Teraphim were physical objects kept in homes and used in family religious practice throughout the Old Testament period. Rachel hid her father Laban's teraphim (Genesis 31), Micah set them up alongside an ephod (Judges 17), and David's wife Michal placed one in his bed to fake his presence (1 Samuel 19). The LXX most often renders the word as εἴδωλον, the standard Greek term for an idol, suggesting ancient translators viewed these straightforwardly as idolatrous images, though one occurrence is rendered δῆλος, a word associated with oracular revelation, hinting at their divinatory function.
caution: The root connection to רָפָא ('to heal') is uncertain, the meaning of the singular form is disputed, and scholars remain divided on exactly what teraphim looked like and how they were used — hence the low confidence rating.

definition: An Aramaic word meaning 'kind' or 'sort,' used to categorize types of things.
article: This Aramaic noun means 'kind' or 'sort,' used to classify or categorize something by type. All four of its Old Testament occurrences appear in a single chapter, Daniel 3, where it describes the various kinds of musical instruments played at Nebuchadnezzar's command. Its extremely narrow distribution — one chapter, one book — reflects its status as an Aramaic term embedded in the Aramaic sections of Daniel rather than a standard Hebrew word.
caution: Confidence is low: this is a rare Aramaic term with only 4 occurrences in a single chapter, and Strong's links it to a Hebrew counterpart that is itself unlisted, leaving its broader semantic range difficult to verify.

definition: To wither or dry up, describing vegetation that fades and dies.
article: קָמַל describes the wilting or withering of plants, appearing only twice in the Old Testament, both times in Isaiah. In Isaiah 19:6 it pictures the reeds and rushes of Egypt's Nile drying up, and in Isaiah 33:9 Lebanon's vegetation withers as a sign of devastation. The KJV renders it once as 'wither' and once as 'hew down,' though the core meaning is consistently about vegetation dying off.
caution: This word occurs only twice, both in Isaiah, making its full semantic range difficult to establish with confidence; the 'hew down' KJV gloss is an unusual rendering that may obscure the word's true meaning.

definition: To burn with strong emotion, especially anger or jealousy, flaring up intensely against a person or situation.
article: חָרָה describes the experience of anger as a kind of heat or fire — the emotion blazes up rather than simply existing. It covers the full range from personal irritation to divine wrath, and appears 90 times across 20 books, with heavy use in narrative-rich books like Genesis, Numbers, and Samuel where interpersonal and divine conflicts are central. The LXX translators split almost evenly between θυμόω (to be enraged) and ὀργίζω (to be angry), both strong Greek words, confirming that ancient readers understood this as genuine, intense anger rather than mild displeasure. The Hithpael stem (4 occurrences) carries a reflexive or iterative sense — working oneself up into anger or competing hotly — adding a nuance of emotional escalation.
caution: The moderate confidence tier likely reflects some uncertainty about the boundary between the literal sense of heat and the figurative sense of anger, and whether certain forms belong to this root or to the related root חָרַר (to burn literally).

definition: An Aramaic word for a day or period of time, functioning identically to its Hebrew counterpart.
article: This is the Aramaic form of the common Hebrew word for 'day,' appearing 16 times in the Old Testament — 11 times in Daniel and 5 times in Ezra, the two books that contain Aramaic sections. It can refer to a literal calendar day or a broader stretch of time, matching the flexible range of its Hebrew equivalent. Ancient translators of the Septuagint consistently rendered it as ἡμέρα, the standard Greek word for 'day,' confirming that its meaning was straightforward and unambiguous to them.
caution: This entry is flagged low confidence, and its sparse attestation — only 16 occurrences across just 2 books — means its full range of use in Biblical Aramaic is difficult to assess with certainty.

definition: A people or nation viewed as a gathered community, often in parallel with similar terms for ethnic or political groups.
article: לְאֹם refers to a community of people bound together, whether as an ethnic group, a nation, or a people. Its range is essentially covered by just two English words — 'nation' and 'people' — which the KJV uses interchangeably to translate it. The word appears almost entirely in poetry and elevated speech: 26 of its 36 occurrences are in Psalms and Isaiah, giving it a distinctly literary register. The LXX most often renders it ἔθνος (nation, 14×) but also λαός (people, 8×), confirming that ancient readers saw it as a near-synonym for both terms, used especially in poetic parallelism.
caution: Confidence is moderate; the root is listed as unused in Hebrew, making the word's precise nuance difficult to pin down with certainty.

definition: A Hebrew personal name meaning 'Yahweh has opened,' borne by several Israelites in the post-exilic period.
article: Pethahiah is a proper name appearing 4 times across Nehemiah, 1 Chronicles, and Ezra — all post-exilic books — indicating it was used among those who returned from Babylon. The name combines the root פָּתַח ('to open') with יָהּ (a short form of Yahweh), expressing the idea that God has 'opened' something, perhaps the womb or a door of blessing. Strong's identifies four distinct individuals bearing this name, including a priestly division leader in 1 Chronicles and a man who stood before the king on Judah's behalf in Nehemiah 11:24.
caution: Because the name refers to multiple individuals across different texts, it can be difficult to determine which occurrences refer to the same person, and the confidence tier for this entry is rated low.

definition: A place name referring to a specific location called Seirath, apparently in the hill country of Ephraim in ancient Palestine.
article: Seirath (שְׂעִירָ֫תָה) is a proper place name that appears only once in the Old Testament, in Judges 3:26, where Ehud escapes to this location after assassinating the Moabite king Eglon. The directional suffix on the form indicates movement toward the place — 'to Seirath.' Strong's connects the name to a root meaning 'roughness,' suggesting perhaps rugged or wooded terrain, consistent with the hill country setting implied in the Judges narrative. The LXX renders the passage with verbs meaning 'to pass by' and 'to be in uproar,' suggesting the translators may have read the word contextually rather than as a clear place name.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon appearing only once in the OT, and the exact location of Seirath is unknown; the LXX translation pattern raises the possibility that ancient readers were uncertain whether this was a proper name or a common noun.

definition: A decorative chain or necklace worn around the neck, used as a royal honor or reward in the ancient Near East.
article: This Aramaic word refers to a chain or necklace, specifically the kind bestowed as a mark of high honor by a king. All six occurrences fall within a single scene in Daniel 5, where Belshazzar promises — and then gives — such a chain to whoever can interpret the mysterious writing on the wall. The word is marked as foreign even within Aramaic, reflecting the multilingual court culture of ancient Babylon.
caution: The word is of uncertain foreign origin (possibly Persian or another ancient Near Eastern language), and its precise form and etymology are disputed; confidence in the translation is low.

definition: Horam, a Canaanite king of Gezer who came to aid Lachish and was defeated by Joshua.
article: Horam is a personal name appearing once in the Old Testament, in Joshua 10:33, where the king of Gezer marches to help Lachish against Israel. Joshua defeats him and his army completely. The LXX renders the surrounding narrative with a word meaning 'to flee' (διαφεύγω), suggesting the ancient translators understood the encounter as a rout. Strong's connects the name to an unused root meaning 'to tower up,' implying a sense of height or elevation, though this etymological detail cannot be confirmed from the text itself.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon — a name appearing only once in the entire Hebrew Old Testament — so nothing beyond its single narrative context can be confirmed.

definition: A proper name referring to two biblical figures: a descendant of Cain and a descendant of Seth, both called Enoch.
article: Chanok (Enoch) is a personal name appearing 16 times across 4 books, concentrated heavily in Genesis (11 times). The name belongs to two distinct individuals: Enoch son of Cain (Genesis 4), after whom a city is named, and Enoch son of Jared (Genesis 5), a figure famous for walking with God. The LXX renders the name as Ἐνώχ nearly every time, but strikingly also uses εὐαρεστέω ('to please well') and μετατίθημι ('to transfer, translate') — Greek words that reflect the tradition about Enoch being taken by God rather than dying (Genesis 5:24).
caution: Strong's connects the name to a root meaning 'initiated,' but the digest flags low confidence, and name-etymology in Hebrew is often uncertain and should not be pressed.

definition: To rush about eagerly or course hungrily, like a predator or a person driven by intense craving or appetite.
article: This rare verb, appearing only 6 times across 5 books, conveys the driven, restless motion of something — or someone — moving urgently out of deep hunger or desire. The KJV renders it variously as 'range,' 'run to and fro,' 'long,' and 'have appetite,' capturing both the physical rushing and the inner craving that drives it. It appears in vivid imagery: a hungry man dreaming of food (Isaiah), a roaring lion or ranging bear (Proverbs), and soldiers swarming a city (Joel). The single LXX rendering as ἀντίληψις ('taking hold of, seizing') leans toward the grasping, acquisitive side of the word's range.
caution: With only 6 occurrences and low confidence assigned, the precise semantic boundaries between physical rushing and metaphorical craving are difficult to draw, and the solitary LXX rendering may not be representative.

definition: An Aramaic word for leg, used once in Daniel's vision of the great statue.
article: This Aramaic term means 'leg' and appears just once in the Old Testament, in Daniel 2:33, describing the iron legs of the colossal statue in Nebuchadnezzar's dream. The KJV consistently renders it as 'leg,' and the word's meaning is straightforward within its context. Its single occurrence makes it one of the rarest words in the Hebrew Bible, functioning as part of the Aramaic sections of Daniel rather than classical Biblical Hebrew.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon with only one occurrence in the entire Old Testament, found exclusively in the Aramaic portions of Daniel, leaving very limited context for confirming its full semantic range.

definition: The skin of a person or animal, or the leather and hides made from animal skin.
article: עוֹר refers to skin in its natural state on a living body, as well as the cured hides and leather made from animal skins. Its range spans both the biological and the crafted: Job uses it to describe his own suffering flesh, while Leviticus — where over half its occurrences appear — uses it extensively for the ritual inspection of skin diseases and for animal hides used in tabernacle construction. The LXX overwhelmingly renders it δέρμα (73 times), the standard Greek word for skin, confirming that ancient readers understood it as a straightforward term for skin and hide across all its contexts.
caution: The two occurrences rendered ξύλινος ('wooden') by the LXX are unexpected and may reflect scribal variation or a difficult reading in those passages.

definition: To swarm, teem, or multiply abundantly — especially of small creatures filling water, land, or air.
article: This verb describes the explosive proliferation of living creatures, particularly the wriggling, crawling, or swimming kind. Its 14 occurrences cluster tightly in Genesis (5×) and Leviticus (5×), where it appears in creation and purity laws — the very contexts where swarming animals matter most. The Septuagint's choice of ἐξάγω ('bring forth') in three instances suggests ancient readers understood the word as emphasizing productive abundance rather than merely the wriggling motion itself. The word covers both the act of swarming and the creatures doing it, which is why it can read as a verb of motion or a description of teeming population.
caution: The confidence tier is rated low, and the LXX renders the word inconsistently — including once as κῆτος ('sea monster') — suggesting ancient translators themselves were uncertain about its precise scope, so the exact nuance in any given verse should be treated cautiously.

definition: A noun meaning tumult or uproar, appearing once in a poetic oracle to describe the sons of Seth or a state of chaos.
article: This word appears only once in the Old Testament, in Balaam's oracle in Numbers 24:17, where it describes 'all the sons of Sheth' or 'all the sons of tumult.' The KJV treats it as a proper name (Sheth), but Strong's roots it in a word meaning tumult, suggesting it may describe a class of people characterized by uproar or disorder. The ancient LXX translators were themselves divided — one rendering reflects the name Seth while another uses a word meaning 'to bless' or 'call happy' — showing that even early readers were uncertain what to do with it.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon with significant scholarly disagreement: it may be a proper name (Seth/Sheth), a common noun meaning tumult, or a descriptor of warlike peoples, and the LXX offers no clear consensus.

definition: A personal name meaning 'God is my defense,' borne by one of David's warriors who joined him at Ziklag.
article: Eluzai is a proper name appearing once in the Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 12:6, in a list of Benjaminite warriors who came to David at Ziklag. The name combines the Hebrew words for 'God' and 'strength/defense,' reflecting the common Hebrew practice of embedding theological confession into personal names. Because it appears only in a genealogical roster, no narrative context illuminates the individual's character or story.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon — occurring only once in the entire Old Testament — so no broader usage can confirm the name's exact form or significance.

definition: A designated place, official order, or census count — depending on context, the word can mean the appointment itself or the specific place or number it produces.
article: This noun derives from the root פָּקַד, which broadly covers mustering, appointing, and oversight. Depending on context, מִפְקָד can refer to a physical location set apart for a purpose, an authoritative command, or the result of a census count. With only 4 occurrences spread across four different books — Samuel, Chronicles, and Ezekiel — its usage is sparse and varied enough that context must guide interpretation in each case. The LXX shows real uncertainty here, rendering the word once as ἀποχωρίζω ("to separate") and once simply as ὀγδοήκοντα ("eighty," a numeral), suggesting even ancient translators struggled to find a consistent equivalent.
caution: With only 4 occurrences and inconsistent LXX renderings (including a bare numeral), the precise semantic range of this word is genuinely uncertain and context-dependent in each instance.

definition: To chop, cut, or carve wood; used of laborers who fell or dress timber.
article: חָטַב refers to the work of cutting or hewing wood, appearing just 9 times across 6 books. Its most concentrated use is in Joshua, where it describes the Gibeonites condemned to be "hewers of wood" — a vivid narrative detail that anchors the word in the context of forced labor and social status. The Pual stem (passive) appears once, suggesting wood that has been dressed or worked over. The LXX evidence and the spread across Deuteronomy, Chronicles, Psalms, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel confirm it stays consistently within the domain of woodcutting work without significant metaphorical extension.
caution: Confidence is rated low, likely due to the word's sparse attestation (only 9 occurrences) and the unusual KJV gloss "polish," which is difficult to reconcile with the core meaning and may reflect a disputed reading in one passage.

definition: A specific stony region in Bashan, east of the Jordan, containing dozens of fortified cities.
article: Argob is a proper geographic name referring to a distinct territory within the kingdom of Bashan, east of the Jordan River. It appears 5 times across Deuteronomy, 1 Kings, and 2 Kings, consistently describing a region notable for its many fortified towns — Deuteronomy counts sixty walled cities within it. The LXX most often renders it with περίχωρος, meaning 'surrounding region' or 'district,' confirming ancient readers understood it as a defined geographic zone rather than a city or person.
caution: Confidence is low: one occurrence carries a personal-name grammatical role rather than a place name, and the LXX renders that instance with λογίζομαι ('to reckon'), suggesting possible confusion in the ancient text tradition over whether Argob is always a place or sometimes a person.

definition: A personal name belonging to an Israelite man listed in the genealogies of Judah in 1 Chronicles.
article: Meonothai is a proper name appearing once in the Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 4:14, as part of the tribal genealogy of Judah. The name appears to be related to the Hebrew root for 'dwelling' or 'habitation,' and Strong's suggests it means 'habitative.' Because it occurs only in a genealogical list and is translated simply as a personal name throughout, its meaning carries no independent theological weight in context.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon — appearing only once in the entire Old Testament — so virtually nothing can be said about the word's usage beyond its role as a proper name in a single genealogical list.

definition: A Hebrew personal name meaning 'work of Yahweh,' borne by multiple distinct individuals in the Old Testament.
article: Maaseiah is a proper name appearing 23 times across 5 books, concentrated in Nehemiah, Jeremiah, 2 Chronicles, and Ezra — all texts dealing with the late monarchy, exile, and restoration periods. The name is composed of the Hebrew words for 'work' and the divine name Yah, so it functions as a statement of devotion. Strong's identifies at least sixteen different individuals bearing this name, which explains its spread across so many distinct historical contexts. The single LXX rendering as διάδοχος ('successor') likely reflects a specific contextual translation choice rather than the name's general meaning.
caution: Because at least sixteen different people share this name in the OT, readers should take care not to conflate distinct individuals appearing in different books.

definition: A word covering three distinct ideas: a door-hinge, a messenger or envoy, and sharp physical or emotional pain.
article: This single Hebrew root carries three surprisingly different meanings depending on context: a hinge on which a door pivots (Proverbs 26:14), a diplomatic messenger or ambassador (Proverbs 13:17, 25:13; Isaiah, Obadiah), and the sharp pangs of pain — especially birth-like agony (Isaiah 13:8, 1 Samuel 4:19). The LXX twice renders it with ὠδίν, the Greek word for birth-pangs or labor pains, which confirms ancient readers understood the pain sense as vivid and physical. The word appears most often in Isaiah (5 times), where the messenger and anguish senses both feature prominently across poetic and prophetic contexts.
caution: Scholarly confidence is rated low, likely because the three meanings seem unrelated and the underlying connection between them — whether all derive from the same root — remains disputed.

definition: An Aramaic word for peace or prosperity, used in formal greetings in official letters and royal decrees.
article: This is the Aramaic form of the familiar Hebrew שָׁלוֹם, appearing only 4 times in the Old Testament, all in the Aramaic sections of Ezra and Daniel. Its occurrences are clustered in formal, official contexts — royal correspondence and edicts — where it functions as a salutation wishing the recipient peace or well-being. The KJV consistently renders it simply as 'peace,' reflecting its use as a standard greeting formula in ancient Near Eastern official documents.
caution: With only 4 occurrences across 2 books, all in Aramaic rather than Hebrew, the full semantic range cannot be confidently established from biblical evidence alone.

definition: To be cut off, appearing once in the Psalms in the Niphal (passive) stem.
article: גָּרַז means to cut off, and its single occurrence in the Old Testament is in Psalm 31:23, where the Niphal stem gives it a passive sense — 'I am cut off.' The word appears only once across the entire Hebrew Bible, making it a hapax legomenon. Because the evidence is so limited, its full semantic range is impossible to establish, but in context it expresses a sense of being severed or excluded, likely from God's presence or care.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon, occurring only once in the Old Testament; its precise meaning relies heavily on context and ancient versional evidence rather than broad usage patterns.

definition: A cluster or bunch of grapes hanging together on a vine, sometimes used figuratively for fruitfulness or abundance.
article: אֶשְׁכּוֹל refers to a bunch or cluster of grapes, and the KJV consistently translates it as 'cluster of grapes' across all 9 occurrences. The word appears most often in Song of Solomon (3×) and Numbers (2×), where the famous cluster from the Valley of Eshcol was so large it required two men to carry it on a pole. The ancient Greek translators uniformly chose βότρυς, the standard Greek word for a grape cluster, confirming there was no ambiguity about its meaning. In Deuteronomy and Isaiah it appears in poetic contexts describing vines, suggesting the word could carry a figurative weight in elevated speech.
caution: The root derivation is uncertain and marked as low confidence, though the word's meaning as a grape cluster is itself consistently clear.

definition: A personal name referring to a minor Levite figure mentioned in a genealogical list in Chronicles.
article: Zizah appears only once in the Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 23:11, as the name of a son of Shimei from the tribe of Levi. Strong's notes it as an alternate form of the name Ziza (H2124), suggesting these may be variant spellings of the same name. The KJV renders it simply as 'Zizah,' and there is no LXX translation evidence to draw on for broader meaning. Its sole occurrence is in a genealogical passage, which is the most common context for obscure personal names in Chronicles.
caution: This name occurs only once in the entire Old Testament and appears to be a variant spelling of a closely related name (Ziza), making any independent analysis of this form essentially impossible.

definition: An Aramaic word meaning a part or share of something, used in the context of portions or allotments.
article: This Aramaic term appears only 3 times in the Old Testament, all in the Aramaic sections of Daniel and Ezra. It carries the straightforward sense of a part or portion of something larger. Its extremely limited distribution — confined to just two books — reflects its status as an Aramaic loanword rather than native Hebrew vocabulary.
caution: Confidence is low due to very sparse attestation (only 3 occurrences across 2 books), and the root is Aramaic rather than Hebrew, making its full semantic range difficult to establish from biblical evidence alone.

definition: Gideon, the Israelite judge and military leader who defeated the Midianites, whose name suggests a warrior or one who cuts down.
article: Gideon is a personal name belonging to the famous judge of Israel whose story fills most of the book of Judges (chapters 6–8). All 39 occurrences appear in Judges alone, and the LXX consistently renders the name as Γεδεών, the form familiar from the New Testament's Hall of Faith in Hebrews 11. The name itself likely connects to a root meaning 'to cut down' or 'fell,' fitting his role as a warrior who dismantled Midianite power, though readers encounter the name simply as a proper noun throughout the text.
caution: The name's precise meaning is moderately uncertain — Strong's links it to a root meaning 'feller,' but the connection is etymological inference rather than direct textual evidence.

definition: A wilderness campsite on the Israelite exodus route, whose name means 'pomegranate of the breach' or 'pomegranate of the gap.'
article: Rimmon-Perets is a proper place name referring to one of the stopping points during Israel's wilderness journey, mentioned only in Numbers 33:19–20 as a camp between Rithmah and Libnah. The name combines the Hebrew words for 'pomegranate' and 'breach' or 'gap,' though the exact significance of that combination for this location is unknown. The Septuagint simply transliterates the second element as Φάρες rather than translating it, suggesting the ancient Greek translators treated it as an opaque proper name rather than a meaningful description.
caution: The site's exact location is entirely unknown and cannot be identified with any archaeological or geographical certainty; confidence is rated low.

definition: The Aramaic word for heart, referring to the inner seat of thought, will, and understanding.
article: This is the Aramaic form of the Hebrew word for heart, appearing all 7 of its Old Testament occurrences in the book of Daniel. It refers to the inner life — thoughts, intentions, and understanding — rather than the physical organ. Notably, the Septuagint twice renders it with the Greek word θεωρέω, meaning 'to perceive or observe,' suggesting ancient translators sometimes read it as the seat of mental perception rather than emotion.
caution: This is an Aramaic entry with only 7 occurrences confined to Daniel, and the LXX's unusual rendering with θεωρέω creates some uncertainty about the word's precise semantic range in context.

definition: Sculptured or carved decorative figures, used of ornamental work in the Temple.
article: This rare noun appears only once in the entire Old Testament, in 2 Chronicles 3:10, describing the crafted figures — likely the two cherubim — made for the inner sanctuary of Solomon's Temple. Strong's connects it to an unused root meaning to bestrew or cover with carvings, suggesting elaborate sculptural decoration rather than a simple image. The KJV renders it 'image work,' pointing to the ornate, artistic character of the Temple furnishings being described.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon, appearing only once in the OT, and its root is not attested elsewhere in Hebrew, making the precise meaning uncertain and dependent largely on context and etymology.

definition: A break or gap in a wall, barrier, or relationship — a rupture that lets something burst through or spill out.
article: פָּ֫רֶץ names the result of a violent breaking — most concretely a gap torn in a wall or fortification, but also the sudden overwhelming outburst of divine force. Its 19 occurrences spread across 11 books, appearing in narrative, prophecy, and poetry alike. The LXX translates it as φραγμός ('fence, barrier') three times and πτῶμα ('fall, collapse') three times, showing ancient readers saw both the physical gap and the catastrophic event of collapse as central. The name of Judah's son Perez (Genesis 38:29) comes from this same word, commemorating a dramatic 'breaking out' at birth.
caution: The confidence tier is marked low, and the LXX renders one instance as πλοῖον ('ship'), which is difficult to explain and may reflect a variant text or a translator's uncertainty, so at least one occurrence remains semantically disputed.

definition: A Persian proper name identifying one of the ten sons of Haman killed by the Jews in Esther.
article: Aspatha is a Persian personal name appearing only once in the Old Testament, in Esther 9:7, as one of the ten sons of Haman who were slain during the Jewish defense authorized by King Ahasuerus. The name is of Persian derivation, though its precise meaning is not recoverable from the biblical text alone. Because it is a proper name with a single occurrence, its entire biblical significance is tied to this one narrative moment in Esther.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon and a Persian loanword whose original meaning remains uncertain; no LXX translation evidence is available to clarify ancient interpretation of the name.

definition: Jotbathah is a place name referring to a desert campsite visited by the Israelites during their wilderness wanderings.
article: Jotbathah is a proper place name identifying a location in the desert where the Israelites stopped during their Exodus journey. It appears three times across two books — twice in Numbers 33 as part of the itinerary list of campsites, and once in Deuteronomy 10:7. The KJV renders it as both "Jotbath" and "Jotbathah," reflecting slight variation in transliteration rather than any difference in meaning.
caution: The exact location of Jotbathah is unknown; no archaeological site has been confidently identified with it, and the spelling variation between KJV renderings reflects underlying textual uncertainty.

definition: A departure from what is right; a turning aside into moral wrong or rebellion.
article: סֵטִים refers to a turning aside from what is right — essentially a straying into wrongdoing or rebellion. It appears only once in the Old Testament, in Hosea 5:2, a passage condemning Israel's corrupt leadership and idolatry. The KJV renders it as 'revolters' and 'that turn aside,' both capturing the sense of deliberate deviation. The LXX's split between ἀγρεύω ('to hunt' or 'ensnare') and παιδευτής ('discipliner') suggests ancient translators were uncertain how to render this rare word, reading the context in very different ways.
caution: This word occurs only once in the entire Old Testament (a hapax legomenon), and the sharply divergent LXX renderings signal that ancient translators themselves were unsure of its precise meaning; significant uncertainty remains.

definition: To be morally loose or worthless, often expressed as excessive, wasteful eating and shameful conduct.
article: This verb covers a range from literal shaking or quaking to the idea of being morally loose, worthless, or prodigal. In Proverbs, where it appears three times, it consistently describes the glutton or riotous eater — someone whose self-indulgence leads to ruin. The Niphal stem leans toward the sense of being treated as vile or worthless, which fits Lamentations and Jeremiah's use in contexts of national humiliation. Interestingly, the LXX translators twice chose τρόμος (trembling, terror) and once ἀνάξιος (unworthy), suggesting ancient readers saw both the physical and moral dimensions of the word as genuinely distinct.
caution: With only 8 occurrences and a low confidence tier, the connection between the physical sense of shaking and the moral sense of loose living remains uncertain, and the LXX translations point in noticeably different directions from each other.

definition: A specific type of strong, tough tree, likely ash or a similar hardwood, mentioned in a woodworking context.
article: This word appears only once in the entire Old Testament, in Isaiah 44:14, where the prophet describes someone cutting down trees to make idols. Strong's connects the word to a root meaning strength or toughness, suggesting a hardy hardwood tree. The KJV translates it simply as 'ash,' though the exact species is uncertain given the single occurrence and the challenges of identifying ancient Near Eastern tree names.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon (appearing only once in the OT), making its precise species identification uncertain — some scholars question whether 'ash' is the correct tree, and other translations suggest alternatives such as cedar or pine.

definition: To gather in a troop or mob, and also to slash or gash oneself, especially in mourning rituals.
article: This verb carries two distinct but possibly related senses: assembling in a crowd or band, and cutting or slashing oneself, the latter appearing prominently in ritual mourning contexts. The Hithpolel stem, which is reflexive or iterative, accounts for 5 of the 6 verbal occurrences, suggesting the dominant usage is 'cutting oneself' or 'banding together' as a self-directed act. Its appearance in 1 Kings 18:28 — where the prophets of Baal slash themselves — and in Jeremiah and Deuteronomy in the context of mourning rites gives the word a strong association with forbidden self-harm. Notably, the LXX translators chose κλαίω, meaning 'to weep,' on two occasions, suggesting ancient readers sometimes understood the action as part of broader grief expression rather than isolating the physical cutting.
caution: Confidence is rated low, and the connection between the 'gather in troops' sense and the 'gash oneself' sense is etymologically debated; some scholars treat these as two distinct roots that were conflated.

definition: To fall into a deep, stunning sleep — often an overwhelming, helpless unconsciousness rather than ordinary rest.
article: רָדַם describes a profound, overpowering sleep that renders a person completely insensible — closer to being 'stunned' than simply resting. It appears 7 times across 5 books, always in the Niphal stem (passive/reflexive), which underscores that this sleep happens *to* a person rather than being chosen. The spread of contexts is telling: Sisera sleeps this way before Jael strikes (Judges 4:21), Jonah is found dead asleep in the ship's hold, and Daniel is overcome while receiving a vision — in each case the sleep is dramatic and total. The LXX evidence aligns with this heaviness, consistently choosing Greek words for deep or stupefied sleep rather than ordinary slumber.
caution: Confidence is rated low, the root is rare (only 7 occurrences), and the precise nuance separating it from ordinary sleep terms like יָשֵׁן is not fully settled among scholars.

definition: Capricious, vexing behavior or persons — those who act arbitrarily, bringing frustration or oppression.
article: This rare word appears only twice in Isaiah (3:4 and 66:4), making it one of the least-attested nouns in the Hebrew Bible. Its core idea seems to involve erratic, willful, or capriciously harmful action — the kind that frustrates and vexes those subjected to it. The KJV rendered it as both
caution: babe

definition: A preposition and adverb meaning 'under,' 'below,' or 'in place of,' covering both physical position beneath something and substitution or exchange.
article: תָּחַת is one of the most common words in the Hebrew Bible, appearing 511 times across 36 books, and it carries two distinct but related ideas: physical location beneath something (under the sky, under one's feet) and substitution or exchange (one thing in place of another). The same spatial intuition — one thing occupying the position of another — underlies both uses. The LXX translators captured this split well, using ὑπό and ὑποκάτω for the spatial sense ('under') and ἀντί for the substitution sense ('instead of'), that last Greek word being the same one used in the NT phrase 'an eye for an eye.' Its heavy presence in legal and narrative books like Exodus, Kings, and Chronicles reflects how often Hebrew writers needed to specify both physical placement and one-for-one replacement.

definition: To treat someone as worthless or contemptible — to despise, demean, or hold in low esteem.
article: This word expresses the act of treating a person as beneath respect or honor — roughly what English captures with 'despise' or 'hold in contempt.' It appears only 6 times across 4 books, functioning as both a noun (carrying the sense of dishonor or shame) and a verb in Niphal and Hiphil stems. The LXX translators most often chose ἀτιμάζω ('to dishonor') and ἔντιμος ('honorable,' used antithetically), confirming that the word sits squarely in the domain of social honor and shame — as seen in Deuteronomy's laws protecting dignity and in 1 Samuel 18:23 where David is called a 'base' man.
caution: Confidence is rated low, the word is rare (only 6 occurrences), and the LXX shows unusual variation — including μαστιγόω ('to flog') and προσδέομαι ('to need') — suggesting translators were not always certain of the meaning, leaving some glosses genuinely uncertain.

definition: An ornamental accessory worn by women, either a decorative sash or headband used as adornment.
article: This rare word refers to some kind of decorative item worn by women as personal adornment. It appears only twice in the Old Testament — once in Isaiah 3:20 (in a list of women's luxury items) and once in Jeremiah 2:32 (where a bride's adornments are mentioned). The KJV translates it as both 'attire' and 'headband,' reflecting genuine uncertainty about whether it was worn around the waist or the head. The root קָשַׁר means 'to bind,' suggesting something tied or fastened to the body.
caution: With only 2 occurrences and KJV translators disagreeing between 'headband' and 'attire,' the precise nature of this garment or accessory remains uncertain; scholarly confidence is low.

definition: A designated place where waste or ashes are emptied out, such as an ash-heap outside the camp.
article: שֶׁפֶך refers to a specific location where refuse or ashes are poured out, derived from the root meaning 'to pour out' or 'to shed.' Its only two occurrences are both in Leviticus 4:12, describing the place outside the Israelite camp where the remains of a sin offering were to be disposed of. The word is so rare that the KJV doesn't even translate it as a noun — it renders the phrase as 'are poured out,' absorbing the word into a verb phrase rather than naming the location directly.
caution: This word occurs only twice, both in the same verse, making it effectively a hapax legomenon in terms of context; its precise meaning depends almost entirely on the root etymology rather than varied usage.

definition: An Aramaic conjunction meaning 'also' or 'even,' used to add emphasis or include an additional element.
article: This Aramaic particle functions as an additive conjunction, equivalent to 'also' or 'even' in English. It appears only 4 times in the Old Testament, entirely in the Aramaic sections of Ezra (3 times) and Daniel (once), reflecting the limited Aramaic portions of Scripture. The KJV consistently renders it as 'also,' suggesting a straightforward additive role with no significant variation in usage across its occurrences.
caution: With only 4 occurrences across 2 books, attestation is very sparse, and the entry is marked low confidence; its meaning is inferred largely from its correspondence to the Hebrew particle אַף and consistent KJV rendering.

definition: Laughter or derision — ranging from genuine joy and merriment to contemptuous mockery and scorn.
article: שְׂחוֹק covers the full spectrum from heartfelt, joyful laughter to bitter contemptuous mockery, and context is everything in deciding which end of that range is meant. In Psalm 126:2, it describes the elated laughter of restored exiles; in Jeremiah and Lamentations, it shades into being a laughingstock — an object of derision before enemies. The LXX translators most often chose γέλως (8 of 15 times), the standard Greek word for laughter, which confirms that the core sense is laughter itself, with social or emotional coloring supplied by the surrounding context. The word appears heavily in wisdom and poetic literature — Job, Ecclesiastes, Proverbs, Psalms — suggesting it often carries a reflective or evaluative tone rather than simply describing a physical reaction.
caution: Confidence is rated low for this lemma, likely reflecting disputed interpretation in some contexts, particularly where the line between joyful laughter and contemptuous derision is unclear; the KJV gloss 'sport' hints at further nuance that is not fully settled.

definition: A place name identifying a location on the northern boundary of the promised land as described to Moses.
article: Ziphron appears only once in the Old Testament, in Numbers 34:9, where it marks a point along the northern border of the land God promised to Israel. It is a proper geographical name and carries no broader semantic range beyond this single boundary reference. Because it occurs just once, its precise location remains uncertain to modern scholars, though ancient boundary lists like this one were practical administrative documents.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon appearing only in Numbers 34:9, and the site's exact geographical location has not been identified with certainty.

definition: An Aramaic demonstrative pronoun meaning 'this' or 'another,' used exclusively in the Aramaic sections of Daniel.
article: This is an Aramaic word, not Hebrew, appearing only 6 times and entirely within the book of Daniel. It functions as a demonstrative pronoun pointing to something near or just mentioned — essentially the Aramaic equivalent of 'this.' Its narrow range of use reflects Daniel's well-known bilingual nature, where portions of the book are written in Aramaic rather than Hebrew.
caution: Confidence is low: the KJV gloss range is extremely sparse, the word is Aramaic with only 6 occurrences in a single book, and the grammatical role marked 'd' in one instance adds slight ambiguity to its full range of function.

definition: A place name in ancient Palestine, meaning 'fountain of gardens,' occurring in the tribal territory lists of Joshua.
article: En-gannim is a proper geographic name referring to one or more settlements in ancient Palestine. It appears all 6 times in the book of Joshua, in the context of tribal boundary and city allotment lists — once for Judah (Joshua 15) and once for Issachar (Joshua 19), with the Issachar site also listed among Levitical cities (Joshua 21). The name itself combines the Hebrew words for 'spring' or 'fountain' and 'gardens,' suggesting a well-watered locale, though the KJV simply transliterates it throughout as 'En-gannim' without attempting a translation.
caution: Confidence is rated low, likely because scholars debate whether the two En-gannims in Joshua refer to the same site or two distinct locations, and precise modern identification remains uncertain.

definition: To judge, govern, or plead the cause of someone, especially in a legal or ruling sense.
article: The verb דִּין carries the core idea of exercising judgment or legal authority — deciding a case, vindicating someone, or ruling over others. It appears 24 times across 11 books, with the heaviest concentration in Psalms (8×) and Jeremiah (4×), suggesting it is comfortable in both poetic and prophetic contexts. The Septuagint most often renders it with κρίνω (9×), the standard Greek word for judging or deciding a legal case, which confirms that ancient readers understood it primarily in a judicial sense. The Qal stem accounts for nearly all uses (17×), with only one Niphal occurrence.
caution: The Strong's definition and KJV gloss supplied in the digest ('sail direct,' 'come with a straight course') appear to belong to a different or confused entry, creating moderate uncertainty; the LXX evidence for κρίνω is the more reliable guide to meaning here.

definition: Heavy labor burdens imposed on forced workers, especially the crushing toil assigned to enslaved people.
article: סִבְלֹת refers to the oppressive burdens or heavy labor assigned to enslaved workers. All 6 occurrences are found exclusively in Exodus, where the word describes the backbreaking toil forced upon the Israelites in Egypt. The KJV consistently renders it 'burden,' and the LXX's use of τύπτω ('to strike/beat') in one instance is striking — suggesting ancient translators sometimes understood the word in terms of the physical punishment accompanying forced labor rather than the load itself.
caution: Confidence is rated low, and the word's narrow attestation (6 occurrences, one book only) limits certainty about its full semantic range; its root connection to סֵבֶל is assumed but the exact nuance of 'porterage' versus broader forced labor remains somewhat uncertain.

definition: Fat ashes left from burnt offerings, or the richness and abundance that fatness symbolizes.
article: דָּשֶׁן refers primarily to the greasy ashes remaining after animal sacrifices were burned on the altar — a very concrete, priestly concern found five times in Leviticus alone. Beyond the altar, the word stretches metaphorically to mean lush abundance or richness, the way fatness signals plenty in the ancient world. The LXX translators chose πιότης (richness, fatness) five times, showing they read the figurative sense as primary in poetic and prophetic contexts like Psalms and Isaiah. The distribution — priestly law on one end, poetry on the other — captures the word's full range well.
caution: The low confidence tier and the LXX's use of ῥήγνυμι (to break, burst) twice suggests some passages were puzzling even to ancient translators, indicating genuine uncertainty about the word's precise sense in those contexts.

definition: A cooling place or room, likely a chamber designed to provide relief from summer heat.
article: This rare word appears only twice, both in Judges 3, describing the room where Eglon the king of Moab was sitting when Ehud assassinated him. Strong's connects it to a root meaning 'cooling off,' suggesting a specially ventilated chamber — essentially a summer room built for heat relief. The LXX translators rendered it inconsistently, using words meaning 'sitting,' 'near,' and 'rising up,' suggesting they were uncertain of the precise architectural term, which is a sign that even ancient readers found it obscure.
caution: This word occurs only twice in a single narrative passage, and the LXX translators show clear uncertainty about its meaning, so the 'cool chamber' interpretation, while widely accepted, cannot be considered fully settled.

definition: Silence or stillness, especially the quiet of death or the grave, as opposed to living speech and praise.
article: דּוּמָה refers to a deep, death-associated silence — the kind where no voice is heard at all. Both of its Old Testament occurrences are in Psalms, where the word appears in the context of death and the inability of the dead to praise God (Ps 115:17) and the danger of falling into that permanent quiet (Ps 94:17). The LXX renders the word with terms related to silence and the underworld, reinforcing its connection to the stillness of death rather than ordinary quietness.
caution: This word occurs only twice, both in Psalms, and derives from an otherwise unused Hebrew root, making its full semantic range difficult to establish with confidence.

definition: To tie or bind something physically, or to bind people together in a conspiracy or close loyalty.
article: קָשַׁר covers both the literal act of tying or fastening something—like binding a cord around the wrist (Gen 38:28) or tying words to your hand (Deut 6:8)—and the figurative act of people binding themselves together in a plot or coup. In fact, more than a third of its occurrences appear in 2 Kings and 2 Chronicles, almost always describing palace conspiracies against a king. The Septuagint's most frequent choice, συστρέφω (
caution: to gather together, band around someone"), captures both senses well, suggesting ancient readers heard both the physical and social dimensions of the word at once.The root also appears in Proverbs describing loyal attachment, as when love or wisdom is

definition: A personal name referring to several distinct individuals in the Old Testament, most prominently a companion of Moses.
article: Hur is a personal name borne by at least four Israelites and one Midianite across the Old Testament. The most prominent is the Hur who appears alongside Aaron in supporting Moses' hands during the battle against Amalek (Exodus 17) and who was left in charge with Aaron while Moses ascended Sinai (Exodus 24). He also appears as the grandfather of Bezalel, the chief craftsman of the tabernacle (Exodus 31, 35). Five of the fifteen occurrences appear in 1 Chronicles, reflecting genealogical records that mention other individuals who share the name.
caution: The LXX translates the name inconsistently with common Greek words rather than a fixed transliteration, suggesting ancient translators sometimes treated the name contextually, making precise identification of referents uncertain in a few passages.

definition: An Aramaic word for an elder or senior leader, used of community authorities in the post-exilic period.
article: This Aramaic term refers to elders — respected authority figures representing a community. All 5 of its Old Testament occurrences are clustered in a single book, Ezra, where these elders appear as the recognized leaders of the Jewish community during the rebuilding of the temple under Persian rule. The word's tight concentration in Ezra reflects the Aramaic administrative language of that era, as official correspondence with Persian authorities was conducted in Aramaic.
caution: The Strong's entry simply states this word 'corresponds to' a Hebrew root without defining it independently, and with only 5 occurrences in one book, the full range of its meaning is difficult to establish with confidence.

definition: A spoken word, utterance, or promise — what is declared or said aloud.
article: This noun refers to something spoken — a word, utterance, or solemn promise. Its six occurrences are concentrated in poetic books (four in Psalms, one in Job, one in Habakkuk), suggesting it belongs to an elevated, literary register rather than ordinary prose speech. Psalm 19:3–4 uses it memorably to describe the silent yet real 'speech' of the heavens, showing the word can stretch beyond literal vocal sound to any meaningful declaration. The LXX's inconsistent renderings — once as ἔνδυμα ('garment') and once as παραβολή ('parable' or 'proverb') — are unusual and do not clearly illuminate the word's core meaning.
caution: Confidence is rated low, the LXX renderings are difficult to reconcile with the standard meaning, and Strong's simply cross-references a related lemma rather than defining this word independently — so the precise nuance remains uncertain.

definition: A layer or deposit — of dew on the ground or of semen in a sexual act.
article: This noun comes from the root meaning 'to lie down' and covers two distinct physical realities: a spread-out layer (as when dew settles on the ground, Exodus 16:13–14) and the discharge or act involved in sexual relations (Leviticus 15 and Numbers). All 9 occurrences are confined to legal and narrative prose in the Torah, never appearing in poetry. The Greek translators consistently chose κοίτη, a word that in Greek likewise spans both 'bed/lying place' and sexual context, confirming the ancient understanding of the word's double range.
caution: The low confidence tier and small sample size (9 occurrences, 3 books) mean the full semantic range is difficult to pin down with certainty, and the KJV glosses — 'carnally,' 'copulation,' 'lay,' 'seed' — reflect translators navigating genuine ambiguity in context rather than lexical clarity.

definition: A strong inner longing or craving, ranging from wholesome desire to dangerous lust, often with a sense of delight in what is wanted.
article: תַּאֲוָה describes an intense desire or appetite — the pull a person feels toward something they want. Its range runs from neutral or positive longing (a pleasant thing, something delightful) all the way to dangerous craving, as in the wilderness episode where Israel lusted after meat (Numbers 11:4). The word clusters heavily in Psalms and Proverbs (16 of its 21 occurrences), suggesting it was especially useful to wisdom and poetic writers reflecting on human appetite and motivation. Ancient Greek translators most often chose ἐπιθυμία (7 times), the same word the New Testament uses for both desire and sinful lust, which shows they understood the word as describing a deep, driving inner want.
caution: The moderate confidence tier and the unusually varied LXX renderings — including 'better,' 'pleasing,' 'liar,' and 'consider' — suggest translators sometimes struggled with the word's precise nuance in context, so individual occurrences may carry more specific shading than a single definition can capture.

definition: A leader or commander who holds authority to decide and direct, ranging from military captain to civil ruler.
article: קָצִין describes a person in charge — someone with recognized authority to lead, command, or decide. The KJV renders it as captain, guide, prince, and ruler, reflecting a range that covers both battlefield command and civic governance. The LXX most often chooses ἀρχηγός (5×), meaning 'leader' or 'chief,' which shows ancient readers understood the word as broadly authoritative rather than narrowly military. Notably, Proverbs 6:7 applies it to the ant, which has no קָצִין over it — suggesting the word carried the ordinary sense of an overseer or boss that even a common reader would instantly recognize.
caution: Confidence is rated low, and the LXX offers some puzzling renderings (including words meaning 'compel,' 'farmland,' and 'far off') that suggest translators were not always sure what the word meant in certain contexts.

definition: The head of a person or animal, and by extension the top, front, chief, or beginning of almost anything.
article: רֹאשׁ is one of the most versatile nouns in Biblical Hebrew, appearing 600 times across 35 books. Its physical sense — the head of a living creature — extends naturally into spatial meaning (the top of a mountain or tower), rank (a chief or ruler), and sequence (the first or beginning of something). The LXX translators reached for κεφαλή ('head') 265 times but switched to ἄρχων ('ruler, prince') 51 times and ἀρχή ('beginning, authority') 28 times, showing that ancient readers recognized all three conceptual clusters as genuinely present in the Hebrew word. Its heavy concentration in Numbers, Leviticus, and Chronicles often reflects its use for tribal and priestly leaders, while in Psalms and poetry it tends toward the spatial or metaphorical.

definition: Ambushes or acts of lying in wait, used as a plural feminine noun referring to concealed military attacks.
article: This word appears only once in the entire Old Testament, at Isaiah 25:11, where the KJV renders it 'spoils' — though Strong's defines it as the plural of a root meaning ambuscades, that is, military ambushes or surprise attacks from concealment. The tension between the KJV gloss 'spoils' and the lexical definition 'ambushes' reflects genuine interpretive difficulty in this single occurrence. Because it appears only in Isaiah 25:11, within a poetic passage of judgment, the precise nuance is hard to pin down with confidence.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon with only one OT occurrence, and the KJV translation 'spoils' diverges noticeably from the lexical definition 'ambushes,' leaving its exact meaning genuinely uncertain.

definition: A box or chest used as a container, specifically for carrying objects alongside the ark of God.
article: This rare word refers to a carrying box or chest. All three of its Old Testament occurrences appear in a single passage in 1 Samuel 6, where the Philistines use it to transport golden objects alongside the returned ark of the LORD. The KJV consistently renders it 'coffer,' and the word's narrow usage in this single episode makes its meaning fairly concrete even if its root is uncertain.
