The KJV simply transliterates it as "Dophkah," and the underlying Hebrew root suggests the meaning "knock" or "beat," though this is its function as a place name, not a common noun. Its precise geographic location in the Sinai desert remains unidentified today.
caution: Dophkah occurs only twice in a single chapter and is otherwise unattested in the OT; its exact location is unknown and scholars have proposed various identifications without consensus.

definition: A spoken incantation or the practice of seeking omens through magical arts.
article: נַ֫חַשׁ refers to the act or words of enchantment — either an incantation spoken to achieve an effect or the practice of reading omens. Its only two occurrences are both in Numbers 23–24, in the oracles of Balaam, where the point is that such practices have no power over Israel. The LXX translators handled the word differently each time — once with ἔθω (custom or habit) and once with ἐπιτελέω (to carry out or accomplish) — suggesting even ancient readers were uncertain whether the focus was the ritual act or its spoken formula.
caution: With only 2 occurrences confined to a single passage, and LXX translators rendering it two different ways, the precise meaning is uncertain and should be held loosely.

definition: A division or assigned section, specifically referring to a rotational group of Levites organized for temple service.
article: This Aramaic word appears only once in the Old Testament, in Ezra 6:18, where it describes the organized sections of Levites set up for worship at the restored Jerusalem temple. The KJV renders it 'course,' capturing the idea of a rotating assignment group rather than a physical division. Its single use is in an Aramaic portion of Ezra (Ezra 4–6 is written in Aramaic), reflecting administrative temple language of the Persian period.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon — appearing only once in the entire Old Testament — so its precise nuance rests entirely on a single context, limiting certainty about its full range.

definition: A rounded or hemispherical cap worn by ordinary Aaronic priests as part of their prescribed ceremonial dress.
article: This word refers to the rounded caps assigned to Aaron's sons as part their official priestly vestments, distinct from the more elaborate turban (מִצְנֶפֶת) worn by the high priest. All four occurrences are clustered tightly in the Exodus and Leviticus passages describing the construction and donning of priestly garments, giving it an exclusively liturgical context. Interestingly, the Septuagint translators rendered the word with περιτίθημι ('to place around') and τελειόω ('to complete/consecrate'), suggesting they treated these caps less as a standalone object and more as part of the act of investiture itself.
caution: The LXX does not use a consistent Greek noun for this item, which makes the precise shape and style of the cap difficult to confirm, and the low-confidence rating reflects genuine uncertainty about its exact form.

definition: A place name in ancient Palestine, meaning 'spring of the apple tree,' located on a boundary of Manasseh.
article: En-tappuach is a geographical location mentioned twice in Joshua 17:7, where it marks a boundary point of the tribe of Manasseh. The name combines the Hebrew words for 'spring' or 'eye' and 'apple tree,' suggesting a settlement near a natural water source. The KJV simply preserves the Hebrew name as 'En-tappuah' without translation, which is the standard practice for proper place names.
caution: The site appears only in Joshua 17:7 and its exact modern location has not been identified with certainty, making geographical reconstruction difficult.

definition: An Aramaic verb meaning to see, gaze upon, or behold, including visionary and dream-sight.
article: This Aramaic verb is the standard word for seeing and beholding in the biblical Aramaic portions of the Old Testament. Its 31 occurrences are concentrated almost entirely in Daniel (30×), where it frequently describes the seeing of visions and dream-images — making visionary perception its dominant use in context. The LXX renders it with standard Greek words for sight, reflecting that ancient translators understood it as real visual experience, whether literal or visionary. The single Hiphil occurrence in Ezra 4:14 carries the sense of what is fitting or customary to see, which is the unusual "seem" or "be wont" sense Strong's notes.
caution: The "be usual" or "seem" gloss is poorly attested and semantically distant from the core meaning, suggesting either a disputed usage or a contextually forced reading in Ezra 4:14.

definition: A Hebrew personal name meaning 'God is my help,' borne by multiple individuals in the Old Testament.
article: Eliezer is a proper name appearing 14 times across 5 books, with the heaviest concentration in 1 Chronicles (7 times) and Ezra (4 times). The name is borne by at least eleven different individuals, the most prominent being Abraham's servant mentioned in Genesis 15:2 and Moses's son named in Exodus 18:4. The Septuagint consistently renders it as Ἐλιέζερ, a straightforward transliteration showing ancient translators made no attempt to interpret or adapt it — they simply carried the name across as-is.
caution: The low confidence tier assigned to this entry may reflect uncertainty in distinguishing which occurrences refer to which individual, since at least eleven different people share this name across the Old Testament.

definition: An Aramaic word meaning strength or military force, used to describe armies, power, or loudness of voice.
article: This is the Aramaic form of the Hebrew word חַיִל, and it carries a similarly broad range covering armies, raw strength, and even the force behind a loud voice. It appears only 7 times in the Old Testament, confined to just two books: Daniel (6 times) and Ezra (once). The KJV translates it in notably different ways — 'army,' 'power,' 'most mighty,' and even 'aloud' — reflecting how the same Aramaic root could describe both physical forces and the sheer force of sound. In Daniel 3:20, for instance, it describes the 'most mighty' soldiers commanded by Nebuchadnezzar.
caution: Confidence is low due to sparse attestation (only 7 occurrences in 2 books), and the gloss 'aloud' is a somewhat unusual extension of the core meaning that may reflect an idiomatic Aramaic phrase rather than a direct semantic sense of the word itself.

definition: A personal name — one of Abraham's sons by Keturah, meaning 'he will leave.'
article: Jishbak (also spelled Ishbak) is a personal name appearing just twice in the Old Testament — once in the Genesis account of Abraham's descendants by Keturah (Genesis 25:2) and once in the parallel genealogy in 1 Chronicles 1:32. The name is consistently translated as a proper noun in both Hebrew and the KJV, with no other semantic usage. Strong's connects it to an unused root meaning 'to leave,' making 'he will leave' the proposed meaning behind the name, though the root itself does not otherwise appear in the Hebrew Bible.
caution: The underlying root is unattested in Biblical Hebrew, making the proposed meaning 'he will leave' difficult to verify with confidence.

definition: To look intently or gaze at something, often with deliberate attention, care, or emotional regard.
article: נָבַט means more than a casual glance — it describes a focused, purposeful act of looking, frequently carrying the sense of attention, concern, or even longing. It appears 70 times across 16 books, with its heaviest use in Psalms (17×), Isaiah (15×), and Lamentations (7×), where the emotional weight of looking — whether toward God, toward suffering, or toward a distant hope — is especially prominent. Notably, all 39 verb forms appear in the Hiphil stem, which in Hebrew typically conveys a directed, active sense: one is *causing* oneself to look, reinforcing the idea of deliberate attention. The LXX most often renders it ἐπιβλέπω (24×), a Greek word meaning to look upon with focused attention or favor, confirming that ancient readers understood this as more than mere seeing.
caution: The moderate confidence tier reflects some uncertainty about the precise nuance in individual contexts — whether the word stresses the act of looking, the emotional disposition behind it, or both — and scholars do not always agree on the boundaries between this root and other Hebrew vision verbs.

definition: To be right or fitting, and by extension to succeed or prosper in what one undertakes.
article: This verb carries the idea of something being straight, right, or acceptable, and extends naturally into the sense of succeeding or going well. It appears only 4 times across two books — Ecclesiastes and Esther — making it quite rare. In Ecclesiastes 10:10 the word is used to describe the advantage gained by skill, where the Hiphil stem gives it a causative force: making something work well or succeed. The LXX rendering with δυναμόω (to strengthen or empower) in one place and στοιχέω (to proceed or advance rightly) in another reflects both the fitness and the prospering dimensions of the word.
caution: With only 4 occurrences across 2 books, the semantic range is difficult to pin down with confidence, and scholarly opinion on precise nuances remains uncertain.

definition: A Moabite deity—Baal of Peor—whose worship led Israel into a notorious apostasy in the wilderness.
article: Baal-Peor is a proper name for a Moabite god worshipped at the site of Peor, appearing 12 times across Numbers, Deuteronomy, Psalms, and Hosea—always in the context of Israel's catastrophic idolatry in the wilderness (Numbers 25) and the warnings or laments that followed. The name combines the common Semitic word for 'lord' or 'master' (baal) with Peor, likely a place name. The LXX's occasional use of τελέω ('to complete' or 'to initiate into rites') hints that ancient translators may have associated this worship with initiation ceremonies or ritual acts, which aligns with the sexually charged nature of the incident in Numbers 25. Its appearances in Hosea and Psalms show that this episode remained a defining symbol of unfaithfulness long after the original event.
caution: The LXX translation choices (τελέω and οἰκεῖος) are unusual and not fully explained, and the precise nature of Baal-Peor's cult is historically uncertain; the confidence tier for this entry is rated low.

definition: To be, exist, become, or come to pass — covering both simple existence and events unfolding over time.
article: הָיָה is one of the most common verbs in the Hebrew Bible, appearing 3,575 times across all 39 books, and it does far more than simply link a subject to a predicate. It carries the full weight of existence, transformation, and occurrence — what English splits across 'be,' 'become,' and 'happen.' The LXX translators captured this range by using two distinct Greek verbs: εἰμί (to be, 2,127 times) and γίνομαι (to become or come about, 1,304 times), a split that reveals how ancient readers heard both static existence and dynamic change in the same Hebrew word. Its heaviest use in Ezekiel (341 times) and the narrative books reflects how central it is to the prophetic formula 'the word of the LORD came' and to storytelling itself.

definition: An adjective meaning short or limited in extent — whether in patience, lifespan, physical size, or number.
article: קְצַר describes something that falls short of a full or adequate measure, and the context determines what dimension is in view. In Proverbs it appears twice in close proximity to describe a person who is quick to anger — short of patience — contrasted with one who is slow and controlled. Job uses it of human life being short and troubled, while 2 Kings and Isaiah apply it to things that are few or feeble. The LXX's choice of ὀλιγόψυχος (

definition: To give milk or nurse young; used of lactating animals still feeding their offspring.
article: This verb describes animals that are actively nursing or giving milk to their young. All five occurrences are in the Qal stem and refer to livestock — notably nursing cows in 1 Samuel 6 and nursing ewes in Genesis 33 and Psalm 78. The range is narrow: this is a practical agricultural term for lactating animals, not a metaphorical or theological one. Interestingly, the LXX renders it once with καταδιώκω ("to pursue"), which fits poorly and suggests the ancient Greek translators may have struggled with this rare word.
caution: Confidence is low due to only 5 occurrences and an LXX rendering that does not clearly match the expected meaning, leaving some uncertainty about the word's precise semantic range.

definition: A place name referring to a single town called Atroth-Shophan, located in the territory east of the Jordan River.
article: Atroth-Shophan appears only in Numbers 32:35, where it is listed among the towns built by the tribe of Gad in the Transjordan region. The name appears to combine 'Atroth' (meaning crowns) with 'Shophan' (from a root meaning hidden). The KJV treated it as two separate places — 'Atroth' and 'Shophan' — but most interpreters read it as a single compound place name, making the KJV split a potential translation error.
caution: This word occurs only in one verse (counted twice due to the split reading), the site has not been securely identified archaeologically, and scholarly confidence in the exact reading and meaning of the name remains low.

definition: To cherish or hold dear, with the sense of embracing someone close, as in holding to one's bosom.
article: חָבַב appears only once in the entire Old Testament, in Deuteronomy 33:3, where it describes God's love for his people. Strong's connects the root to the idea of hiding something in the bosom — that is, holding it protectively close — giving the word a warmth and intimacy beyond ordinary affection. The KJV renders it simply as 'love,' but the underlying image is more physical and tender, closer to 'embrace' or 'hold dear.' Its single occurrence in the Qal stem makes it extremely rare, and the LXX evidence would be particularly useful here for confirmation, though the context in Moses' blessing strongly supports a sense of devoted, sheltering love.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon — appearing only once in the Hebrew Bible — so its precise nuance cannot be confirmed by comparing other uses; the meaning rests almost entirely on context and root comparison.

definition: An angelic watcher or heavenly guardian being, as used in Aramaic visionary literature.
article: This Aramaic noun appears only 3 times in the Old Testament, all in Daniel 4, where it describes supernatural beings who descend from heaven and announce divine decrees. The word is consistently translated 'watcher' in the KJV, and the LXX renders it with Greek terms for a watcher or one who is awake, reinforcing the idea of a vigilant heavenly guardian. Its use is tightly confined to Nebuchadnezzar's dream vision, where these figures act as agents carrying out God's judgments on earth.
caution: This word occurs only 3 times in a single book, all in Aramaic rather than Hebrew, and its precise nature as a class of angelic being is drawn from a very narrow textual base, leaving its fuller meaning uncertain.

definition: An abundance or rich supply of resources, used once to describe overflowing natural wealth.
article: שֶׁפַע appears only once in the Old Testament, in Deuteronomy 33:19, in the context of blessing and natural wealth drawn from the sea. Its root carries the sense of overflowing abundance or plentiful resources. The LXX translators rendered it in two different ways — ἐμπόριον (marketplace, trading wealth) and παράλιος (coastal, seaside) — suggesting they interpreted the abundance as tied to maritime commerce and geography. The KJV simply renders it 'abundance,' which captures the core idea without the geographical nuance the Greek translators saw.
caution: This word occurs only once in the Hebrew Bible (a hapax legomenon), and the two divergent LXX translation choices suggest ancient uncertainty about its precise meaning.

definition: Gomorrah, one of the infamous cities of the plain destroyed by God alongside Sodom, whose name became a lasting symbol of divine judgment on wickedness.
article: Gomorrah is a place name appearing 19 times across 6 books, concentrated most heavily in Genesis (9 times), where its destruction is narrated, and then echoed in the prophets Isaiah, Jeremiah, Amos, and Zephaniah as a shorthand for catastrophic divine judgment. The word functions both as a straightforward proper name and as a powerful rhetorical symbol — prophets invoke Gomorrah to warn audiences that a similar fate awaits unrepentant communities. The LXX almost universally renders it as Γόμοῤῥα (17 times), cementing this name's transmission directly into Greek and later into New Testament usage, though one instance is rendered with the Greek word for "overthrow" or "destruction," hinting at how ancient readers associated the name itself with ruin.
caution: The underlying Hebrew root and the precise original meaning of the name are uncertain, and the confidence tier for this entry is rated low, meaning the root derivation and any built-in semantic nuance remain disputed.

definition: A noun meaning freedom or liberty, specifically referring to release from the condition of slavery.
article: חֻפְשָׁה refers to the state of freedom or liberty, particularly in the context of release from slavery. It appears only once in the Old Testament, in Leviticus 19:20, which discusses a slave woman who has not yet been given her freedom. The LXX renders it with ἐλευθερία, the standard Greek word for liberty and freedom, confirming that ancient translators understood it as a concrete legal status, not a metaphor.
caution: This word is a hapax legomenon, occurring only once in the entire Old Testament, so its full semantic range cannot be established with confidence beyond this single context.

definition: To encounter or meet someone or something, whether by chance, by design, or in a hostile confrontation.
article: This verb covers the full range of meeting or encountering — from a casual, unplanned crossing of paths to a deliberate or even violent confrontation. Its spread across KJV glosses like "befall," "happen," "meet," and "fall out" reflects that breadth. The LXX most often renders it with ἀπάντησις or συνάντησις, both standard Greek words for a meeting or encounter, confirming that ancient readers understood it primarily in terms of coming face-to-face with someone or something. Its heaviest concentration is in 1 Samuel (20 of 37 occurrences), where encounters — friendly, accidental, and hostile — are a constant feature of the narrative.
caution: The moderate confidence rating likely reflects ambiguity in individual passages between an accidental happening and an intentional meeting, and the single LXX rendering as φόνος ("slaughter") in one case suggests at least one context was read as violent confrontation, adding some uncertainty to the word's exact nuance in those instances.

definition: A farming tool, likely a hoe or plowshare, used for tilling the soil.
article: This word appears only once in the Old Testament, at 1 Samuel 13:20, in a passage describing Israelites going to Philistine smiths to sharpen their farm implements. The root חָרַשׁ relates to cutting or engraving, suggesting a tool that breaks or works the ground. The KJV renders it 'share' (a plowshare), while Strong's suggests 'hoe,' leaving the exact implement somewhat uncertain.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon — appearing only once in the entire Old Testament — so its precise meaning cannot be confirmed by comparing other contexts, and the exact implement it names remains disputed.

definition: A pedestal, stand, or fixed base used to support an object or mark an established place.
article: מְכוֹנָה refers primarily to a physical base or stand, and its 24 occurrences are heavily concentrated in 1 Kings (15 times), where it describes the elaborate bronze wheeled stands Solomon had crafted for the Temple's lavers. The word can also carry the broader sense of a fixed or established place, as seen in its use in Jeremiah and Ezra. The LXX renders it with στῦλος (pillar or column) nine times, suggesting ancient readers associated it closely with upright structural supports, though the Temple context clearly points to wheeled cart-like bases rather than simple pillars. This tension in the LXX translations — including puzzling choices like πῆχυς (cubit) and μῆκος (length) — reflects real interpretive difficulty with these complex Temple furnishings.
caution: The moderate confidence rating and the scattered LXX translation choices (five different Greek words) suggest genuine uncertainty about the word's full semantic range beyond the Temple stand context.

definition: To go or turn to the left, moving or directing oneself in the leftward direction.
article: This rare verb appears only 5 times across 5 books, always meaning to go or turn to the left. Both verb occurrences are in the Hiphil stem, suggesting a causative or directed sense — actively turning or steering leftward. The LXX evidence aligns with this directional meaning, and the KJV consistently renders it as 'go left' or 'turn to the left.' The spread across narrative, prophetic, and historical books suggests it was a standard but infrequently needed directional term.
caution: With only 5 occurrences and a denominative root derived from the noun for 'left hand,' the verb's full range is difficult to establish; confidence is rated low.

definition: A divinely mandated release or cancellation of debts, and the suspension of agricultural labor, occurring every seventh year in Israel.
article: This word refers to the seventh-year institution commanded in Deuteronomy, covering both the release of financial debts and the suspension of normal land use. All five occurrences are in Deuteronomy alone, clustered in chapters 15 and 31, making it a highly specific legal term rather than a general word. The LXX consistently translates it as ἄφεσις, meaning 'release' or 'forgiveness' — the same Greek word later used in the New Testament for forgiveness of sins, suggesting ancient readers heard a broad liberating force in the concept.
caution: Confidence is rated low, likely because the root שָׁמַט appears in other contexts meaning 'to let drop' or 'release,' leaving some uncertainty about the precise scope of this derived noun's meaning beyond its Deuteronomy context.

definition: A proper name referring to a place in Canaan and at least two Israelite individuals in the Old Testament.
article: Sheba appears 10 times across 3 books — 2 Samuel (8 times), Joshua (1 time), and 1 Chronicles (1 time). The name is shared by a town allotted to Simeon in Joshua 19:2 and by at least two individuals, most notably the rebel who led a revolt against David in 2 Samuel 20. Strong's notes the name is identical in form to the common Hebrew word for 'seven,' but in these passages it functions exclusively as a proper name. The KJV consistently renders it 'Sheba' throughout.
caution: Confidence is rated low, likely because the identical spelling of this name and the common word for 'seven' creates ambiguity, and the referents across the three passages may not all be the same individual or place.

definition: To soar or fly, used of a bird mounting up powerfully into the sky.
article: This verb appears only once in the entire Old Testament, in Job 39:26, where God challenges Job by asking whether it is by human wisdom that the hawk soars and spreads its wings toward the south. The Hiphil stem suggests a causative or energetic sense — not merely fluttering but actively launching into flight. Its single occurrence in the poetic and dramatic context of God's speeches in Job fits the elevated, vivid imagery of that book perfectly.
caution: With only one occurrence in the entire Hebrew Bible, the full semantic range of this verb cannot be determined with confidence; it is effectively a hapax legomenon.

definition: A specific city in Moab, used as a proper place name in ancient Near Eastern geography.
article: Ar is a proper name referring to a city in Moab, appearing 6 times across Numbers, Deuteronomy, and Isaiah. It consistently functions as a geographic landmark in texts describing Israel's wilderness journey and boundaries near Moabite territory. The KJV always renders it simply as 'Ar,' treating it as a place name throughout, though Strong's notes it shares a root with the common Hebrew word for 'city.' Interestingly, the LXX once renders it with the Greek word meaning 'swallow up' or 'engulf,' suggesting at least one ancient translator read the word differently in its context.
caution: Confidence is rated low, and the single LXX rendering as 'swallow up' rather than a place name raises a genuine question about whether every occurrence is truly a proper noun or whether one instance may carry a different sense.

definition: To wrap or cover over, and by extension to faint, languish, or be overwhelmed — ranging from physical covering to emotional collapse.
article: This verb moves across two related ideas: physically shrouding or covering something, and the weakening or collapse that darkness and heaviness suggest — faintness, swooning, or being overwhelmed. The KJV renders it as 'cover,' 'faint,' 'overwhelmed,' and even 'feebler,' showing how wide the range is. Its concentration in Psalms (8 of 16 occurrences) and Lamentations (3 occurrences) signals a poetic and often emotionally intense register — the soul fainting, the valleys clothed with grain. The LXX's use of ἐκλύω ('to grow faint, give out') confirms that ancient readers understood the weakening sense as central.
caution: The word's low confidence tier and scattered LXX renderings — including the seemingly opposite glosses ἄσημος ('obscure') and ἐπίσημος ('notable') — suggest the ancient translators themselves were uncertain, and the precise meaning in some verses remains disputed.

definition: A writing ink used to inscribe words on a scroll or document.
article: This word refers simply to ink, the liquid medium used for writing. It appears only once in the entire Old Testament, in Jeremiah 36:18, where Baruch describes writing Jeremiah's dictated words onto a scroll. The word's derivation is uncertain, and Strong's notes this explicitly, though its meaning in context is straightforward.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon — appearing only once in the Hebrew Bible — and its origin is of uncertain derivation, making full confidence in its semantic range impossible.

definition: A person or thing exempt from bondage or obligation, most often describing a freed slave released from servitude.
article: חָפְשִׁי describes the state of being free — particularly a slave who has been legally released from bondage. It appears 17 times across 7 books, with its heaviest concentration in Exodus 21 and Deuteronomy 15, where the laws governing the release of Hebrew servants are laid out. The most common LXX rendering is ἐλεύθερος ("free person"), used 8 times, confirming that ancient translators understood this as genuine liberation from servitude. Job and Psalms use the word in more poetic contexts, where freedom from care or constraint is in view rather than literal manumission.
caution: The confidence tier is rated low, and the LXX also renders this word with Greek terms meaning "prophesy" and "dream" in several instances, suggesting either a difficult Hebrew text or that some occurrences may belong to a different word entirely — readers should treat those minority renderings with caution.

definition: The stripped-off equipment or armor taken from a defeated enemy as spoil or plunder.
article: This rare noun appears only twice in the Old Testament, once in Judges and once in 2 Samuel, and in both cases it refers to armor or gear taken from a slain enemy. The KJV consistently renders it as 'armour,' reflecting the specific idea of equipment stripped from a fallen soldier. Interestingly, the LXX translators used different Greek words across renderings — including 'panoply' (full battle gear) and words meaning 'to strike' — suggesting ancient readers understood the term in a military stripping or spoil context.
caution: This word occurs only twice in the OT and carries a low confidence rating, making its precise nuance uncertain; the varied LXX translations add further ambiguity about whether the focus is on the armor itself or the act of stripping it.

definition: The personal name Job, the patriarch at the center of the book bearing his name, known for enduring great suffering.
article: אּיּוֹב is almost exclusively a proper name referring to the biblical patriarch Job, appearing 56 of its 58 Old Testament occurrences in the book of Job itself, with just 2 appearances in Ezekiel (14:14, 14:20) where he is cited alongside Noah and Daniel as an example of righteousness. The ancient Greek translators of the LXX consistently rendered the name as Ἰώβ, the direct Greek equivalent, confirming it was understood as a personal name rather than a common noun. Strong's connects the name to a root meaning 'hated' or 'persecuted,' which would give the name a fitting irony given the character's story, though name etymologies in Hebrew are often uncertain.
caution: The proposed etymology linking the name to a root meaning 'hated' or 'persecuted' is a scholarly inference, not a settled fact, and the name's true origin remains disputed.

definition: An exclamation that arrests attention, equivalent to 'Look!' or 'See!' — directing the reader to notice what follows.
article: הִנֵּה is one of the most common words in the Hebrew Bible, appearing 843 times across 35 books, and it functions like a spoken gesture — a sharp 'Look!' or 'See this!' that makes the reader pay attention to the next statement. It is especially frequent in narrative books like Genesis (118×), 1 Samuel (74×), and Ezekiel (78×), where speakers use it to introduce dramatic announcements, divine declarations, or surprising observations. The Septuagint almost always translates it as ἰδού (649×), the same Greek word used in the New Testament for 'behold,' which shows how consistently ancient readers heard this as a pure attention marker. English readers encounter it most often as 'behold' in older translations, but 'look,' 'see,' or even an exclamation point can capture the same effect in modern English.

definition: A physical image, likeness, or representative figure — ranging from idols to the human form made in God's image.
article: The word צֶלֶם refers to a concrete representation or likeness of something — most famously used five times in Genesis for the 'image of God' in which humans are made and bear. In historical and prophetic books it typically describes physical idol-images, as in Ezekiel and 2 Kings. The LXX overwhelmingly chose εἰκών ('icon,' 'image') to render it, which is exactly the word Paul and other NT writers later used for Christ as the 'image' of God — a meaningful translation choice. The two Psalms occurrences may carry a more shadowy, illusory sense, closer to the root meaning of a phantom or fleeting form.
caution: The root is listed as unused, meaning the word's derivation is reconstructed rather than directly attested, and the relationship between its 'idol' sense and its 'divine image' sense remains genuinely disputed among scholars.

definition: An Aramaic word for a threshing floor, a large open area where grain was beaten and winnowed.
article: This Aramaic term appears only once in the entire Old Testament, in Daniel 2:35, where it describes the threshing floor as the place where the crushed remains of the great statue were scattered by the wind. The word carries the sense of something ample or spacious, fitting the image of a broad, open floor used for processing grain. The LXX evidence aligns with this single concrete meaning, and no other translation choices exist in the KJV beyond 'threshingfloor.'
caution: This is a hapax legomenon appearing only once in the Old Testament, and as an Aramaic loanword with a single attestation, its full semantic range cannot be firmly established from biblical usage alone.

definition: To store away or hoard something, keeping it hidden and reserved for future use.
article: כָּמַס appears only once in the Old Testament, in Deuteronomy 32:34, where God speaks of vengeance sealed up and stored away in his treasury. The word carries the sense of something deliberately set aside and kept hidden until the right moment. Because it occurs just this once, the KJV renders it simply as "lay up in store," and Strong's notes a figurative extension toward storing something in memory, though the Deuteronomy context is concrete and vivid.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon — appearing only once in the entire Hebrew Old Testament — so its precise semantic range cannot be confirmed through comparison with other passages.

definition: A flower or blossom, used once in Isaiah as an image of something beautiful but short-lived.
article: צִיצָה means a flower or blossom, and it appears only once in the Old Testament, in Isaiah 28:4, where it describes the fading glory of Samaria. It is the feminine form of the related noun צִיץ. The LXX is notably inconsistent here, rendering it with two different Greek words — πρόδρομος (forerunner, or early fig) and σῦκον (fig) — suggesting ancient translators associated the image with early, perishable fruit rather than a literal flower.
caution: This word occurs only once in the entire Old Testament (a near-hapax), and the LXX's divergent renderings introduce genuine uncertainty about its precise meaning in context.

definition: Set apart as sacred, whether a person, place, object, or God himself — the quality of being wholly devoted to and distinct for the divine.
article: קָדוֹשׁ describes something or someone consecrated to God and therefore distinct from the ordinary or common. It functions both as an adjective — describing holy offerings, a holy nation, a holy Sabbath — and as a noun referring to God himself ('the Holy One'), angels, or human beings set apart for God. The word appears 119 times across 20 books, with Isaiah alone accounting for 38 of those, largely because of his signature title 'the Holy One of Israel.' The LXX's overwhelming choice of ἅγιος (88 times) is highly significant, because that same Greek word became the standard New Testament term for 'holy' and 'saints,' showing direct continuity between the Hebrew concept and early Christian usage.

definition: The lower legs (from knee to ankle) of animals, humans, or locusts, used especially in ritual butchery contexts.
article: This word refers specifically to the lower portion of a leg — from knee to ankle — and appears almost exclusively in cultic, priestly contexts. Six of its nine occurrences are in Leviticus, with two more in Exodus, describing how sacrificial animals were to be washed or arranged before burning on the altar. The Amos reference (3:12) uses the word vividly, comparing a shepherd rescuing only a fragment of a sheep to Israel's desperate situation. Interestingly, the LXX renders it both as πούς ('foot/leg') and σκέλος ('leg/shank'), suggesting ancient translators themselves were slightly uncertain about the exact anatomical boundary the word intended.
caution: Confidence is rated low, likely because the word occurs only 9 times and always in the dual form, making its precise anatomical range (versus related leg vocabulary) difficult to pin down with certainty.

definition: Pressure or distress, used figuratively for the crushing weight of hardship or affliction.
article: מוּעָקָה refers to the experience of being pressed down or squeezed, used figuratively for intense distress or affliction. It appears only once in the Old Testament, in Psalm 66:11, where the poet describes God bringing his people through a place of crushing difficulty. Because it occurs in a psalm, the word carries a vivid, physical metaphor — the feeling of being trapped under pressure — applied to spiritual and communal suffering.
caution: This word occurs only once in the entire Old Testament (a hapax legomenon), making its precise nuance difficult to confirm beyond the general sense of pressure or distress.

definition: A proper name referring to one of several Israelite border towns, most often the city on the edge of the Arnon River gorge in Transjordan.
article: Aroer is a place name applied to at least three distinct locations in or near ancient Palestine, though the Arnon-edge settlement in Transjordan dominates the count, appearing repeatedly in boundary descriptions in Deuteronomy, Numbers, and Joshua. Its 16 occurrences spread across 10 books are almost entirely geographical markers in tribal allotment and military campaign texts. The KJV renders it uniformly as 'Aroer,' reflecting that ancient translators made no attempt to translate its underlying sense. Strong's notes the root meaning suggests 'nudity of situation,' possibly describing an exposed or bare geographic setting, though this etymology does not affect how the name functions in the text.
caution: The association with three separate locations makes individual references potentially ambiguous, and the low-confidence tier signals uncertainty about whether all 16 occurrences refer to the same site or are reliably distinguished in the manuscript tradition.

definition: A specific low-lying hollow or depression in Jerusalem, used as a place name in Zechariah's prophecy of judgment.
article: מַכְתֵּשׁ (Maktesh) appears only once in the Old Testament, in Zephaniah 1:11, where its inhabitants are called to wail because of coming destruction. The name likely reflects the common Hebrew noun for a mortar or hollow, describing a bowl-shaped district of Jerusalem, probably a commercial quarter. The KJV simply transliterates it as 'Maktesh,' treating it as a proper name rather than translating the geographical description.
caution: This word occurs only once in the entire Old Testament (a hapax legomenon as a place name), and the exact location of this district within Jerusalem remains uncertain among scholars.

definition: An Aramaic word meaning seed or offspring, used once in Daniel to describe dynastic intermarriage.
article: This is the Aramaic form of the common Hebrew root for 'seed,' appearing only once in the Old Testament, in Daniel 2:43. There it refers to the mixing of royal lineages through intermarriage — a political strategy of blending dynasties. The LXX translators rendered it with two different Greek words: εὐνοέω (to be well-disposed) and συγκεράννυμι (to mix together), suggesting ancient readers understood the verse as describing an attempt at political union or reconciliation through intermarriage.
caution: This word occurs only once in the entire Old Testament (a hapax in Aramaic), making its precise semantic range very difficult to confirm; scholarly confidence is limited.

definition: A round or circular thing — covering a flat river plain, a round loaf of bread, or a talent (a large unit of weight or money).
article: The word כִּכָּר shares one unifying idea: roundness or circularity. In Genesis it refers to the flat plain of the Jordan valley — the well-watered region Lot chose — while in Exodus and the books of Kings and Chronicles it almost always means a talent, the largest standard unit of weight used for silver, gold, or bronze. The LXX translators rendered it as τάλαντον (talent) 37 times, showing that the monetary-weight sense dominated ancient readers' understanding. The geographic sense appears mainly in Genesis narratives about the Jordan plain, and the bread-loaf sense is comparatively rare, appearing only a handful of times in narrative texts.
caution: The single root covering three such different referents (landscape, bread, and monetary weight) reflects assumed shared shape, but the connection between senses is not always self-evident, and the moderate confidence tier signals some uncertainty in tracing all uses back to a unified meaning.

definition: A foreign deity worshipped by the Avites, mentioned once in the Old Testament.
article: Nibchaz is a proper name referring to a god worshipped by the Avites, a people resettled in Samaria by the Assyrians, as recorded in 2 Kings 17:31. The word appears only this single time in the entire Old Testament, making it a hapax legomenon with extremely limited context. Strong's identifies it as a foreign loanword, consistent with its role as the name of a non-Israelite deity whose origins lie outside the Hebrew tradition.
caution: Because this is a hapax legomenon of acknowledged foreign origin, virtually nothing is known about the nature or background of this deity beyond its single brief mention.

definition: A proper name for a well dug by Isaac's servants, whose name evokes hostility or accusation.
article: Sitnah is the name of a specific well dug by Isaac's servants in Genesis 26:21, given because Philistine herdsmen quarreled over it. The name is related to the Hebrew root for opposition or accusation, making it a meaningful place name that reflects the conflict surrounding it. The LXX renders it with ἀπαίρω, meaning 'to depart,' suggesting the ancient translators focused on Isaac moving on from the dispute rather than preserving the place name directly.
caution: This word occurs only once in the entire Old Testament, making it a hapax as a proper noun; its connection to the root for 'hostility' is assumed by most scholars but the name's precise etymology cannot be fully verified from this single occurrence.

definition: A personal name referring to an Israelite man sent to inquire of the priests and prophets in Zechariah's time.
article: Regem-Melek is a personal name appearing twice in a single verse (Zechariah 7:2), where he is sent along with Sharezer to the house of God to seek a word from the Lord. The name's component parts suggest a meaning like 'king's heap' or 'king's friend,' though in context it functions purely as an individual's proper name. The KJV consistently renders it as 'Regem-melech' without translation, and the LXX evidence offers little additional insight into how ancient readers interpreted the name itself.
caution: With only 2 occurrences in a single verse of one book, this is essentially a hapax-level proper name, and nothing certain can be said about the person beyond his brief mention in Zechariah 7:2.

definition: A personal name referring to one of David's elite warriors, spelled Naharai or Nahari in English Bibles.
article: Naharai (also spelled Nahari) is the name of one of David's thirty mighty warriors, appearing just twice in the Old Testament — once in the list in 2 Samuel 23:37 and once in the parallel list in 1 Chronicles 11:39. He is identified as the armor-bearer of Joab, which places him in a position of particular trust and proximity to David's commander. The two occurrences are essentially a duplicate record of the same individual, making this a very narrow attestation.
caution: The name's underlying Hebrew root and its precise meaning are uncertain; Strong's suggests a connection to a word for 'snoring,' but this etymology is speculative and the confidence tier for this entry is rated low.

definition: To leap suddenly in alarm, conveying a sense of being startled or dismayed with fear.
article: This rare Hebrew verb appears only once in the Old Testament, in Psalm 18:46, where it describes a reaction of fearful dismay. Strong's connects the root idea to a sudden leaping motion, suggesting the physical jolt of being startled — the body's involuntary response to terror. The KJV renders it simply as 'be afraid,' but the underlying image is more vivid than ordinary fear. Its single occurrence in the poetic Psalms fits well with that book's tendency toward expressive, physical descriptions of emotion.
caution: This word is a hapax legomenon, appearing only once in the entire Hebrew Old Testament, so its precise meaning rests on etymology and context alone rather than comparative usage.

definition: A pit or trap, used as an image of deadly danger or destruction into which one falls.
article: This rare noun appears only twice in the Old Testament — once in Psalms and once in Lamentations — both in poetic contexts where life-threatening peril is in view. The core image is a physical pitfall or snare, but both occurrences lean toward the figurative sense of inescapable destruction. The KJV renders it as both 'pit' and 'destruction,' reflecting this dual literal-figurative range, and the poetic distribution suggests the word carried an elevated, dramatic register rather than everyday use.
caution: With only 2 occurrences across the entire Old Testament, the full semantic range of this word cannot be confidently established, and its precise meaning in each context remains somewhat uncertain.

definition: A ritual waving or presenting of an offering before God, and by extension any brandishing or forceful swinging motion.
article: תְּנוּפָה refers primarily to the ceremonial gesture of presenting a sacrificial portion — grain, animal breast, or precious metal — by waving or lifting it before God. Almost all of its 30 occurrences fall in the priestly legislation of Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers, confirming it as technical cultic vocabulary tied to the Tabernacle system. In Isaiah's two uses, the word shifts toward a more vivid image of brandishing or shaking, as when God's arm swings in judgment. The LXX often renders it with ἀφορίζω, meaning "to set apart" or "consecrate," suggesting ancient readers understood the gesture primarily as an act of dedication rather than a physical description of the waving motion itself.
caution: The precise choreography of the waving gesture remains uncertain — scholars debate whether it involved horizontal back-and-forth movement, a lifting motion, or both — and the LXX's inconsistent translations reflect that same ancient uncertainty.

definition: To hire or bargain with someone, particularly by offering payment as a mercenary inducement.
article: This rare verb appears only twice in the book of Hosea, both times in the same chapter (Hos 8:9–10), where it describes Israel's practice of seeking foreign alliances by paying for them — framed in the metaphor of hiring lovers. The Qal and Hiphil stems are both attested, suggesting both the basic act and a causative or purposeful dimension of the transaction. The LXX renders the word with εἰσδέχομαι, meaning 'to receive' or 'accept,' which may reflect a slightly different reading of the context, though the core idea of a paid arrangement remains consistent with the Hebrew.
caution: This word appears only twice and only in Hosea, making its semantic range very difficult to establish with confidence; Strong's limits it specifically to bargaining with a harlot, but the broader context may support a wider sense of mercenary negotiation.

definition: Tiphsach, a place name referring to a ford or crossing point, appearing in two distinct Old Testament contexts.
article: Tiphsach (also spelled Tipsah in the KJV) appears twice in the Old Testament — once in 1 Kings as a geographic boundary marker and once in 2 Kings in a military context. The underlying root suggests a place associated with a ford or river crossing, likely the famous crossing point on the Euphrates River in Mesopotamia. Its two appearances in Kings give it a thin but consistent profile as a real geographic landmark used to describe territorial extent or military movement.
caution: With only 2 occurrences and appearing in different contexts (boundary description vs. military atrocity), scholars debate whether both verses refer to the same location, making identification uncertain.

definition: Something sweet, whether a literal sweet food or a figuratively sweet, delightful quality.
article: This rare noun comes from the root meaning 'to be sweet' and refers to something that is sweet, either as an actual food or in a more figurative sense. In Nehemiah 8:10, it appears alongside eating rich food and drinking sweet drinks as part of a festive celebration. In Song of Solomon 5:16, it describes the beloved's mouth as 'most sweet,' illustrating the word's figurative reach. The LXX renders the Song of Solomon instance with a Greek word for sweetness, confirming that ancient readers understood the term in both concrete and poetic registers.
caution: With only 2 occurrences across the entire Old Testament, the full semantic range of this word cannot be established with confidence, and its precise shade of meaning in each context remains somewhat uncertain.

definition: To fear or be afraid, ranging from terror and dread to reverent awe before God or a powerful person.
article: יָרֵא covers the full spectrum from raw, visceral fear to the worshipful awe a person shows before God — what English often splits into 'afraid' and 'reverent' is a single concept in Hebrew. With 329 occurrences across 34 books, it is one of the most common emotional verbs in the Old Testament, appearing most heavily in Psalms (46×), Deuteronomy (36×), and Isaiah (25×). The Niphal stem (23×) typically carries the sense of being held in awe or inspiring dread, while the Qal handles both ordinary fright and reverence. The LXX almost always uses φοβέω (222×), the same root behind the NT word 'phobia,' confirming that ancient readers heard both terror and reverence in this single Hebrew word.

definition: A personal name meaning 'goodness of Yahweh,' borne by several individuals in the post-exilic period.
article: Tobiah (or Tobijah) is a Hebrew personal name combining the roots for 'good' and 'Yahweh.' It appears 18 times across 4 books, with the vast majority of occurrences (14) in Nehemiah, where a man named Tobiah the Ammonite is a persistent opponent of Nehemiah's rebuilding efforts. The name also appears in Zechariah, Ezra, and 2 Chronicles, referring to different individuals. The LXX rendering offers little semantic help here, as proper names were typically transliterated rather than translated.
caution: Confidence is rated low, possibly reflecting uncertainty about whether all occurrences refer to distinct individuals or about the exact vocalization and form of the name.

definition: Interest charged on a loan, specifically the practice of lending money or goods at a rate that profits the lender at the borrower's expense.
article: נֶשֶׁך refers to interest charged on a debt and appears 12 times across 6 books, concentrated especially in Ezekiel and the Mosaic law books (Leviticus, Deuteronomy, Exodus). The Law consistently prohibits Israelites from charging it to fellow Israelites, though Deuteronomy permits it when lending to foreigners. The LXX renders it as τόκος in 10 of its occurrences — a Greek word meaning 'offspring' applied to money that 'breeds' more money — showing that ancient readers understood it as profit generated by lending.
caution: The confidence tier for this entry is marked low, and the word's precise distinction from a related term for increase or profit (sometimes paired with it in the same verse) is debated; scholars are uncertain whether the two terms are fully synonymous or describe different aspects of interest.

definition: To trim or prune a grapevine by cutting back its branches to promote growth.
article: This verb refers specifically to the agricultural practice of pruning grapevines, appearing only 3 times across Leviticus and Isaiah. In Leviticus it governs the sabbatical year laws, prohibiting pruning during the seventh year of the land's rest. The LXX translators rendered the word as ἄμπελος, the Greek word for 'vine' itself, suggesting they understood the term so closely tied to viticulture that the vine and the act of pruning it were nearly inseparable concepts.
caution: Confidence is low due to very sparse attestation (only 3 occurrences), and the root closely resembles other Hebrew roots, making precise definition difficult without broader contextual evidence.

definition: A fragrant wood or plant used for its pleasant scent, most likely aloe or a similar aromatic substance.
article: אֲהָלִים refers to a fragrant substance — almost certainly aloe wood or a similar aromatic plant material — used in perfuming garments, beds, and sacred spaces. All 4 of its occurrences appear in poetic or elevated contexts: Numbers (Balaam's oracle), Psalms, Proverbs, and Song of Solomon, suggesting it carried a rich, luxurious connotation. The KJV consistently renders it 'aloes,' and the word appears to be of foreign origin according to Strong's, pointing to an exotic import. Interestingly, the LXX translators rendered it using ὡσεί ('like' or 'as'), suggesting they treated it as part of a simile rather than translating the plant name directly.
caution: The word's foreign origin is noted but unspecified, its exact botanical identity remains uncertain, and the low confidence tier reflects genuine scholarly dispute about which plant or tree is meant.

definition: The temple of the head — the thin, vulnerable side of the skull between eye and ear.
article: רַקַּת refers specifically to the temple, the thin-boned side of the head. Its 5 occurrences fall across just two books: Judges and Song of Solomon, showing up in both violent narrative and love poetry. In Judges, it describes the spot where Jael drives a tent peg through Sisera's skull (4:21–22; 5:26), while in Song of Solomon it appears as a site of beauty in descriptions of the beloved (4:3; 6:7) — a striking contrast of vulnerability and loveliness in the same anatomical term. The LXX consistently renders it with words for the temple or cheek region, confirming the physical referent.
caution: The word appears only 5 times in the entire Old Testament, making its precise boundaries with related terms for 'cheek' or 'jaw' difficult to fix with certainty.

definition: A divinely-given vision, dream, or prophetic revelation received and reported by a prophet or seer.
article: חָזוֹן refers to the visionary experience through which a prophet receives communication from God — covering what we might call a waking vision, a dream-like revelation, or a spoken oracle. Its concentration in Daniel (12 times) and Ezekiel (7 times) reflects how central this word is to the great prophetic and apocalyptic literature of the Old Testament. The LXX translators most often chose ὅρασις (20 times), meaning a seeing or sight, confirming that ancient readers understood this word as a genuine perceptual or visionary experience, not merely a mental impression. The famous line in Proverbs 29:18 — where the absence of חָזוֹן leads to disorder — shows the word could also carry the broader sense of prophetic guidance sustaining a community.
caution: The moderate confidence rating reflects some uncertainty about whether every occurrence denotes a full visionary experience or simply an authoritative prophetic word, especially in contexts where no vision narrative follows.

definition: A place name referring to a location in the Jordan Valley region of ancient Palestine, mentioned in boundary and administrative contexts.
article: Tsarethan (also spelled Zarthan) is a geographical location in Palestine appearing just 3 times across Joshua and 1 Kings. It is referenced in Joshua 3:16 in connection with the Jordan River stopping its flow, and in 1 Kings in administrative and construction contexts under Solomon. The LXX rendering σφοδρῶς ('greatly, vehemently') in one instance suggests the ancient translators may have read the passage differently or connected it to a different term altogether, which adds to the uncertainty surrounding this name.
caution: Confidence is low: the exact identification and location of Tsarethan remain uncertain, Strong's notes it may be a variant of a different place name (Tseredah), and the LXX's unexpected Greek rendering raises questions about the textual tradition.

definition: To wrap a belt or girdle around someone or something, often as an act of equipping or empowering for action.
article: אָזַר means to gird or belt — to wrap something tightly around the waist or body, typically in preparation for battle, labor, or divine empowerment. Its range runs from literal belting (as with Elijah's leather belt in 2 Kings 1:8) to metaphorical clothing with strength or power (as in the Psalms and Isaiah). The Hithpael stem, used 3 times, carries a reflexive sense of girding oneself up. The LXX's primary rendering περιζώννυμι (
caution: to wrap around) confirms this core sense, though one puzzling rendering as παραπικραίνω (

definition: An outer garment or covering worn over the body, used as clothing.
article: This rare word refers to some kind of clothing or covering, appearing only twice in the Old Testament — both occurrences in Genesis 49:11, the poetic blessing of Judah. Its narrow attestation makes the meaning hard to pin down with precision. The LXX rendered it with δεσμεύω, a word meaning "to bind" or "tie," which suggests the ancient Greek translators may have understood it as something fastened or wrapped around the body rather than simply a garment in the generic sense.
caution: This word occurs only in a single poetic verse (Genesis 49:11), making it nearly a hapax legomenon; its precise meaning is uncertain, and the LXX translation choice diverges enough from the Hebrew sense of 'clothing' to leave scholars uncertain about the word's exact referent.

definition: Dibri is a personal name belonging to an Israelite man mentioned once in the Old Testament.
article: Dibri is an Israelite personal name appearing only once in the Old Testament, in Leviticus 24:11, where he is identified as the father of a man who blasphemed during a conflict in the camp. Strong's connects the name to the Hebrew root for 'word' or 'speech,' suggesting a meaning like 'wordy,' though such name-meaning connections are often uncertain. The KJV renders it simply as the proper name Dibri, with no translation attempted.
caution: This word occurs only once in the entire Old Testament (a hapax legomenon as a name), so nothing can be confirmed about its meaning beyond its function as a personal identifier.

definition: A bag or pouch, possibly also a decorative accessory, used for carrying valuables or personal items.
article: This rare noun appears only twice in the Old Testament — once in 2 Kings 5:23, where Naaman packs silver into bags for Gehazi, and once in Isaiah 3:22, where it appears in a list of women's luxury items. The KJV translates it as 'bag' in 2 Kings but oddly as 'crisping pins' in Isaiah, suggesting translators were uncertain what the word meant in that decorative context. The root idea, according to Strong's, is something 'cut out or hollowed,' pointing to a pouch or receptacle shape as the core concept.
caution: With only 2 occurrences and a split KJV translation ('bag' vs. 'crisping pins'), the precise meaning — especially in the Isaiah luxury-items list — remains genuinely uncertain, and this entry carries a low confidence rating.

definition: A personal name borne by one of David's sons, listed in genealogical records in Chronicles.
article: Nogah is a proper name appearing exactly twice in the Old Testament, both times in 1 Chronicles — once in the royal genealogy (3:7) and once in the parallel list of David's sons born in Jerusalem (14:6). It is exclusively a personal name with no other semantic function in the text. The name itself shares its form with the common Hebrew noun meaning brightness or radiance, but in these passages it functions only as an identifier within David's family records.
caution: With only 2 occurrences both in the same book and serving only as a proper name, nothing can be said about the word's meaning beyond its use as a personal name; the underlying noun's connection to the name's choice is not explained in the text.

definition: A personal name meaning 'Yahweh is great,' belonging to an Israelite man mentioned in Jeremiah.
article: Yigdalyahu is a proper name appearing once in the Old Testament, in Jeremiah 35:4, where a man named Igdaliah is identified as the father of Hanan, whose chamber was in the temple. The name is a compound of the root גָּדַל ('to be great') and יָהּ (a shortened form of Yahweh), giving it the meaning 'Yahweh has magnified' or 'Yahweh is great.' Because it occurs only once and the KJV renders it simply as 'Igdaliah,' there is no translation variation to analyze.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon — appearing only once in the entire Old Testament — so nothing beyond the name itself and its bearer's identity can be established from usage.

definition: A judge or magistrate who adjudicates legal disputes, though context sometimes suggests the concept of judgment itself.
article: This rare word appears only 3 times across Exodus, Deuteronomy, and Job, making it difficult to pin down its precise range with confidence. In Exodus 21:22 it refers to arbitration by judges in a legal dispute, while Job 31:11 uses it in a context of moral reckoning. The LXX translators rendered it quite differently in each case — once as 'unrestrained' (ἀκατάσχετος) and once as 'foolish' (ἀνόητος) — suggesting ancient interpreters themselves were uncertain how to handle the word, and those choices diverge sharply from the straightforward 'judge' that Strong's and KJV supply.
caution: With only 3 occurrences and LXX translations that diverge significantly from each other and from the standard 'judge' gloss, the precise meaning of this word is genuinely uncertain and should be treated with caution.

definition: A proper name referring to a Levitical city in Israel and to several Israelite individuals, meaning something like 'servitude' or 'service.'
article: Abdon functions as both a personal name and a place name in the Old Testament, appearing 8 times across Joshua, Judges, 1 Chronicles, and 2 Chronicles. As a personal name it identifies at least four different Israelites, including a judge of Israel mentioned in Judges 12. As a place name it refers to a Levitical city assigned to the tribe of Asher. The KJV consistently renders it simply as 'Abdon' without translation, which is standard practice for proper names.
caution: The underlying root meaning 'servitude' is inferred from the related verb, but whether ancient bearers of this name understood it that way is uncertain; scholarly confidence in the precise sense is rated low.

definition: To tear or rip something apart, especially clothing as a gesture of grief, distress, or horror.
article: קָרַע means to tear or rip, and in the Old Testament it appears most often in the context of people tearing their garments as an outward expression of intense emotion — grief, repentance, or moral outrage. With 63 occurrences across 21 books, it is well attested, and the heaviest concentration in Kings and Samuel reflects the narrative-heavy contexts where leaders tear their clothes in response to disaster, death, or prophetic judgment. The Qal stem accounts for the majority of uses (22×), with the Niphal appearing 4 times in a passive sense (something being torn). Interestingly, Strong's notes a figurative extension to painting or enlarging the eyes, though the dominant use throughout the OT is plainly physical tearing of fabric.
caution: The LXX renders this word only once with περιΐστημι, which means to stand around or avoid — a puzzling translation choice that offers little help in clarifying the word's range, and the moderate confidence tier suggests some nuances remain uncertain.

definition: Dawn or daybreak, referring to the first light of morning.
article: מִשְׁחָר means dawn or the breaking of day, derived from a root associated with the appearance of morning light. It occurs only once in the Old Testament, in Psalm 110:3, a poetic and royal psalm, which fits the elevated, literary register typical of the Psalter. Its single occurrence makes it essentially a hapax legomenon within the Hebrew Bible, and the surrounding context of Psalm 110:3 is notoriously difficult to translate, making the precise nuance of the word hard to pin down with certainty.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon appearing only in Psalm 110:3, a verse widely regarded as one of the most textually difficult in the Psalter, so its exact meaning and grammatical role remain uncertain.

definition: A prepositional form meaning 'with me' or 'alongside me,' expressing accompaniment, association, or close relation to the speaker.
article: עִמָּדִי is an extended form of the preposition עִם ('with'), specifically attached to the first-person singular — essentially 'with me.' It appears 44 times across 9 books, with heavy concentration in Genesis (14×) and Job (14×), where characters frequently speak of God or others being with them or acting toward them. The LXX overwhelmingly translates it with Greek first-person pronouns (ἐμοῦ and ἐμέ together accounting for 28 of 44 renderings), confirming its core sense of personal accompaniment or relation. The KJV gloss range — including 'against,' 'from,' and 'with' — reflects the natural flexibility of Hebrew prepositions, which can shade from close companionship to opposition depending on context.
caution: The moderate confidence rating likely reflects the prepositional flexibility: the same form can mean 'with me,' 'from me,' or even 'against me,' and context must determine which relational nuance is intended.

definition: An Aramaic word for a flat, open plain or valley, used in Daniel's account of the plain of Dura.
article: This Aramaic term refers to a broad, flat plain or valley. It appears only once in the Old Testament, in Daniel 3:1, describing the plain of Dura where Nebuchadnezzar set up his golden statue. The KJV consistently renders it as 'plain,' reflecting its straightforward geographical meaning. Its Hebrew counterpart carries the same sense of a wide, open lowland between hills or mountains.
caution: This word occurs only once in the entire Old Testament (a hapax legomenon in Aramaic), so its semantic range cannot be confirmed from additional biblical contexts.

definition: A retreat or flight, describing the act of fleeing or running away from danger.
article: מְנוּסָה means a fleeing or retreat — the act of running away from threat or danger. It appears only twice in the Old Testament, once in Leviticus 26:36, where God warns that the unfaithful will flee in panic even when no one pursues them, and once in Isaiah 52:12, where Israel is promised they will not need to flee in haste. The contrast between these two uses is striking: panicked flight as a curse versus confident departure without flight as a blessing.
caution: With only 2 occurrences across the entire Old Testament, the full semantic range of this noun cannot be established with confidence.

definition: A round, flat cake baked directly on hot coals or ashes, a basic form of bread in ancient Israel.
article: עֻגָה refers to a simple round cake of bread cooked on heated coals or ashes, representing one of the most basic methods of baking in the ancient Near East. Its 7 occurrences spread across narrative and prophetic books show it appearing in everyday contexts: Abraham's hospitality to visitors (Genesis 18), the hasty Exodus departure (Exodus 12), Elijah's miraculous provision (1 Kings 17 and 19), and Hosea's prophetic imagery. Notably, the LXX translators did not settle on a single consistent Greek equivalent, which may reflect uncertainty about the precise form of this food item even in antiquity.
caution: The LXX renders this word with two unrelated Greek verbs (including θαρσέω, meaning 'take courage') rather than a consistent food term, suggesting ancient translators themselves were sometimes uncertain how to handle it; confidence in the precise meaning is accordingly low.

definition: A kiss, specifically the physical gesture of lips touching as an expression of affection or greeting.
article: This word means simply a kiss, appearing only twice in the Old Testament — once in Proverbs and once in Song of Solomon, both poetic books. Its meaning is narrow and consistent: the physical act of kissing as an expression of love or intimate greeting. The LXX renders it as φίλημα, the standard Greek word for a kiss, confirming ancient readers understood it in exactly this straightforward sense.
caution: With only 2 occurrences both in poetic literature, the full range of contexts this word could appear in remains largely unknown, keeping confidence low.

definition: A road marker or signpost erected as a visible waypoint for travelers finding their way home.
article: This word appears only once in the entire Old Testament, in Jeremiah 31:21, where God calls Israel to set up road markers on their way into exile so they can find the way back home. Strong's connects it to the root behind תָּמָר (tamar), suggesting something erected upright, likely a pillar or post used as a guide-board along a route. The KJV renders it 'high heaps,' which points to a visible, raised structure, though 'signpost' or 'road marker' better captures the wayfinding function the context clearly demands.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon — appearing only once in the OT — so its precise meaning depends heavily on root inference and context rather than a broad pattern of usage.

definition: Baldness or a shaved head, especially as a public sign of mourning or grief.
article: The word refers to the condition of a bare, hairless head, whether natural or deliberately induced. In most of its 11 occurrences it describes a ritual act: shaving or tearing out the hair as a visible expression of deep mourning or lamentation. Leviticus 21:5 uses it in a prohibition against priests making themselves bald, while the prophets Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Amos, and Micah all invoke it as an image of communal grief. The LXX frequently renders it with words for baldness or shaving, reinforcing that ancient readers understood this primarily as a sign of mourning rather than a medical or cosmetic condition.
caution: Confidence is rated low, possibly because one form (qorcha in Ezekiel 27:31) represents a slight spelling variant, and the small sample of 11 occurrences limits certainty about the full semantic range.

definition: An adverb meaning together, at the same time, or all at once — emphasizing unity or simultaneity of persons or actions.
article: יָ֫חַד primarily functions as an adverb (over 120 of its 142 occurrences) expressing that two or more parties act together or at the same time. Its range covers both physical togetherness — people walking or dwelling in the same place — and a sense of unified action or shared experience. The LXX translators most often chose ἅμα ("at the same time," 38×) but also used ὁμοθυμαδόν ("with one mind/accord," 15×), showing that ancient readers heard both a temporal and a relational-unity dimension in the word. It appears heavily in Isaiah, Psalms, and Jeremiah, suggesting a particular affinity for poetic and prophetic contexts where collective action or shared fate is being emphasized.

definition: An Aramaic term for a consumption tax or excise duty levied on goods, appearing only in the book of Ezra.
article: This Aramaic noun refers to a specific type of tax — an excise or consumption levy — distinct from other forms of tribute mentioned in the same context. It appears all 3 of its Old Testament occurrences in the book of Ezra, always in Aramaic administrative correspondence with the Persian court, reflecting the bureaucratic language of the empire. The narrow, technical context makes its meaning reasonably clear: it is one item in a list of fiscal obligations that subject peoples owed to the king.
caution: Confidence is low: the root is reconstructed from an Aramaic cognate, the word occurs only 3 times in a single book, and the precise distinction between this tax and the other levies listed alongside it in Ezra 4 remains uncertain.

definition: A preposition/conjunction expressing cause or purpose: 'because of,' 'for the sake of,' or 'in order that.'
article: עֲבוּר functions as a preposition or conjunction linking an action to its reason or goal — it can look backward at a cause ('because of you') or forward at a purpose ('in order that'). Its range in English requires phrases like 'for the sake of,' 'on account of,' 'because of,' and 'so that,' but in Hebrew it is a single compact word. Its heaviest use is in Genesis (15 times) and 2 Samuel (12 times), appearing most often in narrative prose rather than poetry. The LXX translators capture this dual function well, using ἕνεκα ('on account of') 13 times for the causal sense and ὅπως and ἵνα (together 14 times) for the purposive sense, confirming that ancient readers recognized both directions of meaning.
caution: The moderate confidence tier reflects some uncertainty about the word's precise boundaries with overlapping prepositions; Strong's derivation from a passive participle of עָבַר ('to cross') is a reconstruction, and not all scholars accept that etymology as determinative for meaning.

definition: A poor or destitute person, used in Ecclesiastes to describe someone of low economic and social standing.
article: מִסְכֵּן describes a person who is poor or indigent — someone lacking material resources and social status. All four of its appearances in the Hebrew Bible are found in Ecclesiastes, making it a distinctively Wisdom-literature term. The LXX consistently renders it as πένης, the standard Greek word for a laboring poor person, confirming that ancient readers understood it as straightforwardly economic poverty. Most memorably, Ecclesiastes 9:15–16 uses it for the overlooked wise poor man whose wisdom saves a city yet earns him no lasting recognition.
caution: Confidence is low, likely due to the very rare occurrence (only 4 times, all in one book) and an uncertain root connection; the word may be a loanword or have a disputed etymology.

definition: A rare word for terror or dread, likely evoking a sense of reeling or overwhelming fear.
article: חָגָּא refers to an intense, overwhelming fear, appearing only once in the Old Testament — in Isaiah 19:17, where Judah becomes a source of terror to Egypt. Strong's connects the root to the idea of revolving or vertigo, suggesting fear so intense it makes one reel. The Septuagint translates it with φόβητρον, a Greek word meaning a frightening thing or object of terror, confirming the sense of dread directed outward at something alarming.
caution: This word is a hapax legomenon, occurring only once in the entire Old Testament, so its precise meaning rests on a reconstructed unused root and a single translation instance.

definition: A Hebrew root meaning to be firm, used in the Old Testament only as a passive participle describing something made of cedar wood.
article: This root appears only once in the entire Old Testament, in Ezekiel 27:24, where it describes goods made of cedar. Strong's identifies it as a primitive root meaning 'to be firm,' but in practice it functions as a denominative — a verb derived from the noun for cedar — and occurs only in its passive participle form. The single occurrence in Ezekiel's lament over Tyre places it in a commercial context, describing luxury trade goods. Because it appears only this one time, its full range is essentially defined by that single usage.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon — appearing only once in the entire Hebrew Old Testament — so its meaning rests entirely on one occurrence and the connection to the cedar noun, making confident definition difficult.

definition: To do, make, or accomplish something — covering virtually any human or divine action, creation, or execution of a task.
article: עָשָׂה is one of the most common verbs in the Hebrew Bible, appearing 2,640 times across all 39 books — making it essential vocabulary for any Bible reader. Its range is extraordinarily broad, covering everything from God creating the world to a king building a palace to a person preparing a feast or carrying out a command. The Septuagint translators rendered it as ποιέω ("to do/make") an overwhelming 2,252 times, which is the same Greek verb that shows up throughout the New Testament for human and divine action alike. The Qal stem accounts for the vast majority of uses (1,477×), with the Niphal (passive: "be done, be made") adding 84 more instances where the focus shifts to what gets accomplished rather than who does it.

definition: Smoothness used as a trap — slippery ground that causes falls, or flattering words that deceive and manipulate.
article: This rare word, appearing only 4 times across Psalms, Jeremiah, and Daniel, conveys dangerous smoothness in both literal and figurative senses. In Psalm 35:6 the image is of a path made slippery underfoot, while in Jeremiah 23:12 false prophets are sent onto such treacherous ground. In Daniel 11:21 and 11:34 the word shifts toward smooth, flattering speech used to seize power through deception. The LXX renders the Daniel passages with terms for slipperiness and deceit, confirming that ancient readers felt both the physical and rhetorical danger compressed into this one word.
caution: This word appears only 4 times in the OT and is formed by reduplication of a root, making its precise nuance in each context uncertain; confidence is rated low.

definition: To move away or become old, covering physical relocation, aging, and the copying or transcribing of text.
article: This rare verb appears only 9 times across 4 books, with more than half its occurrences in Job. Its core idea seems to involve something shifting from its place — whether that is a mountain being moved (Job 9:5), a person moving on (Genesis 26:22), or text being copied from one place to another (Proverbs 25:1). The LXX consistently renders it with παλαιόω, a Greek word meaning 'to make old' or 'to wear out,' suggesting ancient readers leaned heavily toward the aging and deterioration sense, though the relocation and transcription senses appear clearly in context.
caution: Confidence is rated low, and the three distinct senses — movement, aging, and transcription — sit uneasily together under one root, leaving the precise semantic unity of this verb genuinely uncertain.

definition: A collective gentile adjective referring to the descendants of Pun, an otherwise unknown figure in the tribe of Issachar.
article: Punite (פּוּנִי) appears exactly once in the Old Testament, in Numbers 26:23, as part of the census listing of clans descended from Issachar. It functions as a patronymic — a family name derived from an ancestor — identifying the descendants of someone named Pun, though that individual is never mentioned anywhere else in the Bible. The KJV renders it simply as "Punites," and there is no LXX evidence that adds further clarity to the name's meaning or origin.
caution: The ancestor 'Pun' from whom this clan name derives is completely unknown outside this single verse, making the name's meaning and background impossible to verify.

definition: Karkas, one of the seven eunuchs serving King Xerxes (Ahasuerus) in the book of Esther.
article: Karkas is a proper name appearing exactly once in the Old Testament, in Esther 1:10, as one of the seven eunuchs sent by King Xerxes to bring Queen Vashti before his banquet guests. Strong's identifies it as a name of Persian origin, though the precise meaning of the underlying Persian word is not established in the evidence. Because it functions solely as a personal name in a single narrative moment, its semantic range is entirely limited to this one individual.
caution: This is a hapax legomenon appearing only once in the entire Old Testament, and its exact Persian etymology is uncertain.
